docs.title: a) Functional Requirements
docs.text:
• The new information system should allow staff to manage and update the museum’s fossil collection, including new fossils either borrowed from other museums, or obtained from suppliers.
  • Staff will be able to update the national history room’s information to ensure that it is up to date.
  • The new system will allow staff to maintain the gift shop’s stock, ensuring that basic functionality is permitted, such as adding new items, tracking stock levels and updating prices on products or admission fees, as well as allowing staff to generate, print and provide customers with receipts.
  • To maintain a level of sufficient security, user levels should be implemented to establish the various permission levels needed to facilitate the different areas of museum.

docs.title: b) User Stories
docs.text:
• As a customer, I want to be able to have access to various payment formats such as a choice between cash, card or both when purchasing products from the gift shop.
  • As a stock manager, I want to be able to easily see the available stock, and which items may need to be ordered so that an accurate up-to-date stock level can be maintained and be able to account for any increases in purchasing that may occur.
  • As a customer I want to be issued with a receipt so that if the product I have purchased, needs to be returned, for example if there is a problem or fault with it then I want to be able to use a receipt to be able to return or exchange the product to the gift shop.

docs.title: c) Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text:
• The museums new system should be able to handle, any influxes in activity such as if there is a school trip the system should be able to accurately maintain functionality due to the increase of usage.
  • The new system must be able to be cost-effective to be able to fit and be maintainable within the limited budget provided for its creation.
  • The system should be easy to use, so that it is easy for staff or customers to be able to use as necessary and to make relevant information easily available.
  • The system should comply with any relevant legislation.

docs.title: i) Must Have
docs.text:
• The system must comply with relevant legislation.
  • The system must have the relevant user levels and permissions to maintain security.
  • The system must be cost-efficient to fit within the limitations of the budget.
  • The system must be user-friendly for the staff and customers.
  • The system must be able to handle influxes in functionality, due to increased usage such as when school trips occur.
  • The system must have support for maintainability and maintenance of the gift shops stock levels.

docs.title: ii) Should Have
docs.text:
• The system should have the ability to allow staff to manage the information related to any fossils in the museum that have been borrowed.
  • The system should have the necessary functionality, to maintain stock in the gift shop, ensuring that basic operations are in place to support it effectively.

docs.title: iii) Could Have
docs.text:
• The system could have additional features for managing borrowed fossils such as tracking return dates or the conditions in which the fossils are in.
  • Additional security levels, such as two factor authentication for staff to ensure that only the relevant staff have access to higher level permissions.

docs.title: iv) Won't Have
docs.text:
• The system won’t have advanced features that are beyond the basic functional requirements needed to run the museum effectively.
  • The system won’t have advanced monitoring systems that can handle temporary increases in activity.
  • The system won’t have highly specialised software that wouldn’t fit the museum’s purpose.

docs.title: a) Lifecycle Options
docs.text:
There are SDLCs (Software Development Life Cycles) that fit specific use cases. Different methodologies behind the development of software can include:

The Waterfall methodology, which takes a sequential approach to creating a piece of software, as it requires a lot of planning and research into the various problems that exist with a system, in order to be effective during the developmental and production stages during usage. As a model, it requires a lot of consideration regarding the type of project it is being used on and requires reassurance in the project that its requirements are unlikely to change in a way that is significantly substantial to the designs of the project, as this could hinder its effectiveness. Due to this for the museum, it may fit, as its inability to be a flexible strategy, may not pose a risk as the museum is unlikely to have its requirements vastly change in a way that would make it not ideal. (1)

The Agile methodology is an iterative and incremental approach to software development, which prioritises flexibility and customer feedback in its strategy, allowing the possibility of requirements to change, in varying numerous substantial ways, which means that in projects more likely to alter the requirements and design features of the software it is being used to create, leads to a more sustainable pace for the teams using it. However, a downside to the Agile methodology is that as a result of its flexibility it leads to more confusion regarding its endpoint, which can be detrimental to health of workers, as it can be demotivating to have a lack of an end. Due to the Agile methodology’s structure, it would not be an effective or ideal strategy for the museum to use. (1)

docs.title: b) Importance of User Input
docs.text: The value of user input is imperative and invaluable during the process of designing and implementing a new system, as it allows that the experience the end user has, meets and validates the requirements set for the system’s end goal, as well as providing helpful feedback from users in improving the existing user experience, to make it easier and more viable for usage. User input is also important as understanding the user’s needs are vital to the success or failure of a new system during its implementation stage, as user’s can state positive and negative aspects and suggest improvements based on their feedback. A downside to this is that the feedback given may be biased, due to the basis of that it is based around a user’s opinion. Another benefit that user input can provide is that it can help identify issues early, which allows for a more reliable and effective system in the long run. By actively communicating with user’s this can help enforce a sense of trust and collaboration around the developers of the new system and its processes and its consumers, allowing for a high level of transparency and clarity. In conclusion by embracing user input and feedback it can allow for a more user-centric system to be developed allowing them to be more successful and impactful long term.

docs.title: Match the stages of normalisation to the short explanation of the stage
docs.text:
1) First Normal Form - There are no transitive dependencies in the structure.
2) Second Normal Form - The data is aesthetically pleasing.
3) Third Normal Form - There are no repeating groups in the structure.
4) UNF - The data is completely un-normalised.

Note

Options for each: - There are no transitive dependencies in the structure. - There are no repeating groups in the structure. - The data is aesthetically pleasing. - The data is completely un-normalised. - The data values are alphabetically sorted. - There are no part-key dependencies in the structure.

Incorrect

docs.title: Which description best matches the approach to installing systems?
docs.text:
1) Direct Approach - The new system is gradually installed, based on components or increments.
2) Phrased Approach - The new system is installed in one branch or department only for a period of time.
3) Parallel Approach - The old and the new system co-exist for a period of time.
4) Single Location Approach - The new system is installed in half of the branches or departments first.

Note

Options for each: - The new system is gradually installed, based on components or increments. - The new system is installed, but the old system is kept in the disaster recovery site. - The old and new system co-exist for a period of time. - The new system is installed in half of the branches or departments first. - The new system is installed in one branch or department only for a period of time.

Incorrect

FEEDBACK FROM ASSESSOR

Overall, a good effort but there are a number of holes in the testing that mean the code fails a sizeable number of hidden tests.

Tests appear to follow an AAA (Arrange-Act-Assert) sequence, but this is not labelled using comments. Tests follow the naming convention outlined in lectures.

For L1R6 test cases, there's no need to specify an expectedState parameter because it must match either the initial state (for valid transitions) or the current state (for invalid transitions).

In addition, you should avoid using 'if' instructions in a test. Firstly, tests need to be minimal and simple to ensure that they don't themselves contain bugs; secondly, if there are two possible actions then these actions will represent different equivalence partitions and should therefore have separate tests.

The Manager interface should start with 'I', to distinguish it from the actual Manager class (which will exist during integration tests).

The dependency object properties should be private, not public. This is only a very minor issue because they have not been accessed directly from outside the class; however, in future work you should ensure that public members are restricted to those specified in the class diagram and requirements.

NSubstitute has been used effectively for creating stubs and mocks.

Some parameterised test cases are included but these only cover a few of the possible inputs. The L1R6 test cases fail to cover all of the possible valid (and invalid) fire transitions. For future work, try to be exhaustive where a limited set of test cases exist.

Hidden tests for L1R5, L1R6 and L1R7 fail because the production code does not transition to "closed" correctly. Hidden test for L2R2 fails completely because the constructor does not set an initial currentState. Hidden test for L2R3 fails because the statuss report string is in the wrong format.

The L3R4 hidden test will fail because EmailService.SendMail() is mis-named as SendEmail(). This will cause a compilation error at a future point when it is integrated with the actual EmailService class. For future work, be careful to check that code matches specifications accurately.

The submitted video runs over 3 minutes past the specified 10-minute time. For this assignment we have decided against penalising students for failure to follow submission instructions, but we must warn that when a limit is stated then it should be adhered-to -- and that future penalties for exceeeding limits could be more serious.

using SmartOffice;
using System;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Linq;
using System.Text;
using System.Threading.Tasks;

namespace TDDAssignment
{
    public class OfficeController
    {
        private string officeID; // L1R1
        private string currentState; // L1R2
        private string previousState;


        public ILightManager? lightManager = null; // L2R2
        public IFireAlarmManager? fireAlarmManager = null; // L2R2
        public IDoorManager? doorManager; // L2R2
        public IWebService? webService = null; // L2R2
        public IEmailService? emailService = null; // L2R2

        // L1R1
        public OfficeController(string id)
        {
            officeID = id.ToLower();
            currentState = "out of hours";
            lightManager = null;
            fireAlarmManager = null;
            doorManager = null;
            webService = null;
            emailService = null;
        }

        // L1R2
        public string GetOfficeID()
        {
            return officeID.ToLower();
        }

        // L1R3
        public void SetOfficeID(string id)
        {
            officeID = id.ToLower();
        }

        public string GetCurrentState()
        {
            return currentState.ToLower();
        }

        // L1R4
        public bool SetCurrentState(string newState)
        {
            // Convert to lowercase for case-insensitive comparison
            string lowerNewState = newState.ToLower();

            // Define all valid states
            string[] validStates = { "closed", "out of hours", "open", "fire drill", "fire alarm" };
            string[] normalStates = { "open", "out of hours", "closed" };
            string[] emergencyStates = { "fire drill", "fire alarm" };

            // Check if the new state is valid
            if (!Array.Exists(validStates, state => state == lowerNewState))
            {
                return false;
            }

            if (lowerNewState == currentState)
            {
                return true;
            }

            // Case 1: Transition from a normal state to an emergency state
            if (Array.Exists(normalStates, state => state == currentState) && Array.Exists(emergencyStates, state => state == lowerNewState))
            {
                previousState = currentState;
                currentState = lowerNewState;
                return true;
            }

            // Case 2: Transition from an emergency state back to the previous state
            if (Array.Exists(emergencyStates, state => state == currentState) &&
                lowerNewState == previousState)
            {
                if (lowerNewState == "open")
                {
                    if (doorManager == null)
                    {
                        throw new InvalidOperationException("DoorManager is required to set the state to 'open'.");
                    }
                    bool doorsOpened = doorManager.OpenAllDoors();
                    if (!doorsOpened)
                    {
                        return false; // Transition fails if doors can't be opened
                    }
                }
                else if (lowerNewState == "closed")
                {
                    if (doorManager == null || lightManager == null)
                    {
                        throw new InvalidOperationException("DoorManager and LightManager are required to set the state to 'closed'.");
                    }
                    bool doorsLocked = doorManager.LockAllDoors();
                    if (!doorsLocked)
                    {
                        return false; // Transition fails if doors can't be locked
                    }
                    bool lightsOff = lightManager.SetAllLights(false);
                    if (!lightsOff)
                    {
                        return false; // Transition fails if lights can't be turned off
                    }
                }
                currentState = lowerNewState; // Set the state back to the previous state
                return true;
            }

            // Case 3: Transition within normal states (based on a state transition diagram)
            if (Array.Exists(normalStates, state => state == currentState) && Array.Exists(normalStates, state => state == lowerNewState))
            {
                bool transitionAllowed = false;
                switch (currentState)
                {
                    case "open":
                        if (lowerNewState == "out of hours")
                            transitionAllowed = true;
                        break;
                    case "out of hours":
                        if (new[] { "open", "closed" }.Contains(lowerNewState))
                            transitionAllowed = true;
                        break;
                    case "closed":
                        if (lowerNewState == "out of hours")
                            transitionAllowed = true;
                        break;
                }
                if (!transitionAllowed)
                {
                    return false;
                }

                if (lowerNewState == "open")
                {
                    if (doorManager == null)
                    {
                        throw new InvalidOperationException("DoorManager is required to set the state to 'open'.");
                    }
                    bool doorsOpened = doorManager.OpenAllDoors();
                    if (!doorsOpened)
                    {
                        return false;
                    }
                }
                else if (lowerNewState == "closed")
                {
                    if (doorManager == null || lightManager == null)
                    {
                        throw new InvalidOperationException("DoorManager and LightManager are required to set the state to 'closed'.");
                    }
                    bool doorsLocked = doorManager.LockAllDoors();
                    if (!doorsLocked)
                    {
                        return false;
                    }
                    bool lightsOff = lightManager.SetAllLights(false);
                    if (!lightsOff)
                    {
                        return false;
                    }
                }
                currentState = lowerNewState;
                return true;
            }

            return false;
        }

        // L2R1
        public OfficeController(string id, string startState)
        {
            string lowerId = id.ToLower();
            string lowerStartState = startState.ToLower();

            SetOfficeID(id);
            SetCurrentState(startState);

            lightManager = null; // L2R2
            fireAlarmManager = null; // L2R2
            doorManager = null; // L2R2
            webService = null; // L2R2
            emailService = null; // L2R2
        }

        // L2R2
        public OfficeController(string id, ILightManager iLightManager, IFireAlarmManager iFireAlarmManager, IDoorManager iDoorManager, IWebService iWebService, IEmailService iEmailService)
        {
            officeID = id.ToLower();
            currentState = "out of hours"; // initial state
            lightManager = iLightManager;
            fireAlarmManager = iFireAlarmManager;
            doorManager = iDoorManager;
            webService = iWebService;
            emailService = iEmailService;
        }

        // L2R3
        public string GetStatusReport()
        {
            string lightStatus = lightManager.GetStatus();
            string fireAlarmStatus = fireAlarmManager.GetStatus();
            string doorStatus = doorManager.GetStatus();
            return $"Office: {officeID}, State: {currentState}, Lights: {lightStatus}, Doors: {doorStatus}, Fire Alarm: {fireAlarmStatus}";
        }
    }
}

    public void L1R6_SetCurrentState_StateTransitionRules_ValidatesCurrentState(string initialState, string newState, string expectedState)

        }
        else
        {

using System;
using System.Threading;
using ClockSystem.Model;
using MVC_ClockSystem._02_View;

namespace ClockSystem.Controller
{
  public class ClockController
  {
    private ClockModel _model;

    private ClockView _view;

    public ClockController(ClockModel model, ClockView view)
    {
      _model = model;
      _view = view;
    }

    public void StartClock()
    {
      while (true)
      {
        _model.UpdateTime(); // Update the model's time
        _view.DisplayTime(_model.Hours, _model.Minutes, _model.Seconds); // Display the updated time in the view
        Thread.Sleep(1000); // Wait for 1 second
      }
    }
  }
}

using DataAccessLayer;
using System.Collections.Generic;
using System.Reflection;

namespace BusinessLogicLayer
{
  public class CModuleService
  {
    private readonly IModuleRepository moduleRepository;

    public CModuleService(IModuleRepository repository)
    {
      moduleRepository = repository;
    }
    
    // Add a module if not already registered
    public bool RegisterModule(string moduleCode, string moduleName)
    {
      var existingModules = moduleRepository.GetModules();

      if (existingModules.Exists(m => m.ModuleCode == moduleCode))
      {
        return false; // Duplicate module code
      }

      var newModule = new CModule
      {
        ModuleCode = moduleCode,
        ModuleName = moduleName
      };
      
      moduleRepository.AddModule(newModule);
      
      return true;
    }

    // Retrieve all registered modules
    public List<CModule> GetRegisteredModules()
    {
      return moduleRepository.GetModules();
    }
  }
}

docs.title: What is Software?
docs.text: Software is a computer program associated with documentation. If software is made for a specific requirement it is called a software product.

docs.title: What is Software Development?
docs.text:
One of the main activities in software engineering is the process of software development, in which a software product is built using well-defined scientific principles, methods, and procedures.

It requires extensive research and requirement gathering to be able to design, model, and develop the software product.

Diagram of Software Engineering process.

docs.title: Requirements Engineering and Use Case Modelling
What are Requirements?
docs.text:
• Requirements are descriptions of the services that a software system must provide and the constraints under which it must operate.
  • Requirement Specification is a structured document that sets out the services the system is expected to provide. Therefore should be precise so that it can act as a contract between the system procurer and the software developer.

docs.title: Understanding Requirements
docs.text:
• Whose requirement?
  • A system's property that provides value to its stakeholder
  • To understand requirements you need to understand your stakeholders.

Image above Stakeholders in a software product.

docs.title: User Requirements
docs.text:
• Statements in natural language plus diagrams of the services the system provides and its operational constraints
  • Written for customers

docs.title: System Requirements
docs.text:
• A structured document setting out detailed descriptions of the system's functions, services, and operational constraints
  • Defines what should be implemented so may be part of a contract between client and contractor.

docs.title: User VS System Requirements
docs.text: The following is an example regarding a system called MentCare, that handles mental health care patient information.

docs.title: User Requirement Definition
docs.text: 1. The MentCare system shall generate monthly management reports showing the cost of drugs prescribed by each clinic during that month.

docs.title: System Requirements Specification
docs.text:
• 1.1 A summary page of the drugs prescribed, their cost and the prescribing clinics should be provided on the last working day of each month.
  • 1.2 The system shall generate the report for printing after 17:30 on the last working day of the month.
  • 1.3 A report shall be created for each clinic and shall list the individual drug names, the total number of prescriptions, the number of doses prescribed and the total cost of the prescribed drugs

docs.title: Requirements Engineering (RE)
docs.text:
RE is the process of understanding and defining what services are required from the system and identifying the constraints on the system's operation and development. Critical stage in the software process, as such that a mistake in this stage inevitably lead to later problems during the system's design and functionality.

The RE Process includes the following: - Feasibility Study - Requirements Elicitation and Analysis - Requirements Specification - Requirements Validation - Requirements Management

docs.title: Feasibility Study
docs.text:
Before beginning requirements engineering (RE) a company may conduct a feasibility study.

The feasibility study mains to answer three main questions: 1) Does the system contribute to the overall objectives to the organisation? 2) Can the system be implemented within schedule and budget using current technology? 3) Can the system be integrated with other systems that are used?

docs.title: Requirements Elicitation and Analysis
docs.text:
it is an iterative process that can be represented as as a circular process of activities.

Two approaches to requirement elicitations include: - Interview - Observation or ethnography

Requirements Elicitation Diagram

docs.title: Requirements Specification
docs.text:
A process to formally document the user and system requirements when creating a software requirement document.

It can be written in a variety of ways: - Natural language specification: Expressive and universal but could be vague, ambiguous or misinterpreted - Structured specification: Written in a standard way e.g. using templates - Use cases: A way to describe the user and the system interactions - Software requirements document: an official statement of what software developers should implement.

docs.title: Requirements Validation
docs.text: A process of checking the requirement for: - Validity: check that the requirements reflect what the real needs of the system users - Consistency: there shouldn't be different descriptions of the same system function - Completeness: the requirement document should include requirements that define all functions and constraints intended by the system user. - Realism: using current knowledge of technology, check that requirement can be implemented within the budget. - Verifiability: Conduct tests to demonstrate that the delivered system meets each of the specified requirements

docs.title: Requirements Management
docs.text:
Requirements management is the process of understanding and controlling changes to system requirements.

Planning is an essential first stage in the requirements management process and therefore tools can be used to support it for: - Requirements storage - Traceability management - Change management

Diagram of requirements management

docs.title: Agile Methods and Requirements
docs.text:
Many agile methods argue that producing detailed system requirements is a waste of time as the requirements change so quickly.

Agile methods usually use incremental requirements engineering and may express requirements as 'user stories'.

While this is practical for business systems, it poses problematic for systems that require pre-delivery analysis (e.g. critical systems) or systems developed by several teams. Agile Methods

In practice RE (Requirements Engineering) is an iterative process. The output of an RE process is a system requirements document.

The early process most effort is focused toward understanding: - High-Level business requirement and non-functional requirements - User requirements for the system

Within the outer rings of the diagram below more effort will be devoted to eliciting and understanding: - Non-Functional Requirements - Detailed System Requirements

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
User Stories: - Brief Statement of actor, need and purpose.

Structured Requirements Document: - Complete, consistent set of requirements in structured language.

Use Case Model: - Set of use case descriptions - Diagram of actors and use case names

docs.title: Functional and Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text:
Software system requirements are often classified as functional and non-functional requirements.

Functional requirements are a statement of services the system should provide: - How the system should react to particular inputs - How the system should behave in particular situations

Non-functional requirements are constraints on the services or functions offered by the system. This includes: - Time constraints - Constraints on the development process

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text:
Describes what the system should do. System services or functionality.

These requirements depend on: - The type of software - The expected users of the software - The general approach taken by organisation when writing the requirements

When expressed as user requirements functional requirements should be written in natural language so that users and managers can understand them. They should describe the functional system requirements: - System functions - System inputs and outputs and exceptions in detail.

docs.title: Example Functional Requirements for MentCare System
docs.text:
A user shall be able to search for the appointments lists for all clinics.

The system shall generate each day, for each clinic, a list of patients who are expected to attend appointments that day.

Each staff member using the system should be uniquely be identied by their 8-digit employee number.

docs.title: Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text:
Non functional requirements that are those not directly concerned with the specific services delivered by the system to its users. These define system constraints and properties such as: - Reliability - Response time and storage requirements

Non-functional requirements may be more critical than functional requirements. If these are not met, the system may be useless.

Product Requirements: Requirements which specify that the delivered product must behave in a particular way e.g. execution speed, reliability, etc.

Organisation Requirements: Requirements which are consequence of organisational policies and procedures. E.g. process standards used, implementation features, etc.

External Requirements: Requirements which arise from factors which are external to the system and its development process. e.g. interoperability requirements, legislative requirements, etc

docs.title: Non-Functional Requirement Types
docs.text: Non-Functional Requirements

docs.title: Example Non-Functional Requirements for MentCare
docs.text:
Product Requirement: The MHC-PMS shall be available to all clinics during normal working hours (Mon-Fri 8:30-17:30). Downtime within normal working hours shall not exceed five seconds in any one day.

Organisational Requirement: Users of the MHC-PMS system shall authenticate themselves using their health authority identity card.

External Requirements: The system shall implement patient privacy provisions as set out in NStan-03-2006 priv.

docs.title: System Requirement Document
docs.text:
1) Introduction: Purpose, Scope, Overview

2) System Overview: - Functional Requirements - Usability Requirements - Performance Requirements - System Interface, Operations, Modes and states, physical characteristics - System Security - Information management - Policies and regulations

3) Verification (Checking): same structure as section 2 4) Appendices: Assumptions and Dependencies; abbreviations.

docs.title: Requirement Language
docs.text:
Writing software requirements involves using a structured and specific language to articulate the functionalities, constraints and characteristics of a software system.

The language is crucial for effective communication between stakeholders, including developers, testers and end-users.

Requirements that are mandatory and therefore the language used to describe them should indicate such, therefore it is recommended to use the word shall. Preferences or goals that are desirable should use the word should. Anything else can use may. MoSCoW Analysis is another way of writing this.

docs.title: Guidelines for Writing Requirements
docs.text:
• Use text highlighting to identify key parts of the requirement
  • Avoid the use of computer terminology
  • Include an explanation (rationale) of why a requirement is necessary

docs.title: Requirements should be:
docs.text:
• Unambiguous
  • Consistent with other requirements
  • Complete: measurable and detailed
  • Includes only one requirement
  • Feasible
  • Verifiable

docs.title: Syntax of Requirements
docs.text:
[Condition], [Subject], [Action], [Object], [Constraint]

  • When a hostile plane is detected, the system shall launch the missile within 0.002 seconds.
  • If the student is enrolled, the system shall register the student on the module.
  • The system shall display the results at midnight.
  • The light shall flash within 2 seconds.

docs.title: Stakeholder Requirements Document
docs.text:
Introduction: - Purpose, Scope, Overview, Stakeholders

Business Management Requirements: - Business Context, Goals, Information Context

Business Operational Requirements: - Processes, Policies, Rules, Constraints, Quality

User Requirements Concept of Proposed System Project Constraints

docs.title: Problems with Requirement Elicitation
docs.text:
Stakeholders don't really know what they want, and therefore they express requirements within their own terms. Different stakeholders may have conflicting requirements, as a result.

Organisation and politcial factors may influence the system requirements.

The requirements may change during the analysis process, as well as new stakeholders may emerge and therefore the business environment may change, which leads to the requirements potentially needing changing along with it.

docs.title: Introduction to Unified Modelling Language (UML)
docs.text:
A set of standard notations for modelling object-oriented systems. It is not a methodology as it defines diagrams and does not defined how to build a system.

UML is a language used for software-intrusive systems, aspects include: - Visualising - Specifying - Designing - Constructing - Documenting

A model is an abstract representation of something that is too complex to work with in its entirety.

UML can be used across all phases of the SLC (Software Development Life-Cycle): - During analysis used to document business processes - During implementation used to document methods and attributes of a class - During deployment used to document hardware components of a syste

docs.title: UML Diagrams for Analysis
docs.text:
Use Case Model: Diagram and Descriptions - Functional System Behaviour - as seen by the user

Activity Diagrams: - Models business activities (processes)

Class Diagrams: (Design Not Specification) - Static Structure of the system - Objects, Attributes, and Operations

docs.title: Use Case Model
docs.text:
System behaviour from a user perspective. - Use Cases: Descriptions off interaction with user - Diagram to summarise use cases and actors

Uses - Defines what should be implemented - Estimate overall project size - Plan increments - Help create test cases: define desired behaviour

docs.title: Use Case Diagrams
docs.text:
Use case diagrams show the user's main interactions with the system. Example of a use case diagram for a student management system

Actors represented as stick figures could be humans or other systems.

The box around the diagram (except actors) indicates the system boundary.

Lines are what links the actors with the interactions.

Class of interactions* are represented as a named ellipse.

docs.title: Use Case Text
docs.text: Title Info Name UC-1: Mark Coursework Summary Summary Lecturer attaches feedback and marks to a student’s work. Rationale Student will read feedback. Marks contribute to the module mark. Primary Actor Lecturer Users Lecturer Preconditions Student has submitted work, and the Lecturer is logged in. Basic Process 1. Lecturer opens work. 2. Lecturer checks for plagiarism. 3. Lecturer reads work, adding comments. 4. Lecturer allocates a mark to the work. Alternative Paths 1. In step 1, if the work cannot be opened, notify the student. 2. In step 2, if plagiarism is detected, arrange a cheat interview. Postconditions Feedback is available for the student. Mark has been recorded.

UML a set of diagramming tools to model/describe a system - Can be used from requirements not engineering - Through to domain analysis - Through to system design

Use Case Models used to describe a system's functionality and users interactions with the system - From a user perspective, can be understood by the client - Can be used in both traditional and agile development.

Architecture Patterns - Address higher level design decisions affecting the overall system structure - Help to define and maintain the overall structure of the entire system.

Categories of architectural patterns Applicatrion Landscape Patterns e.g N-tier - N represents the number of layers in the approach

Application Structure Patterns

docs.title: Recap (CO2401 Lecture 1 - Introduction to Requirements & Use Cases)
docs.text: Requirements are formal descriptions of what software should do. They outline the functionalities, features, constraints, and characteristics that a software must have to meet the needs and expectations of users and stakeholders.

docs.title: OO (Object-Oriented) Analysis and Design
docs.text:
Why draw diagrams?

Before building something, we often create drawings to describe its look and behaviour. - Plans / Blueprints

UML is a language that was discussed in the first lecture.

The purpose of modelling a language is to represent the key features of a system.

docs.title: Candidate Classes
docs.text:
Deciding the overall architecture of an OO (Object Oriented) system can be hard. - What objects/classes should we create? - How many objects should we create? - Should we use inheritance/abstract classes

There are numerous ways to build a system, a way of deciding how objects/classes maybe needed is by looking at the User Stories and Use Case model.

docs.title: Class, Responsibility and Collaborators - CRC Cards
docs.text:
A collaborative approach to determining the overall system architecture.

Empty CRC Card Example

Describe each class on a small card with the following details: - Name of class - List of responsibilities - Things it knows - Things it does

Collaborators (Deprived Classes) - Other classes used by this class.

docs.title: Purpose of CRC Cards
docs.text:
Used as a collaborative medium to brainstorm division of a programs components.

Allows the team to build a common mental model of how a program might work.

Allows quick visual test of alternative approaches/architecture before development begins.

Can be useful when changing/restructuring a program.

docs.title: OO Design with CRC Cards
docs.text:
Identify User Stories/Use Cases (Scenarios)

Finding entities in the system - Things in specification or domain or description

Filter out duplicate and insignificant entities

Assign responsibilities to classes - The operations that a class supports

Identifying collaborations between classes - Represent relationships between classes

Check that structure will support scenarios

docs.title: Using CRC Cards
docs.text:
Use to develop and check design - Walk through typical scenarios 'Use Cases'

Expect to modify

Use in group discussion: - Anthropomorphise - Pretend the class is 'alive' an active participate - Keep related cards close together - Allows for different perspectives to be heard - Identify common patterns/outliers

docs.title: CRC Cards Advantages
docs.text:
Suited to iterative development

Easy to add/remove and rearrange cards

Good for collaborative communication

Can be used very easily in development - e.g. in foundations stage of DSDM

Finished OO (Object Oriented) analysis with CRC cards can provide architectural design guidelines.

Encourages development team to 'role play' through different usage scenarios.

New issues can be identified e.g. missing component

docs.title: CRC Cards Disadvantages
docs.text:
Requires team participation

Both from business side and developers

Can become difficult to manage with very large systems

Too many cards to manage

Does not track sequence when running through scenarios

Lacks detail

Some organisations will require more formal representation of overall architecture

docs.title: Example: CRC analysis
docs.text:
Perform a CRC analysis for a library:

Scenarios: - User returns book - User borrows a recording - User searches catalogue for a journal - Damaged item is removed from the catalogue

Expand use cases or user stories.

Identify candidate classes.

Create CRC Cards

Walk through scenarios.

docs.title: User Stories (Library Example)
docs.text:
Tip: Look for nouns

As a user I want to be able to get a return receipt for my book so that I don't get mistakenly fined.

As a user I want to be able to borrow a recording so I can watch it at home.

As a student I want to be able to search the catalogue for a journal so I can get a good mark on my assignment.

As a librarian I want to remove a damaged item from the catalogue so that it can be repaired.

docs.title: Walk through scenario
docs.text:
User borrows a book (has a library card number and a book number to borrow)

How do we know they are a registered user?

With the current CRC cards we don't.

CRC Cards now with User List.

User borrows a book (has a library card number and a book number to borrow) - we check UserList for details on that specific user (collaborates with user class to return user object for that user) if that user exists. - User object checked for what items they already have (can they borrow more?) if eligible to borrow. - We check catalogue for item to be borrowed? if item exists then return item object of the appropriate book. - Item object checked for reference only: if not reference only - Item object checked if it is out on loan: if available - User object borrows item - adds item to their borrowed items list - sets items borrowed status to "borrowed"

docs.title: Formalising CRC Cards
docs.text:
Swap responsibilities for properties/methods

Properties (things for class knows) can also be written on the back of the card.

docs.title: Why Use CRC Cards
docs.text:
Simplicity.

At a high level they can be used with clients.

CRC cards encourage discussion as it promotes learning between team members.

Participants can experience how the system will work.

Check consistency of structure and use cases

Incremental - in early design don't worry about details - in detailed design can record properties on back

docs.title: Class Diagram
docs.text:
Shows the different objects, their relationship, their behaviours, and attributes.

Provide visual representation of the structure and relationship of classes in a system.

Classes are the building block of objects - Class diagrams are the building blocks of UML

docs.title: Why Class Diagram?
docs.text:
To illustrate data models for information systems, no matter how simple or complex

To understand the general overview of the schematics of an application.

Visually express any specific needs of a system and that information to achieve business goals.

docs.title: Key Software Development Concepts
docs.text:
Abstraction: Using the right level of detail hiding irrelevant details

Modularity: Structuring a system into interacting components (modules) through decomposition of the system.

Coupling: Links between modules (Loose Coupling is good)

Cohesion: The simplicity of the purpose of module (High Cohesion is good)

docs.title: Object Oriented Design
docs.text:
Break system into classes of objects with: - Data (attributes) - Functionality (methods) to manipulate the data

Helps provide a better match to reality than other development approaches.

Other objects interact (Collaborate) via: - Calling each other's methods - Must not directly change another objects data

Requirements are captured by a set of Use Cases - Objects collaborate to deliver each Use Case.

docs.title: Advantages of Object Orientation
docs.text:
Encourages good software engineering principles - Abstraction: - Modelling of only appropriate domain entities in the code - Design Level (focus on 'what'.)

  • Encapsulation
  • Combining data and functionality in one entity
  • Hiding of inner workings from other entities that don't need to see it

  • Implementation Level (focus on flow)

  • Loose Coupling

  • Objects have minimum knowledge of each other

  • Tight Cohesion

  • A good object has a single purpose

docs.title: Design: Working out how
docs.text:
UML diagrams become more detailed: - Communication is aimed at developers not clients - Detailed class diagrams - Sequence diagrams - Show objects' roles in implementing use cases

  • State diagrams for complex software classes
  • Package diagram showing organisation of software
  • Deployment diagram: physical layout of software

docs.title: Conceptualising the Domain
docs.text: Diagram of conceptualising the domain

docs.title: Identifying Classes
docs.text:
Choosing suitable classes and attributes is crucial - Avoid adding unnecessary complexity to the system

Creative Process - There will be changes as you learn about the domain

Look for things in the text of the requirements: - Objects represent "things" in the system domain so nouns and noun phrases can help identify possible classes - The list of things give candidate classes for further analysis

docs.title: Noun Phrase Example: Car Hire Company
CHC Example Information:
docs.text:
The CHC (Car Hire Company) stocks cars of a number of different models. It may have any number of cars of each model. The system should for each model hold the model's name and engine size. No two models have the same name.

A customer can borrow any car of a particular model that is not currently out on loan. However, no customer can have more than 3 cars on loan at once. A hired car must be returned within 14 days. When a customer returns a car it immediately becomes available on loan to other customers.

Each car has a unique Registration number.

Each customer of the hire company has a unique Customer ID, the system also holds each customer's name.

docs.title: CHC Use Case Analysis (Methods)
docs.text:
Get Number Available: The staff member identifies the model of the car. The system displays the number of cars available.

List Models: The staff member identifies the customer. The system displays a list of models and return date(s) for the car(s) that the customer currently has out on loan.

Hire Car: The staff member identifies the car and the customer who is borrowing it. The system records the fact that it is no longer available for loan, due to the fact that the car is on loan to the member that was identified and the date it was hired.

Return Car: The staff member identifies the car. The system records the fact that this car is now available for loan and that it is no longer hired out to the customer who returned it.

Removing synonyms gives a list of Candidate Classes: - Car Hire Company - Car - number of models - number of cars - model - system - model name - customer - loan - day - registration number - customer number - customer name - staff member - number of cars available - list - return date(s) - fact - date it was hired

docs.title: Brief Description of the Solution
docs.text:
The program I have developed manages smart devices through a command-line interface, enabling users to efficiently create, and a remove home, as well as view a collection of homes. Each home contains rooms, which in turn store individual devices. Users can interact with the system to manage devices, rooms, and homes. For example, allowing them to set the brightness and colour of a Smart Light during its creation.

The development process began with designing the base class of CDevice, which is the foundation of the program, as it is the class that all devices are deprived from, such as CSmartLight, CThermostat. CSmartSpeaker, and CSecurityCamera. After implementing the base device class, I implemented the CRoom class, having it hold a vector of unique pointer variables, that contain the room’s devices. This was to group devices based on the room they were created in. After the rooms were created I created the CHome class, which holds a vector of unique pointers for all the rooms available. CHomeManager was created after CHome which has the purpose of managing the homes and holds the homes as well as enabling the user to create, remove and view homes. When the program ends a function clears all the homes to prevent memory leaks and ensure the unique pointers fall out of scope before the program finishes to ensure reduced memory leaks.

docs.title: Grade Band & Evidence
docs.text:
Program Command Line Interface

Figure 1 demonstrates that the console that appears when the program runs showing the home management system and the options available to the user.

I am aiming for the 62% grade boundary, as I feel my solution meets the core requirements of the assignment in regard to that boundary. I believe my solution meets the “must have” requirements presented in the assignment brief but also incorporates elements of the “should have” criteria..

To assess that my program has met the criteria necessary for the grade I am aiming for, I have completed the “must have” requirements provided by the brief; all devices, rooms, and homes have unique ID numbers. Device, room, and home names do not have to be unique, as is the same with the manufacturer. Every class has a polymorphic implementation of the virtual void function of InteractionEvent method, which simulates a user interaction with the device.

Every device, includes a Boolean attribute for the status of the device, users can active and deactivate the status and the InteractionEvent as specified in the brief, is only interactable when the device is active and otherwise, the user is prompted with a message to activate the device before it can be used. Which depending on the device type as per the polymorphic solution I developed to allow the user to interact individually with the device type depending on the type of device they chose to create, depends on the type of interaction the device part takes in, such as the smart speakers interaction event allows for an adjustment of the volume, while the smart bulb allows adjustment of the brightness and assuming the light colour is RGB allows the user to assign a colour specified in a menu, based on the list of acceptable available colours in the brief. The CThermostat interactionEvent allows the user to interact with the current temperature allowing a setting between 0 and 100 same with the brightness levels.

Room Management Option

As presented above the room management system covers the creation, deletion, viewing all the available rooms in the selected home, viewing a room individually, finding a device, which prompts the user for the name of the device and shows the user the device’ information and prompts the user on the device that it was found in. The user is able to duplicate a room, however an issue with my solution that prevented me from obtaining higher grades in the assignment is that the devices are not copied with the room, which I could of solved with a for loop copying the devices, which all already have unique IDs, to be able to completely duplicate the room into the home.

docs.title: Encapsulation
docs.text:
Encapsulation is the idea of having private and public attributes and methods within a class, which prevents access to the private members or attributes of that class. (Deitel, 2017). Which protects data and hides aspects of the implementation such as methods that are private, therefore allowing more control of within the object.

I used encapsulation with classes to ensure that attributes like the device ID were transferred through polymorphism to the other devices, to ensure that they shared the same attributes and methods. I declared private attributes like the id, manufacturer, and name, that can only be set and get through public the setters and getters for the function.

#include "CHome.h"
#include "CRoom.h"
#include <vector>

const int addNoDups = 1;

/*
Brief: Constructor for CHome class, initializes a home with an ID and name

Parameters:
(in) int id (unique identifier for the home)
(in) string homeName (name of the home)
*/
CHome::CHome(int id, string homeName)
{
    this->homeID = id;
    this->homeName = homeName;
};

/*
Brief: Destructor for CHome class, clears the homeRooms vector to free memory
*/
CHome::~CHome()
{
    this->homeRooms.clear();
}

/*
Brief: Creates a new room and adds it to the homeRooms vector

Parameters:
(in) string roomName (name of the new room)
*/
void CHome::CreateRoom(string roomName)
{
    std::unique_ptr<CRoom> newRoom = std::make_unique<CRoom>(this->homeRooms.size() + addNoDups, roomName);
    this->homeRooms.push_back(std::move(newRoom));
    return;
};

/*
Brief: Generates a new unique ID for a room based on current room count

Parameters:
(out) int (new unique ID for a room)
*/
int CHome::GetNewID()
{
    return this->homeRooms.size() + addNoDups;
}

/*
Brief: Removes a room from the homeRooms vector by its ID

Parameters:
(in) int& id (ID of the room to remove)
*/
void CHome::RemoveRoom(int& id)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < this->homeRooms.size(); i++)
    {
        if (this->homeRooms[i]->GetID() == id)
            homeRooms.erase(homeRooms.begin() + i);
    }
}

/*
Brief: Displays all rooms in the home with their IDs and names
*/
void CHome::ViewAllRooms()
{
    if (this->homeRooms.empty())
    {
        std::cout << "No Rooms Available." << '\n';
        return;
    }

    for (std::unique_ptr<CRoom>& room : homeRooms)
        std::cout << "\nRoom ID: " << room->GetID() << "\nRoom Name: " << room->GetName() << '\n';
    return;
};

/*
Brief: Searches for a device by name within a specified room

Parameters:
(in) std::string& roomName (name of the room to search in)
(in) std::string& deviceName (name of the device to find)
*/
void CHome::FindDevice(std::string& roomName, std::string& deviceName)
{
    bool roomFound = false;
    for (const std::unique_ptr<CRoom>& room : homeRooms)
    {
        if (room->GetName() == roomName)
        {
            roomFound = true;
            const std::vector<std::unique_ptr<CDevice>>& devices = room->GetDevices();
            for (const std::unique_ptr<CDevice>& device : devices)
            {
                if (device->GetName() == deviceName)
                {
                    std::cout << "Device: " << device->GetID() << "\nFound in Room: " << room->GetName() << "\nIn Home: " << this->GetName() << '\n';
                    return;
                }
            }
        }
    }
    if (roomFound)
    {
        std::cout << "Device not found in the specified room.\n";
    }
    else
    {
        std::cout << "Room not found.\n";
    }
}

/*
Brief: Duplicates an existing room by creating a new room with the same name

Parameters:
(in) CRoom* room (pointer to the room to duplicate)
*/
void CHome::DuplicateRoom(CRoom* room)
{
    this->CreateRoom(room->GetName());
    std::cout << "Room " << room->GetID() << " has been duplicated";
    return;
};

/*
Brief: Sets the name of the home

Parameters:
(in) string homeName (new name for the home)
*/
void CHome::SetName(string homeName)
{
    this->homeName = homeName;
    return;
}

/*
Brief: Retrieves the name of the home

Parameters:
(out) string (current name of the home)
*/
string CHome::GetName()
{
    return this->homeName;
}

/*
Brief: Sets the ID of the home

Parameters:
(in) int& id (new ID for the home)
*/
void CHome::SetID(int& id)
{
    this->homeID = id;
}

/*
Brief: Get the Home ID

Parameters:
(out) int (id of the home)
*/
int CHome::GetID()
{
    return this->homeID;
}

/*
Brief: Find a room by its ID

Parameters:
(in) int& id (id of room)
(out) CRoom* (pointer to the found room or nullptr if not found)
*/
CRoom* CHome::GetRoomByID(int& id)
{
    bool roomFound = false;
    for (std::unique_ptr<CRoom>& room : homeRooms)
    {
        if (id == room->GetID())
        {
            roomFound = true;
            return room.get();
        }
    }
    if (!roomFound)
        std::cout << "No Room was found." << '\n';

    return nullptr;
}

        return;

#include "CSmartLight.h"
#include <iostream>

using namespace std;

CSmartLight::CSmartLight(int id, std::string manufacturer, std::string name, int brightnessLevel, string colour) : CDevice(id, manufacturer, name)
{
    this->brightnessLevel = brightnessLevel;
    this->lightColour = colour;
}

void CSmartLight::InteractionEvent(int brightness)
{
    if (brightness > 100)
    {
        std::cout << "Temperature cannot be above 100." << '\n';
        return;
    }
    else if (brightness < 0)
    {
        std::cout << "Temperature cannot be below 0." << '\n';
        return;
    }

    if (this->lightColour == "RGB")
    {
        int colourType = 0;
        do
        {
            cout << "1) Warm White\n2) Cool White\n3) RGB" << '\n';
            cout << "What Colour would you like to set?: " << '\n';
            cin >> colourType;

            if (colourType == 1)
            {
                this->lightColour = "Warm White";
            }
            else if (colourType == 2)
            {
                this->lightColour = "Cool White";
            }
            else if (colourType == 3)
            {
                this->lightColour = "RGB";
            }
        } while (colourType != 1 && colourType != 2 && colourType != 3);

    }

    this->brightnessLevel = brightness;
}

string CSmartLight::GetColour()
{
    return this->lightColour;
}

}

/*

Parameters:
(out) int (current volume value)
*/

{

}

/*

Parameters:
(in) int id (unique identifier for the thermostat)
(in) string manufacturer (manufacturer name of the thermostat)
(in) string name (name assigned to the thermostat)
(in) int temperature (initial temperature setting for the thermostat)
*/
CThermostat::CThermostat(int id, string manufacturer, string name, int temperature) : CDevice(id, manufacturer, name)
{
    this->temperature = temperature;
}

/*
Brief: Overrides InteractionEvent to adjust the thermostat's temperature, with validation

Parameters:
(in) int temperature (new temperature value to set)
*/
void CThermostat::InteractionEvent(int temperature)
{
    if (temperature > 100)
    {
        std::cout << "Temperature cannot be above 100." << '\n';
        return;
    }
    else if (temperature < 0)
    {
        std::cout << "Temperature cannot be below 0." << '\n';
        return;  // Added for consistency
    }

    this->temperature = temperature;
}

/*
Brief: Gets the current temperature of the thermostat

Parameters:
(out) int (current temperature value)
*/
int CThermostat::GetTemperature()
{
    return this->temperature;
}

#include <iostream>

/*
Brief: Returns string in lowercase

Parameters:
(in) stringToLower (String in any case)/
(out) stringToLower (String returned edited into lowercase)
*/
std::string& ToLower(std::string& stringToLower)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < stringToLower.length(); i++)
        stringToLower[i] = tolower(stringToLower[i]); // Pass by reference change to lowercase.
    return stringToLower;
}

/*
Brief: Contains the enum variables for the Home menu options
*/
enum HomeManageMenuOptions {
    CreateHome = 1,
    RemoveHome = 2,
    ShowAllHomes = 3,
    EnterHome = 4,
    Exit = 5
};

/*
Brief: Contains the enum variables for the Room menu options
*/
enum HomeMenuOptions {
    CreateRoom = 1,
    RemoveRoom = 2,
    ShowAllRooms = 3,
    EnterRoom = 4,
    FindADevice = 5,
    ActivateAllDevices = 6,
    DuplicateARoom = 7,
    RoomExit = 8
};

/*
Brief: Contains the enum variables for the Device menu options
*/
enum DeviceMenuOptions {
    CreateDevice = 1,
    RemoveDevice = 2,
    ActivateDevice = 3,
    DeactivateDevice = 4,
    ShowAllDevices = 5,
    InteractionEvent = 6,
    DeviceExit = 7
};

/*
Brief: The room the user has chosen to enter to edit the devices of.

Parameters:
(in) room
*/
void EnterTheRoom(CRoom& room)
{
    int RoomMenuSelect = 0;
    do {
        system("cls");
        std::cout << "Device Management System:\n";
        std::cout << "1) Create Device\n2) Remove Device\n3) Activate Device\n4) Deactivate Device\n5) Show All Devices\n6) Interact with Device\n7) Exit\n";
        std::cout << "\nEnter Menu Option: ";
        std::cin >> RoomMenuSelect;
        if (std::cin.fail()) {
            std::cin.clear();
            std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
            std::cout << "Invalid input. Please enter a number.\n";
            system("pause");
        }
        else {
            std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
            int deviceID = 0;
            switch (RoomMenuSelect)
            {
            case CreateDevice:
            {
                std::string deviceType;
                std::cout << "Security Camera\nThermostat\nSmart Light\nSmart Speaker\n";
                std::cout << "Enter device type: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, deviceType);
                std::string deviceManufacturer;
                std::cout << "Enter Device Manufacturer: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, deviceManufacturer);
                std::string deviceName;
                std::cout << "Enter Device Name: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, deviceName);
                std::unique_ptr<CDevice> newDevice = nullptr;
                if (deviceType == "security camera") {
                    std::string cameraQualityStr;
                    int cameraQuality = 0;
                    do {
                        std::cout << "1) 720p\n2) 1080p\n3) 4K\n";
                        std::cout << "What resolution would you like to set?: ";
                        std::cin >> cameraQuality;
                        if (cameraQuality == 1)
                            cameraQualityStr = "720p";
                        else if (cameraQuality == 2)
                            cameraQualityStr = "1080p";
                        else if (cameraQuality == 3)
                            cameraQualityStr = "4K";
                    } while (cameraQuality < 1 || cameraQuality > 3);
                    std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                    std::string powerSupplyStr;
                    int powerSupply = 0;
                    do {
                        std::cout << "1) Mains Powered\n2) Battery\n3) Mains + Solar\n";
                        std::cout << "What power supply would you like to set?: ";
                        std::cin >> powerSupply;
                        if (powerSupply == 1)
                            powerSupplyStr = "Mains Powered";
                        else if (powerSupply == 2)
                            powerSupplyStr = "Battery";
                        else if (powerSupply == 3)
                            powerSupplyStr = "Mains + Solar";
                    } while (powerSupply < 1 || powerSupply > 3);
                    std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                    newDevice = std::make_unique<CSecurityCamera>(room.GetNewID(), deviceManufacturer, deviceName, cameraQualityStr, powerSupplyStr);
                }
                else if (deviceType == "thermostat") {
                    newDevice = std::make_unique<CThermostat>(room.GetNewID(), deviceManufacturer, deviceName, 20);
                }
                else if (deviceType == "smart light") {
                    std::string colourTypeStr;
                    int colourType = 0;
                    do {
                        std::cout << "1) Warm White\n2) Cool White\n3) RGB\n";
                        std::cout << "What Colour would you like to set?: ";
                        std::cin >> colourType;
                        std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                        if (colourType == 1)
                            colourTypeStr = "Warm White";
                        else if (colourType == 2)
                            colourTypeStr = "Cool White";
                        else if (colourType == 3)
                            colourTypeStr = "RGB";
                    } while (colourType < 1 || colourType > 3);
                    newDevice = std::make_unique<CSmartLight>(room.GetNewID(), deviceManufacturer, deviceName, 50, colourTypeStr);
                }
                else if (deviceType == "smart speaker")
                {
                    int volumeLevel = 0;
                    do {
                        std::cout << "What volume would you like to set? 0 - 100: ";
                        std::cin >> volumeLevel;
                        std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                    } while (volumeLevel > 100 || volumeLevel > 0);
                    newDevice = std::make_unique<CSmartSpeaker>(room.GetNewID(), deviceManufacturer, deviceName, volumeLevel);
                }
                if (newDevice) {
                    room.AddDevice(std::move(newDevice));
                    std::cout << "Device created successfully.\n";
                    system("pause");
                }
                else {
                    std::cout << "Invalid device type. Supported types: security camera, thermostat, smart light.\n";
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            }
            case RemoveDevice:
            {
                std::cout << "Enter Device ID: ";
                std::cin >> deviceID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                room.RemoveDevice(deviceID);
                system("pause");
                break;
            }
            case ShowAllDevices:
                room.ViewAllDevices();
                system("pause");
                break;
            case InteractionEvent:
                std::cout << "Enter Device ID: ";
                std::cin >> deviceID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                if (room.GetDevices().empty()) {
                    std::cout << "Room has no devices.\n";
                    system("pause");
                }
                else {
                    bool found = false;
                    for (const auto& device : room.GetDevices()) {
                        if (deviceID == device->GetID()) {
                            device->InteractionEvent();
                            found = true;
                            system("pause");
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    if (!found) {
                        std::cout << "Device not found.\n";
                        system("pause");
                    }
                }
                break;
            case ActivateDevice:
                std::cout << "Enter Device ID: ";
                std::cin >> deviceID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                {
                    bool found = false;
                    for (const auto& device : room.GetDevices()) {
                        if (deviceID == device->GetID()) {
                            device->Activate();
                            std::cout << "Device activated.\n";
                            found = true;
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    if (!found) {
                        std::cout << "Device not found.\n";
                    }
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            case DeactivateDevice:
                std::cout << "Enter Device ID: ";
                std::cin >> deviceID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                {
                    bool found = false;
                    for (const auto& device : room.GetDevices()) {
                        if (deviceID == device->GetID()) {
                            device->Deactivate();
                            std::cout << "Device deactivated.\n";
                            found = true;
                            break;
                        }
                    }
                    if (!found) {
                        std::cout << "Device not found.\n";
                    }
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            case DeviceExit:
                std::cout << "Exiting Device Management.\n";
                system("pause");
                break;
            default:
                std::cout << "Invalid option. Try again.\n";
                system("pause");
            }
        }
    } while (RoomMenuSelect != DeviceExit);
}

/*
Brief: The home the user has chosen to enter to edit the rooms of.

Parameters:
(in) home
*/
void EnterTheHome(CHome& home)
{
    int HomeMenuSelect = 0;
    do {
        system("cls");
        std::cout << "Room Management System:\n";
        std::cout << "1) Create Room\n2) Remove Room\n3) Show All Rooms\n4) View A Room\n5) Find Device\n6) Activate All Devices\n7) Duplicate A Room\n8) Exit\n";
        std::cout << "Enter Menu Option: ";
        std::cin >> HomeMenuSelect;
        if (std::cin.fail()) {
            std::cin.clear();
            std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
            std::cout << "Invalid input. Please enter a number.\n";
            system("pause");
        }
        else {
            std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
            int roomID = 0;
            string roomName = "";
            string deviceName = "";
            switch (HomeMenuSelect) {
            case CreateRoom:
            {
                std::string roomName;
                std::cout << "Enter Room Name: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, roomName);
                home.CreateRoom(roomName);
                std::cout << "Room created successfully.\n";
                system("pause");
                break;
            }
            case RemoveRoom:
            {
                std::cout << "Enter Room ID: ";
                std::cin >> roomID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                home.RemoveRoom(roomID);
                system("pause");
                break;
            }
            case ShowAllRooms:
                home.ViewAllRooms();
                system("pause");
                break;
            case EnterRoom:
            {
                std::cout << "Enter Room ID: ";
                std::cin >> roomID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                CRoom* room = home.GetRoomByID(roomID);
                if (room != nullptr) {
                    EnterTheRoom(*room);
                }
                else 
                {
                    std::cout << "Room not found.\n";
                    delete room;
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            }
            case FindADevice:
            {
                std::cout << "Enter Room Name: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, roomName);
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');

                std::cout << "Enter Device Name: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, deviceName);
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                home.FindDevice(roomName, deviceName);
                system("pause");
                break; 
            }
            case ActivateAllDevices:
            {
                std::cout << "Enter Room ID: ";
                std::cin >> roomID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                CRoom* room = home.GetRoomByID(roomID);
                if (room) {
                    room->ActivateAll();
                    std::cout << "All devices activated in room.\n";
                    system("pause");
                }
                else {
                    std::cout << "Room not found.\n";
                    delete room;
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            }
            case DuplicateARoom:
            {
                std::cout << "Enter Room ID: ";
                std::cin >> roomID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                CRoom* room = home.GetRoomByID(roomID);
                if (room != nullptr) {
                    home.DuplicateRoom(room);
                    system("pause");
                }
                else {
                    std::cout << "Room not found.\n";
                    delete room; // delete raw pointer to avoid memory leaks.
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            }
            case RoomExit:
                std::cout << "Exiting Room Management.\n";
                system("pause");
                break;
            default:
                std::cout << "Invalid option. Try again.\n";
                system("pause");
            }
        }
    } while (HomeMenuSelect != RoomExit);
}

/*
Brief: Home Manager main starting point.
*/
int main()
{
    int HomeManageMenuSelect = 0;
    std::unique_ptr<CHomeManager> manager = std::make_unique<CHomeManager>();

    do {
        system("cls");
        std::cout << "Home Management System:\n";
        std::cout << "1) Create Home\n2) Remove Home\n3) Show All Homes\n4) View A Home\n5) Exit\n";
        std::cout << "Enter Menu Option: ";
        std::cin >> HomeManageMenuSelect;
        if (std::cin.fail()) {
            std::cin.clear();
            std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
            std::cout << "Invalid input. Please enter a number.\n";
            system("pause");
        }
        else {
            std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
            switch (HomeManageMenuSelect) {
            case CreateHome:
            {
                std::string homeName;
                std::cout << "Enter Home Name: ";
                std::getline(std::cin, homeName);
                manager->CreateHome(manager->GetNewID(), homeName);
                std::cout << "Home created successfully.\n";
                system("pause");
                break;
            }
            case RemoveHome:
            {
                int homeID = 0;
                std::cout << "Enter Home ID: ";
                std::cin >> homeID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                manager->RemoveHome(homeID);
                break;
            }
            case ShowAllHomes:
                manager->ShowAllHomes();
                system("pause");
                break;
            case EnterHome:
            {
                int homeID = 0;
                std::cout << "Enter Home ID: ";
                std::cin >> homeID;
                std::cin.ignore(10000, '\n');
                CHome* home = manager->GetHomeByID(homeID);
                if (home != nullptr) {
                    EnterTheHome(*home);
                }
                else {
                    std::cout << "Home not found.\n";
                    delete home;
                    system("pause");
                }
                break;
            }
            case Exit:
                std::cout << "Exiting Home Management System.\n";
                system("pause");
                break;
            default:
                std::cout << "Invalid option. Try again.\n";
                system("pause");
            }
        }
    } while (HomeManageMenuSelect != Exit);
    manager->ClearHomes();
    _CrtDumpMemoryLeaks();
    return 0;
}

// week 3: debug 
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

const int TOP = 6;

class CPattern
{
private:
    int mSequence[TOP];
public:
    void Initialise(int sequence[TOP]);
    void Display();
    int FindMax();
    void DisplayReversed();
    int FindLocation(int value);
};

// Initialise the array.
// Better to do this as a constructor - if you are confident about constructors then
// convert this method into one
void CPattern::Initialise(int sequence[TOP])
{
    for (int i = 0; i < TOP; ++i)
    {
        mSequence[i] = sequence[i];
    }
}

// Display the array
void CPattern::Display()
{
    for (int i = TOP; i < TOP; ++i)
    {
        cout << mSequence[i] << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
}

// Display the array in reverse order
void CPattern::DisplayReversed()
{
    for (int i = TOP; i > 0; --i)
    {
        cout << mSequence[i] << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
}

// Find maximum value in the array
int CPattern::FindMax()
{
    int max = -100;

    for (int i = 0; i < TOP; ++i)
    {
        if (i > max)
        {
            max = i;
        }
    }
    return max;
}

// Find the location of the first occurence of a value, i.e. it's index
// Return -1 if not found
int CPattern::FindLocation(int value)
{
    int found = -1;
    for (int i = 0; i < TOP; ++i)
    {
        if (found == mSequence[i])
        {
            return found;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

int main()
{
    CPattern* myPattern = new CPattern;
    int testArray[TOP] = { 2, 4, 5, 7, 1, 3 };
    myPattern->Initialise(testArray);

    cout << "Display the array:" << endl;
    myPattern->Display();

    cout << endl << "Display the array in reverse order:" << endl;
    myPattern->DisplayReversed();

    cout << endl << "max element of the array: " << myPattern->FindMax();

    cout << endl << endl;
    cout << "location of the number 7: " << myPattern->FindLocation(7);
    cout << endl;

    system("pause");
}

docs.text:
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

const int SIZE = 3;

class Stack
{
private:
    int  mTop;
    string mData[SIZE];
    bool isFull();
    bool isEmpty();
public:
    void InitialiseStack();
    void Push(string newData);
    void Pop(string& oldData);
    void DisplayStack();
};

int main()
{
    Stack* myStack = new Stack;
    myStack->InitialiseStack();

    myStack->Push("red");
    myStack->Push("green");
    myStack->Push("blue");
    myStack->DisplayStack();
    cout << endl;

    string storedData;
    myStack->Pop(storedData);
    cout << "popped: " << storedData << endl; // blue
    myStack->Pop(storedData);
    cout << "popped: " << storedData << endl; // green
    myStack->Pop(storedData);
    cout << "popped: " << storedData << endl; // red

    delete myStack;
    myStack = nullptr;
}

bool Stack::isFull()
{
    bool result = false;

    if (mTop >= SIZE)
    {
        result = true;
    }
    return result;
}

bool Stack::isEmpty()
{
    bool result = false;

    if (mTop <= 0)
    {
        result = true;
    }

    return result;
}

void Stack::InitialiseStack()
{
    mTop = 0;
}

void Stack::Push(string newData)
{
    //check if not empty
    if (!isFull())
    {
        //push onto stack
        mData[mTop] = newData;
        ++mTop;
    }
    //let the user know stack is full
    else
    {
        cout << "Stack is full" << endl;
    }
}

void Stack::Pop(string& oldData)
{
    // check if Stack is not Empty
    if (!isEmpty())
    {
        //decrease mTop and then return value
        --mTop;
        oldData = mData[mTop];
    }
    // else if Stack is Empty
    else
    {
        cout << "stack is empty" << endl;
        oldData = "";
    }
}

void Stack::DisplayStack()
{
    for (int i = 0; i < mTop; i++)
    {
        cout << mData[i] << endl;
    }
}
