docs.title: What is a Graph?
docs.text:
A visual representation of a set of objects where some of these objects are connected.

The objects are represented by points called vertices and the links that connect the objects are known as edges.

docs.title: A Formal Definition
docs.text:
A graph G can be defined as - G = (V, E) V is the set of vertices in the group. E is the set of edges connecting the vertices. V = {a, b, c, d, e} E = {ab, ac, bd, cd, de}

NB for a non-directional graph. ab & ba are the same. Sets do not include repetition and the edge is only included once.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text: A loop occurs when an edge connects a vertex back to itself. For example, an edge drawn from (a) to (b) would be considered a loop.

docs.title: Degree of Vertex (Valency)
docs.text:
The degree of a vertex (dot) is the number of edges (lines) connected to it.

This is denoted by (deg(V)), where (V) is the vertex in question.

For example, if a vertex has two edges, its degree would be 2.

The Degree Of Vertex for the Vertex (A) is: deg(a) = 2 (2 edges connected to it)

deg(b) = 2 deg© = 2 deg(d) = 3

deg(e) = 1 A Vertex with only 1 degree of vertex is known as the Pendent Vertex.

A loop in a graph counts as having a Valency (Degree of Vertex Number) of 2. In this case deg(e) = 0 and therefore, a vertex with 0 Valency is known as an Isolated Vertex.

docs.title: Degree Sequence
docs.text:
Valency can also be displayed as a degree sequence.

For graph G with the following Degree of Vertex (Valency): - deg(a) = 2 - deg(b) = 3 - deg© = 1 (Pendent Vertex) - deg(d) = 2 - deg(e) = 0 (Isolated Vertex)

The Degree Sequence is as follows: Degree Sequence = {2, 3, 1, 2, 0} (The amount of edges for every vertex in the graph.

docs.title: Directed Graphs
docs.text: For a directed graph, the edges connecting the vertices have a direction associated with them.

docs.title: Degree of Vertex for Directed Graphs
docs.text: In a directed graph each vertex has an indegree and outdegree, their purpose is as follows: - Indegree is the number of edges coming into the vertex. Denoted by deg+(V) - Outdegree is the number of edges leaving the vertex. Denoted by deg-(V)

docs.title: Directed Graph Valency
docs.text:
Indegrees: deg(1) = 0 (Isolated Vertex) deg(2) = 2 deg(3) = 2 deg(4) = 1 (Pendent Vertex)

Outdegrees: deg(1) = 2 deg(2) = 1 (Pendent Vertex) deg(3) = 1 (Pendent Vertex) deg(4) = 1 (Pendent Vertex)

docs.title: Degree of Sequence:
docs.text: Degree of Sequence = {0, 2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1} (Indegrees, Outdegrees)

docs.title: Weighted Graph
docs.text:
A Weighted Graph is a graph in which each branch is given a numerical weight.

A weighted graph is therefore a special type of labelled graph in which the labels are numbers.

docs.title: Simple Graphs
docs.text: A Simple Graph is an unweighted, undirected graph containing no graph loops, or multiple edges. Therefore, a simple graph may be either connected or disconnected.

docs.title: Applications of Graph Theory
docs.text:
Examples usages of Graph Theory:

Electrical Engineering Used For: Designing Circuit Connections.

Computer Science Used For: Study of algorithms such as: - Kruskal's Algorithm - Pim's Algorithm - Dijkstra's Algorithm

Computer Networks Used For: Relationships between interconnected computers in the network.

Science Used For: Molecular and Chemical Structure of a substance i.e. DNS structure of an organism.

docs.title: Google Maps Graph Example
docs.text:
Google Maps is one large graph with the aforementioned Vertices and Edges.

Google utilises an algorithm, such as Dijkstra's Algorithm to calculate the shortest path between 2 vertices.

In this example: - Vertices represent locations, such as intersections, landmarks, or specific addresses - Edges represent the connections or roads between the locations.

docs.title: Traversable Graphs
docs.text: A graph is Traversable if a path can be traced between all vertices without retracing the same path.

docs.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
docs.text:
An algorithm designed for finding the shortest path between nodes in a weighted, possibly directed graph.

e.g. A Road Network

docs.title: Greedy Algorithm
docs.text:
Dijkstra's algorithm, adopts a Greedy Approach to solving the shortest path problem.

At each stage of the process, the best option available is taken. (The edge will the lowest weight).

Unlike the 0/1 Knapsack problem where the Greedy algorithm is not guaranteed to return an optimal solution. However, in this circumstance Greedy returns an optimal solution to the shortest path problem.

docs.title: Breadth First Search & Depth First Search
Search Algorithms
docs.text:
During the lectures the following search algorthms have been discussed: - Linear Search #find-link - Binary Search - Binary Search Trees

This lecture will cover: - Breadth-First Search - Depth-First Search Here’s an enhanced version of your explanation with smoother phrasing and clear structure:

docs.title: Adjacency Matrix
docs.text:
In graph theory, when two vertices are connected by an edge, they are said to be adjacent.

An adjacency matrix is a way to represent adjacency relationships in a graph.

A square matrix is utilised: - 1 indicates that two vertices are connected by an edge (adjacent). - 0 indicates that two vertices are not connected.

docs.title: Properties of Adjacency Matrices:
docs.text:
1. For graphs with no loops, the diagonal of the matrix will always contain 0s, as no vertex connects to itself.
  2. In a non-directed graph, the adjacency matrix is symmetrical. This is because edges in an undirected graph can be traversed in either direction, making the relationship mutuals.

docs.title: Search Space in Algorithms
docs.text: The Search Space is the set of all possible states or solutions that an algorithm must explore in order to solve a problem.

docs.title: Key Regions of Search Space:
docs.text: Explored: These are the regions or states that have already been searched and are already known. Unexplored: These are states that have not yet been discovered or examined. Waiting To Explore (Known as Fridge or Frontier): These are states that have been discovered but not yet explored fully.

docs.title: Shortest Path from Blackburn to Southport
docs.text: BFS takes the shallowest path first. The BFS algorithm is a function which accepts the inital state and the goal as test arguments. The states are ordered alphabetically. Using the FIFO (First-In First-Out) data structure. (Queue to process the Frontier states) Uses a set to hold the done states.

docs.title: BFS - Blackpool to Southport
docs.text:
Add the start state Blackburn to the frontier.

Its adjacent vertices (neighbors) are added to the frontier, ensuring breadth-first exploration

As nodes are explored, they are moved to the done states, meaning they won't be revisited. Continuing with Breadth-First Search Bolton was the first into the queue, so that is processed next. Adding Bolton into the done state, since it is not what we are trying to find. Next Burnley gets added to the done states as it once again isn't the location (Southport) that the BFS is trying to find the shortest path for. Next onto Preston since Soutport is in Preston, as per the diagram presented, the BFS finds Preston, which gets added to the done states.

However, now Preston's neighbours are added to the Frontier of possible options to the shortest path. Rochdale is is added to the done states. This process is continued until options are entered into the done states.

docs.title: Breadth-First Search Cost
docs.text:
Optimal: BFS is optimal if the cost of every step is the same (uniform) (e.g. 1 Step per edge.)

Complete - Yes, the BFS is garanteed to find a solution is the search space is finite.

Time Complexity: (1 + b + b^2 + b^3 + etc + b^n)) (b) is the branching factor (average number of child nodes per node) (n) is the depth of the solution

Implementation: BFS uses a FIFO (First In First Out) queue data structure to manage the Frontier.

docs.title: When to use BFS
docs.text:
Best suited for shallow search spaces.

Can be optimised by caching the previous searches.

docs.title: BFS Cost Example Table
docs.text: Depth Nodes Time Memory (Space) 2 110 .11 miliseconds 107 KB 4 11,110 11 miliseconds 10.6 MB 6 10^6 1.1 seconds 1 GB 8 10^8 2 minutes 103 GB 10 10^10 3 hours 10 TB 12 10^12 13 days 1 PB 14 10^14 3.5 years 99 PB 16 10^15 350 years 10 Exabytes b = 10.1 million nodes per second. 1000 bytes per node.

docs.title: DFS - Blackburn To Southport
docs.text:
Takes the deepest path first approach. The algorithm is a function which accepts an inital state and a goal state. The order of the states will be alphabetical. Uses a LIFO data structure. (Stack to process Frontier states) Uses a set to hold the done states.

As with BFS we start by adding "Blackburn" to the Frontier, since this is not what we are looking for. This will be added to the done states.

Its adjacent vertices are then added to the Frontier. They are pushed onto the Frontier stack in Reverse order.

docs.title: DFS Cost
docs.text:
Optimal: Not guaranteed, as DFS soes not necessarily find the Shortest Path it may get stuck in deeper branches before finding the solution.

Complete: Yes, if the search space is finite, and there's no infinite depth, DFS is complete.

Time Complexity: O(b^n) where: (b) is the branching factor (average number of child nodes per node) (n) is the maximum depth of the search space

Implementation: DFS uses a LIFO Stack to manage the Frontier.

docs.title: When To Use DFS
docs.text:
Best suited for problems where the solution lies deep in the search space otr when memory is a critical constraint.

A drawback to DFS is that it may explore inefficiently if the solution is far from the initally explored path or in shallower areas.

docs.title: DFS Space Advantage
docs.text:
Using the BFS Cost Table from earlier. Recall that: - b = 10 - 1 million nodes per second - 1000 bytes per node.

DFS has an advantage in terms of space over BFS.

Space = O(b*n) Depth = 16

10 x 16 = 160 x 1000 bytes per node = 160,000 bytes. 160,000 / 1024 = (approx) 156 KB

DFS = 156KB BFS = 10 Exabytes

Adaptive Study Planner

BSc (Hons) Software Engineering School of Engineering and Computing University of Lancashire

docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text:
The problem this project seeks to address is that many students struggle with effective time management (Hyseni Duraku, Z., Davis, H. and Hamiti, E. (2023)), particularly when attempting to balance coursework, part-time employment, and exam deadlines. While numerous planning tools exist, that are highly popularised, such as Google Calendar, Notion, and Obsidian, all have the same inherent flaw, that they are manual and require the user to remember and adjust everything change that is necessary. For example, a problem that may arise is updating their calendar for an upcoming exam.

To meet the minimal viable, this project proposes to develop an adaptive study planner, a web-based system designed to pull student information from university-provided sources (e.g. Timetable System) to automate the process of scheduling these activities into the calendar. For examination timetables, optical character recognition, planned to be used as to extract the relevant character data from the image provided, deducing exam dates and adding them to the user's calendar.

The expansive version of this project seeks to use other tools like natural language processing to analyse notes, for keywords or dates that could be recommended to add to the calendar. Further integrating with existing university platforms such as BlackBoard could also be implemented allowing for updates when coursework deadlines are assigned.

docs.title: Ethical Analysis
docs.text:
This analysis seeks to justify any moral or ethical implications associated in the data collection involved the adaptive study planner.

Due to the handling student information, it is important to consider how the data is stored, protected, and processed. The planner will use details such as the timetable, and user-uploaded examination timetables; therefore the collection and storage of this data must handled, in the system by design, in accordance with GDPR legislation (Art. 1 GDPR – subject-matter and objectives (2016)).

All information requested from the user will be limited to what is necessary for the system to function. Data will be encoded during transfer, and encrypted during storage (i.e. if the user permits persistence). User-uploaded images will be deleted immediately after they have been processed by the OCR library to ensure no unnecessary retention of personal data.

Where authentication details are required such as, for accessing the university timetable, they will be encrypted on the backend using a key generated from the user's unique identifier (UUID). The encrypted credentials will be stored securely and decrypted only when necessary to perform scheduled retrieval of the timetable data, ensuring that plaintext credentials are never retrained. Requests to university resources will use secure HTTPS communication.

In-line, with the British Computer Society's (BCS) Code of Conduct (BCS Code of conduct (no date) BCS.) the project will be carried in a way that conforms to the standards of being professional, fair, and inclusive, and will be an important aspect throughout development. The system will be designed to promote equal access to IT by implementing accessibility features for example, a high contrast mode, or font alterations, as to accommodate users regardless of personal circumstances.

docs.title: Risks to Project
docs.text:
The main risks related to the project can be categorised into reliability, data security, and project scope.

Reliability refers to the rise of risks that may arise in integration issues between the university timetable, the OCR library, and the backend, which may hinder the user-interface if not properly handled.

Data Security refers to risks in the chosen method of encryption, or transferring insecurely over the HTTP protocol. If sensitive information, such as timetable details or user credentials were intercepted or improperly encrypted, leading to the exposure of unanonymised data, it could potentially result in a violation of GDPR law (Art. 32 GDPR – security of processing (2016)).

Project Scope refers to the risks around feature creep, described in Wu, Y., et al. (2015) A preliminary analysis and case study of feature-based software customization (Extended abstract) as "A phenomenon of importing and [implementing] redundant features" being potentially unplanned additions or ideas beyond the initially specified scope such as, attempting to implement NLP before the notes system is fully completed which may divert focus, time, and resources of other key areas stalling the project's progress.

docs.title: Risks of Project Failure
docs.text: Project failure could occur for various reasons such as improper time management, underestimation of technical complexity, or security vulnerabilities, such as failure to properly secure user data, leading to a breach of GDPR legislation.

docs.title: Risk Contingency and Preventative Mitigation Measures
docs.text:
To manage the risks mentioned several preventative and contingency measures will be applied throughout the project.

To ensure that the system is reliable each part of it will be unit tested to ensure that independently each feature works within intended behaviour. Early development, designs, and mock-ups will allow me to assess the system in its entirety before development allowing me to identify any compatibility or integration problems before they arise. Another risk is data security, to ensure and maintain secure communications and storage under data protection, I plan to use HTTPS to communicate with the backend, and any data that is stored will be encrypted with an appropriate method (e.g. AES-256).

docs.title: Original Proposal Problem Statement
docs.text:
Problem Statement

The problem this project seeks to address is that many students struggle with effective time management (Hyseni Duraku, Z., Davis, H. and Hamiti, E. (2023)), particularly when attempting to balance coursework, part-time employment, and exam deadlines. While numerous planning tools exist, that are highly popularised, such as Google Calendar, Notion, and Obsidian, all have the same inherent flaw, that they are manual and require the user to remember and adjust everything change that is necessary. For example, a problem that may arise is updating their calendar for an upcoming exam.

To meet the minimal viable, this project proposes to develop an adaptive study planner, a web-based system designed to pull student information from university-provided sources (e.g. Timetable System) to automate the process of scheduling these activities into the calendar. For examination timetables, optical character recognition, planned to be used as to extract the relevant character data from the image provided, deducing exam dates and adding them to the user's calendar.

The expansive version of this project seeks to use other tools like natural language processing to analyse notes, for keywords or dates that could be recommended to add to the calendar. Further integrating with existing university platforms such as BlackBoard could also be implemented allowing for updates when coursework deadlines are assigned.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Students in higher education constantly face significant challenges in organisation, scheduling and cognitive difficulties which adversely, affects their academic performance and overall wellbeing. Two clear problems that stand out are the high demands for executive-functioning of effective and efficient time-management and a heavy reliance on manual data entry, which is common in existing planning tools. These problems are made exceedingly worse under conditions of academic stress, mental health difficulties, or simply dynamic changing nature of university, and personal commitments. The manual-entry problem places a consistent loop of cognitive and temporal burden on students, during academic pressures when executive-function is low.

Many of the widely available mainstream tools, which are widely advertised to students, for instance Google Calendar, Notion, Todoist, Obsidian, and many other platforms, which all suffer from the same inherent limitation of manual data entry, requiring the student to enter every exam, lab, lecture, deadline, reading list, room change, or any other forms of scheduling. In the event of inconsistent notices provided for timetable changes, which leaves students with little time to adjust their planners to account for this change; which as a result may lead to missed deadlines, lectures, lab, etc therefore proceeding to unnecessary stress.

The significance and impact of this problem is board. Poor academic organisation, in particular a consistent failure to sustain up-to-date scheduling information, leading to a repeated cycle of preventable academic stress. As a discussed in a paper (Pascoe, M. C., Hetrick, S. E. and Parker, A. G. (2019)), which assessed the impact of academic stress on students, concluding with the result that academic-related stress has an impact on students leading to a negative academic performance, decreased learning capacity, increased risk of developing mental health problems like depression and anxiety, and sleep disturbances, the paper also clarifies academic stress and burnout to include exhaustion, depersonalisation, cynicism, and inefficacy, or reduced accomplishment stating that “increased stress is associated with substance use among students” (Pascoe, M. C., Hetrick, S. E. and Parker, A. G. (2019)). In contrast, successfully removing this limitation for timetable, deadline, and examination entry would provide immediate and widespread benefit to the student demographic, by providing a web platform which utilises technologies to reduce the amount of manual data entry required by the student, therefore relieving some of the existing cognitive load.

From a legal and ethical perspective, any system that accesses official university timetabling or assessment/examination data must fully comply with UK GDPR and Data Protection Act (2018). Due to the project being developed independently of the university, the only lawful basis for acquiring student's personal information for processing, is obtaining explicit consent under Article 6(1)(a) of General Data Protection Regulation (2016). Robust, and easily revokable consent systems will need to be developed to maintain lawful. For instance under an individual's right of erasure.

docs.title: 1.1. The Project Aim
docs.text: The primary high-level aim of this project is to benefit students through the development of a web-based adaptive student study planner which removes the need for manual data entry, for timetable, and assignment deadlines by securely synchronising with the official university timetable resources, for instance the BlackBoard system for deadline and examination timetable resource collection, thereby reducing some of the preventable academic stress from the student.

docs.title: 1.2. The Project Objectives
docs.text:
1. Investigate all supported ways of exportin data from the BlackBoard Learn platform, university TimeTable system, and other supporting systems. For instance transferring the pre-existing Outlook Calendar schedule and plan a system that can handle and process the supported data types. For example, examination timetables should be images, for OCR to work, to assess and extract the schedule content.
  2. Identify and document, the existing BlackBoard Learn REST API and OAuth for M365 authentication and the current basic authentication process for the existing university TimeTable.
  3. Develop a reliable notes system which can reliable create, edit, and delete notes in markdown format. Saved to the user's account.
  4. Configure an automatic time-based timetable synchronisation service that refreshes the data sources to pull any new data that has not yet been previously added to the user's schedule and updating any pre-existing changes.
  5. Plan and develop a secure encryption system for the user's account information, and markdown notes to ensure proper security for data protection.
  6. Build an adaptive, user-centric dashboard that combines the timetable, upcoming deadlines, recent notes, suggested daily study blocks, and a visual tracking the days notes were created as an indicator of progress.
  7. Ensure the implementation developed is fully GDPR compliant and is transparent in the storage, collection, and removal processes, to inform the user of how to permanently delete all their user data.
  8. Perform comprehensive and thorough unit-testing of each component of the application to ensure full functionality, and proper guard boundaries to avoid anomalous behaviour.
  9. __Some form of student rating thing.

docs.title: 2.1. The Nature and Impact of Academic-Related Stress on Students and Executive Functioning
docs.text:
Academic stress in students has been heavily researched and is well-established as a major issue in higher education. Pascoe, Hetrick and Parker (2020), in a major narrative review that collected data from various studies, including large-scale OECD, PISA surveys of over 540,000 students across 72 countries (OECD, 2017) and national student health data, found that in both secondary and higher education students routinely reported high levels of academic-related stress, primarily driven by the pressure of grade expectations. However, fear of poor performance, heavy workloads, and a difficulty to consistently keep track of changing timetables, deadlines, and personal circumstances can all affect a student’s academic performance. Their analysis showed that ongoing academic demands are strongly associated with poor mental health, such as depression, and anxiety, disrupted sleep, reduced physical activity, and increased substance use. Crucially, the review repeatedly highlights a consistent burden of manually monitoring and updating dynamic schedules, especially during peak times, for instance during an examination period, precisely when cognitive resources are low therefore the constant requirement to reassess scheduling for updates creates a broader cycle of consistent academic stress which directly impacts the physical and mental wellbeing of the student and consequential results in a poorer academic performance (Pascoe, Hetrick and Parker, 2020) overall.

Recent research by Pérez-Jorge, D. et al. (2025) highlights that academic stress has a significant impact on executive functioning, that students in higher education rely on to sustain day-to-day organisation and planning. In a mixed study of 256 undergraduate and postgraduate students at the university of La Laguna, participants completed an adapted version of the SISCO Inventory of Academic Stress with a portion of the group followed by small focus-group sessions. The findings illustrated a relationship between what students considered an excessive number of assignments, exam pressure, and those with self-reported difficulties in concentration, and organisation, in particular, students with family, and work priorities seemed to be the most effected. The results demonstrate how academic stress decreases the cognitive capacity particularly in activities requiring executive functioning of higher education students needed to maintain regular schedules around their timetables, deadlines, and other personal commitments.

The research results illustrate that academic stress has a significant impact on a student’s physical and mental wellbeing, depleting the cognitive energy needed to maintain accurate and up-to-date schedules, especially during peak times when cognitive load, for instance examination, and revision is very high. By creating a cycle of improper scheduling can create a disorganised calendar for the student, which could result in missed deadlines, exams or personal responsibilities, for example part-time work. leading to further depletion of executive functioning and is a contributor to worsening academic performance.

docs.title: 2.2. The Lack of Interoperability in Mainstream Planning Tools
docs.text: The core limitation present in widely available digital planning calendars and tools is their fundamental dependency on manual data entry. For every lecture, deadline, room change, or examination, students must manually enter and update their schedules which may be gathered from a variety of sources such as emails, learning management systems, outlook calendar events, or from numerous alternative sources. This reliance is highlighted in a paper by Banihashem et al. (2022), which discusses that while current learning systems excel at assessing student performance data, once tasks are started, they fail to automate the “pre-action”, being the essential organisation and scheduling linked to executive functioning that is required to begin learning. While this does not directly reflect a student planner system, it does demonstrate the trend of manual data reliance across student systems which continues to deplete executive functioning. Furthermore, many mainstream applications such as Google Calendar, Notion, and Todoist lack native integration with learning management systems like BlackBoard; these platforms operate without any connectivity to a student’s institutional module resources, or timetable, therefore requiring the student to manually change all their planner or scheduling information.

docs.title: 2.3. Data Extraction for Legacy Institutional Systems
docs.text:
A common technical limitation in Higher Education systems is the reliance on legacy web applications, secured by HTTP basic authentication, which despite the essential nature of the data, notable lack public facing API endpoints prevent easy retrieval of the student data. These legacy systems can manage numerous services for example, academic timetabling, student course and personal information, and attendance monitoring. Past research (Bisbal et al. (1999)) which noted that a significant problem in existing interfacing interface approaches in that during that time they were designed exclusively with the browser in focus, therefore lacking a well-documented easily accessible API for external integration with internal systems. Consequently, this means that the legacy system acts as a presentation layer for human interaction rather than a gateway allowing browser, and external API access for instance, for developers. This limitation results in valuable institutional data being produced solely for visual consumption, effectively blocking attempts at automated processing or external retrieval.

To address the rigidity of these legacy systems without the time-consuming, overhead of requesting the university redevelopment their existing systems. The "wrapping" strategy offers a viable solution. Bisbal et al. (1999) describe wrapping as the process of encapsulating existing data or programs within a new interface, essentially providing the legacy component with a modern appearance while retaining its original functionality.

docs.title: 2.4. Secure Note-Taking and GDPR Compliance
docs.text:
Developing independent software for higher education requires strict adherence to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), particularly when processing personal data such as student study habits and private daily or study notes. Voigt and von dem Bussche (2017) emphasise that under the principle of "Privacy by Design", data protection safeguards must be integrated securely into the core development process rather than added as a mere side objective. This is particularly critical for applications that rely on web scraping institutional data, as the system effectively acts as a ‘data controller’ for the information it retrieves and stores. Consequently, the system design must prioritise "Data Minimisation" as mandated under Article 5, ensuring that only the specific data required for scheduling such as module codes and dates is retained, while extraneous personal information is immediately discarded to reduce the application's overall risk profile.

To secure sensitive user-generated content, such as personal revision notes, the system must implement "Encryption at Rest" rather than relying solely on HTTPS for transmission. Bertino and Sandhu (2005) discusses in a paper, that perimeter defences are frequently insufficient to protect plaintext data against more significant internal threats or privilege escalation attacks, such as SQL injection. To mitigate this risk, the design of the system must ensure that user data is inaccessible without the unique decryption key associated with the user's session.

docs.title: 2.5. Gaps in Research
docs.text:
The existing literature on this topic comprehensively links the relationship between academic stress and impaired executive functioning. However, despite significant technological advancements over the last few decades, interventions to relieve this burden, persist. Pascoe, M.C., Hetrick, S.E. and Parker, A.G. (2019), establish in their research that students experience a heightened level of stress during peak academic periods, precisely when cognitive resources for maintaining manual schedules are low, whereas Pérez-Jorge et al. (2025) reported that stress directly compromises the student’s organisational capabilities that are required in effective planning. However, both studies remain general to the problem, identifying the student’s academic cycle of stress and disorganisation, without exploring how a system could be designed to tackle this problem. Consequently, psychologically academic stress in students is well understood, however the technology through automated scheduling could reduce some of the cognitive overhead of the student, remains elusive.

Furthermore, current research on learning management systems identifies critical limitations in ‘pre-action’ support. Banihashem et al. (2022) highlights that existing educational technologies excel at tracking student performance once tasks commence, however tasks that are yet provided have no automation for the beginning organisation and scheduling that executive functioning demands. A way to minimise this gap is to clearly aggregate a student’s relevant information, including timetables, deadlines, assignments, and examination timetables into a unified planning application thereby removing some of the manual-entry requirements as typically seen in mainstream recommendations.

Many higher education institutions rely on legacy systems, which prioritise the presentation layer and do not have any external API endpoints, therefore for data to be collected on these systems the technical concept of ‘wrapping’ being to encapsulate the presentation layer within a modern interface. Bisbal et al. (1999) details principles for encapsulating legacy applications within modern interfaces, demonstrating how existing data can be accessed and integrated into modern systems, without requiring institutional system redevelopment. There is a significantly limited amount of research in applying these wrapping techniques to a student planning application representing a significant gap in the nature of the problem, compared to modern practical implementation.

Finally, no existing solution adequately combines automated institutional data extraction with the privacy-by-design architecture that GDPR compliance mandates. Mainstream planning tools such as Google Calendar, Notion, and Todoist operate without native integration to learning management systems like Blackboard, requiring complete manual data entry while offering limited protection for sensitive student content. Voigt and von dem Bussche (2017) emphasise that data protection must be embedded within core development processes, and Bertino and Sandhu (2005) argue that encryption at rest is essential for protecting against internal threats. Current tools address neither institutional integration nor robust encryption for user-generated study materials, leaving students without a solution that reduces scheduling burden while maintaining appropriate data security.

This research therefore addresses a clearly defined gap within the existing literature: the absence of an integrated, privacy-compliant system that automates schedule aggregation from legacy institutional sources, and learning management systems, thereby reducing the cognitive load that exacerbates academic stress during critical academic periods.

docs.title: 3.1. Problem Analysis (Objectives 1 & 2)
docs.text:
The initial phase of development follows a waterfall approach, which is categorised for its sequential linear progression. Each phase must be fully completed before proceeding to the next. This methodology was selected for the problem as it requires comprehensive requirements gathering prior to any development work occurring, ensuring that the technical constraints of existing systems or implementations are fully understood before decisions are made. Described by Royce (1970) analysis and specifications are imperative during the early stages of a project, which is essential for completing the first two objectives being the investigation of exploring methods for data exploration, authentication processes, and ensuring compatible data handling early on.

The requirements gathering process involves investigating all supported methods of exporting data from the BlackBoard Learn platform, the university timetabling system, and any other necessary integrations such as with Outlook Calendar to sync events in the student planner. This investigation requires thorough documenting of the available data export formats such as CSV, where direct API access is available. As researched in the state of the art Bisbal et al (1999) noted that legacy systems often lack well-documented API endpoints making external integration require alternative methods, which is where the implementation of the wrapping strategy is necessary to ensure proper encapsulation for the data being presented visually to the browser. For examination timetables which are typically provided as images, or PDF documents therefore one requirement for analysis is the implementation of Optical Character Recogniton technology to extract the character data from the image and import this data into the schedule.

The documentation phase involves identifying and recording the existing BlackBoard REST API capabilities, OAuth authentication processes for Microsoft Office 365 integration, and the current HTTP basic authentication solution utilised by the university legacy application timetable system. The documentation phase serves as the foundation in the design phase ensuring the available design accommodates the specific constraints and requirements of the data source from the platform being extracted from. Once analysis of the existing data sources is concluded then proceeded by the design and development phases therefore avoiding unforeseen technical limitations discovered later in  the development process which may stall or hinder the development of the project.

docs.title: 3.2. Privacy-By-Design Ethics (Objectives 3 & 4)
docs.text:
Once the problem analysis phase is complete the project will proceed to establish a robust security-focused design ensuring full compliance with UK GDPR and the data protection act (2018). As emphasised by Voigt, P. and Von dem Bussche, A. (2017) data protection must be integrated into the core development process rather than as a secondary addition, and therefore the security must be planned during the early phases of the project to maintain a secure design across all subsequent and proceeding design phases. The project must maintain privacy-by-design which requires the implementation of encryption-at-rest for all user-generated content, secure session management, and easily revokable consent mechanisms therefore requiring a system that is privacy focused with transparency In the management, storage and collection of data during user registration.

Following the recommendations of Bertino and Sandu (2005) who argue that perimeter defences are insufficient to protect plaintext data against internal threats, and therefore the system must be designed to ensure that user-data remains inaccessible without the unique decryption key associated with that user. To meet this requirement for the project, AES-256 encryption for stored markdown notes and bcrypt hashing for user passwords. The encryption for the project needs to be designed prior to the development of the notes and dashboard systems, ensuring all user-generated content and passwords are securely stored.

In order to fully comply with the GDPR law, the project will follow the principle of data minimisation as described under article 5 of GDPR. Data extraction must only obtain the specific information required for scheduling, for example module codes, names, and resources. The design must also ensure that proper right to erasure mechanisms are in place as to easily allow the user to access, or permanently delete all account information, notes, or calendar notices, allowing users to easily consent and withdraw their consent with the immediate deletion of their data upon termination of user account.

docs.title: 3.3. Core Feature Development (Objectives 5, 6, & 7)
docs.text:
Once the foundational security and data protections are established, the next phase begins with the project shift to core feature development, encompassing the 5th, 6th, and 7th project objectives which primarily focus on two of the most critical components of the entire system, time-based timetable synchronisation and  a fully functional markdown-based note-taking system which integrates into a seamless user dashboard interface which establishes links between the other pages of the web application and the central user dashboard. These two objectives are imperative to the project’s main aim of reducing overall academic stress to help maintain adequate executive functioning for the students day-to-day.

The design and implementation of the timetable synchronisation system begins with the development of a CRUD (Create, Read, Update, and Delete) time-based functions, which will operate in the background to facilitate reliable updates to the user’s schedule. Functions triggered at a specific time interval passing, for example every 3 months and 15 minutes, provide the backbone enabling the system to store newly fetched data, retrieve and display that content onto the user’s dashboard, override any previously cached entries or any with updated information, and clearing out the outdated, for example the time an class has passed and therefore it is now redundant data. The system trigger for these operations will be both user and server driven. For the user when they go to access their schedule an immediate update is sent to ensure all information is accurate and up-to-date as provided by the timetable system, on the other hand, for the system itself will send requests, slowly and incrementally like normal traffic as to not overwhelm the timetable server with requests all at once for all of the users, once every midnight, as to both not disrupt for the performance for the user by significantly using server resources for all of the necessary timetable update requests.

To maintain data integrity within the scheduling system, the server-based timetable synchronisation trigger will begin an iterative loop that scans the database of all registered users individually. This allows the system to evaluate whether any calendar entries, including notes or one-time schedule events, are no longer relevant for instance, a past lab session or expired assignment deadline and should be removed or overwritten with up-to-date data. However, recognising that some users may wish to retain specific events for personal reference or future review, the application will include a user-toggleable setting that allows individuals to toggle this behaviour on or off. This ensures that no valuable scheduling entries are unintentionally deleted as part of the system’s automation, with the user remaining in control of how long their notices persist beyond their original dates.

The user dashboard will be built with responsiveness and a user-centric design in mind. Students logging into the platform will be brought to this interface which will function as the central point for which the timetable and scheduling data will be presented, for example a recent notes list. Through the work of De Vreugd et al (2024) a paper that which discussed the value of visual self-tracking tools to integrate better student awareness into their studies.

To support a data-reliant structured approach, all data sources will be downloadable and converted in .ics as a well-recognised calendar-friendly format for easier integration with the calendar system, and makes importing and exporting of third party schedules data simpler on both the system and user. Due to the timetable system being made and designed as human-interactive, then the data received from the timetable will need to be processed and converted from the HTML content.

In conclusion, this platform hopes to reduce the need for manual work on the student, by enhancing time-awareness, and supports consistent academic involvement in a GDPR complaint and efficient manner. These features form, the core user experience of the application and directly drive toward to the project’s overall aim of reducing the cognitive demand caused by disorganisation and stress in higher education.

docs.title: 3.4. Testing and Evaluation
docs.text:
The final objective in the project will be unit testing which forms the foundations to reassuring quality assurance process and will be repeatedly performed throughout all major components of the development lifecycle ensuring accurate functionality and avoiding anomalous behaviour as features scale. Each key fundamental of the system is to be built around distinct logical modules allowing the testing process to cover them individually while maintaining modularity. The components primarily to be unit testing will be the TimeTable synchronisation, OCR Implementation, Markdown Notes Handling, User Login and Authentication processes, and the AES-256 encryption and decryption for the user data. Testing allows for project errors to be resolved before new modules or systems are layered together removing potential logic errors before it scales and interlinks with the other systems.

Each functionality within the notes subsystem will undergo specific tests to verify note creation, editing, deletion, and markdown rendering in both preview and storage modes. Particular testing focus is placed on verifying that formatting rules render correctly across headings, bold, italics, and list handling syntax, while also ensuring database integrity when back-end encryption is applied to note content at rest. Any numeric or symbolic markdown structures will undergo test parsing and sanitisation for cross-site scripting prevention. All encryption and authentication logic must also withstand brute-force attempts and invalid input strings during testing, ensuring that passwords, scheduling data, and study notes never fall out of encrypted form during processing.

Finally, final unit tests will ensure that GDPR-compliance mechanisms tied to account deletion and data erasure. Once triggered, the test will verify that user-linked data across notes, credentials, and calendar events are fully removed from the system with no residual information retaining.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Minimum Viable Product Stage
docs.text:
The MVP stage was designed to satisfy two foundational design requirements: validating the technical feasibility of the legacy timetable integration prior to any significant frontend investment, and establishing a Privacy-by-Design architecture as the structural baseline from which all subsequent development would extend. To satisfy these constraints, a deliberate specification decision was made to under-invest in the presentation layer, composing it of a single HTML, CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript stack, ensuring that development effort could be concentrated exclusively on the two critical backend mechanisms identified in objectives one and two; the automation of university timetable authentication and data extraction, and the implementation of a secure session-managed backend using ExpressJS. The user navigation wireframe illustrated in Figure 1 was produced at this stage to establish a clear model of the intended user journey, providing sufficient structural context to guide backend API routing decisions without prematurely committing to a full component-based architecture.

Figure 1 - User Navigation Wireframe

The intentionally minimal presentation layer, whilst not aesthetically refined, served its specification purpose precisely; by constraining the UI to a bare HTML, CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript stack, the authentication flow and Express API routing could be verified in isolation, ensuring that the Privacy-by-Design foundations and GDPR data protection obligations were architecturally sound before any feature development commenced.

During this stage of development, the core priority was validating this backend functionality. Due to strict time constraints, the project pivoted from a sequential Waterfall testing methodology to an agile, sprint-based approach. Testing commenced concurrently with code creation, primarily relying on runtime debugging without formal logging. The notable exception to this was the secure API routing, which was systematically verified using Postman (expanded in testing section 5.3).

A primary test of the feasibility of the project was demonstrating a reliable ability to consistently web scrape the timetable data from the university’s timetable system. As previously identified during the initial problem analysis, the legacy-like system operates purely on the presentation layer, comprised of an HTML table containing all the student’s scheduling information, and entirely lacks publicly accessible API endpoints.

To overcome this limitation a custom backend web scraper was created to authenticate into the timetable system posing as a legitimate user request. The legacy timetable application is secured with HTTP basic authentication, therefore the NodeJS script dynamically constructs the ‘Authorization’ header by appending the university’s domain onto the username and then concatenating the university email and password subsequentially encoding the string into the Base64 format.

Once the response successfully passes the authentication check, the cheerio library is utilised to parse the returned raw HTML from the request body. A custom recursive function which utilises a regular expression for matching parsing the string into the matching pattern, is then applied to extract the event strings: Time, Module, Location, Lecturer, and Type, and maps them into a JSON array. By successfully automating the extraction of the timetable events and parsing them into the database, the MVP definitively proved the viability of the legacy integration.

To act as the SOR (Source of Record) for my application the relational database utilising MySQL for application decoupling, was intentionally designed to be simple for the MVP yet highly secure, as illustrated in the diagram (Figure 2). The data in the tables is entirely dependent on the users table, specifically the user’s uuid (universally unique identifier) as the primary key. Under GDPR Right to Erasure, when a user deletes their account, it triggers a process in the database which utilises ON DELETE CASCADE foreign key constraints.

The expanded post-MVP ERD, as illustrated in Figure 5, reflects the additional tables introduced during this phase of development. A notable addition is the user_settings table, which was introduced to allow persistence for user preferences  server-side, including theme selection, time format, date format, and notification preferences, allowing the application to incorporate a broader range of accessibility and personalisation options for the user. The theme preference in particular supports light, dark, and auto system-based modes, which was a deliberate design decision to accommodate users with varying visual accessibility requirements, for instance those with light sensitivity or who prefer reduced contrast environments. Similarly to the MVP ERD, all tables maintain a strict foreign key dependency on the users table via the UUID primary key, ensuring that under GDPR Right to Erasure, account deletion propagates an ON DELETE CASCADE constraint across all dependent tables, permanently removing all associated notes, scheduled events, and user preferences in a single efficient database operation.

docs.title: 4.3 Development Methodology
docs.text:
The methodology outlined in Section 3 specified a sequential Waterfall approach for the requirements gathering, legacy system documentation, and security planning phases, on the basis that the technical constraints of the timetable system and GDPR compliance obligations needed to be fully characterised before any development commenced. In practice, this sequential structure was retained across these foundational phases; however, the architectural complexity of the React migration necessitated a departure from the originally planned downstream testing model, as concurrent sprint-based development became the only viable approach within the available timeframe. This represents the primary divergence between the proposed and actual methodology, and is discussed critically in Section 5.3.

The frontend architecture followed a deliberate two-phase approach. The MVP was intentionally constructed using Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, and CSS as a stepping stone to validate the core backend feasibility, and verify stable functionality, specifically the timetable scraper and Privacy-by-Design foundations, before committing to the full React migration. After demonstration, the backend was confirmed stable, and therefore a dedicated react branch was created to isolate the frontend rewrite from the stable mvp environment. The migration went through several iterations before being successfully merged into master via pull request, with all subsequent features including the TF-IDF search with additional scoring, iCalendar import and export, and the useAuth, useTheme, useNotifications hook developed within this branch.

docs.title: 5.1 Key Problems
docs.text:
The development process encountered numerous problems across both the MVP and post-MVP phases of the project. During the MVP, seemingly straightforward styling issues such as the calendar grid div failing to centre correctly consumed significant debugging time, and the calendar event rendering posed persistent challenges, with overlapping events remaining a partially unresolved issue in the final implementation despite the CSS overflow property being set to auto, which should theoretically have handled the overflow behaviour automatically.

The most significant challenge however was the migration to React itself, which introduced an entirely new set of problems stemming from the fundamental differences between Vanilla JavaScript and React's declarative component model. Understanding React's state management system, the rules around hooks, and the lifecycle of components required a substantial learning curve during development. A particular challenge was designing and implementing custom hooks and contexts from scratch, specifically the AuthContext (Figure 7), which required to be structured correctly to wrap the entirety of App.js as the root provider, ensuring the authenticated user state existed in the global component tree and was accessible to every page component without needing to be passed down manually through props.

During the initial problem analysis and methodology phases, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) was planned as a core feature to allow students to upload examination timetable images, from which the system would automatically extract and import the relevant dates and events into the calendar. However, due to the time constraints imposed by the significant architectural migration to React and the complexity of implementing the core backend features to a satisfactory standard, the OCR feature was descoped from the final implementation. The decision was made to prioritise the reliable completion of the timetable scraper, notes system, and calendar integration over introducing an additional library dependency that could not be adequately tested and validated within the remaining development time, which prioritised creating a stable build for the show and tell demonstration with supervisor.

A further challenge arose because of the strict Privacy-by-Design constraint of storing all notes as AES-128 ciphertext, which prevented the use of MySQL's native full-text search capabilities, as the database can only operate on the encrypted values, making it impossible to query against user input server-side. This necessitated retrieving the full notes array to the client for decryption first, and only then executing the TF-IDF algorithm across the plaintext content to produce scored, ranked results for the search bar. While this preserves the zero-knowledge principle, it introduces a scalability limitation were the processing overhead scales linearly with note volume, a constraint that without the encryption requirement would be trivially resolved through server-side through SQL and indexing.

Figure 6 - APIs & React Hooks - Sequence Diagram.

As shown in Figure 6, the React frontend demonstrates the benefits of the API decoupling design decision. Rather than individual components directly constructing and sending HTTP requests for instance, repeatedly calling the authorisation API (/auth/whoami endpoint) every time to verify a user’s authorisation status each page component interacts with dedicated API endpoints (such as /user/events and /user/notes) through a single centralised module apiHandler.js.

The code presented in Figure 22 (Appendix 4), demonstrates that when the app initially loads through app.js, the AuthProvider immediately runs the checkAuth function which sends a single request to /auth/whoami which verifies the user’s authentication status, based on whether an Express Session exists for their client on the backend. The useAuth function allows other component to access the state data stored in the AuthContext like the user’s uuid and the loading value.

The MemberRoute component shown in Figure 23 (Appendix 4) acts as a protected route wrapper, sharing as the rest of the components, the same, useAuth hook to retrieve the user state cached by the AuthProvider, therefore guarding all restricted pages without making any additional requests to the backend. During the initial load, whilst the /auth/whoami request is still resolving, the loading check prevents the pre-mature redirection of a valid user. Once resolved, if the user is null (as returned by the express backend) it immediately redirects to the login page, otherwise the protected page renders normally.

sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as Client (React Frontend)
    participant UseAuth as UseAuth Hook
    participant Express_Backend as Express Backend
    participant CryptoJS as CryptoJS Engine
    participant DatabaseHandler as DatabaseHandler.js

    Client->>UseAuth: Submit Plaintext Note (Title & Content)
    UseAuth->>Express_Backend: Verify Request
    Express_Backend->>UseAuth: Return Authenticated User UUID
    UseAuth->>CryptoJS: Pass Plaintext Content & UUID (as key)
    CryptoJS->>UseAuth: Return Encrypted Ciphertext
    UseAuth->>DatabaseHandler: INSERT (Plaintext Title, Ciphertext Body)

    Client->>Express_Backend: Fetch Notes
    Express_Backend->>UseAuth: Verify Request
    UseAuth->>Express_Backend: Return Authenticated User UUID
    Express_Backend->>DatabaseHandler: SELECT Notes by UUID
    DatabaseHandler->>Express_Backend: Return Ciphertext Body
    Express_Backend->>CryptoJS: Pass Ciphertext & UUID (as Key)
    CryptoJS->>Express_Backend: Return Decrypted Plaintext
    Express_Backend->>Client: Send JSON Array (Plaintext Content)
Figure 7 - AES-128 Encryption Data Flow Diagram - Notes Example.

To satisfy the project's strict Privacy-by-Design objectives, a robust cryptographic data flow was constructed to guarantee Encryption-at-Rest for all user-generated study notes. As visualised in Figure 4, encryption and decryption are executed entirely within the backend server memory, ensuring the MySQL database acts strictly as a secure storage vault. When a client submits a new note from the React frontend, the Express backend authenticates the request via session middleware, extracting the user's universally unique identifier (UUID). The API controller truncates the plaintext title to satisfy database constraints, while the CryptoJS engine dynamically applies the user's UUID as the secret cryptographic key to encrypt the note's body using an AES-128 algorithm. This payload is subsequently passed to the databaseHandler.js module, which handles the secure MySQL insertion.

Figure 8 - Database Encrypted at Rest

Upon retrieval, the process is inverted. The database handler passes the ciphertext back to the backend, where it is decrypted in runtime using the authenticated user's UUID before being formatted as a JSON array and sent to the client. This architectural design ensures that even in the event of a database compromise, the stored plaintext remains entirely inaccessible without the user's active, authenticated session, and is unusable in case of data breach.

The pseudo code, and flowchart in Appendix 3, illustrate the custom TF-IDF search algorithm that was implemented entirely client-side, operating exclusively on the decrypted notes array already held in the component's state, ensuring no additional requests are made to the backend during a search. The algorithm begins by tokenising the user's query, stripping punctuation and common stop words whilst intentionally retaining technical terms such as "how" and "use" which frequently appear in academic note titles via a hardcoded array of common stop words. To prevent the algorithm failing on queries made of entirely stop words, a fallback tokeniseRaw function is invoked which retains the stop words but removes punctuation, ensuring a result is always returned.

For each note, a base TF-IDF score is calculated across the decrypted title and body content, with additional score bonuses applied post-calculation for exact title matches (+10), partial title matches (+5), and partial content matches (+2), improving the relevance of results. The notes are then sorted in descending order by their final score and returned to the NotesPage component for rendering, maintaining strict Encryption-at-Rest throughout as the search never exposes decrypted content beyond the user's active session.

However, the client-side approach, while privacy-preserving, means computational load scales with note volume entirely within the browser, a limitation that would need to be addressed, likely through server-side indexing, for any production deployment handling large note collections.

docs.title: 5.2 Testing
docs.text:
Due to the time constraints imposed by the React migration the project pivoted away from the sequential Waterfall testing approach originally outlined in the methodology, shifting to a concurrent sprint-based process where testing was performed alongside development rather than as a formal downstream phase. During the MVP phase this primarily meant runtime debugging without formal logging, which while given the circumstances carries the inherent risk of edge-case behaviour going undetected, particularly in the context of the AES-128 encryption and session management logic where undetected boundary conditions could constitute a security risk, and is a limitation that would be addressed through an automated testing framework such as Jest in future iterations of the project.

The notable exception to this approach was the systematic API testing conducted using Postman, which provided a structured and repeatable mechanism for verifying backend endpoint behaviour across all systems of the application, covering a total of fifty-seven test cases documented in full in Appendix 2. The authentication tests confirmed that the system correctly enforces password length validation, rejects duplicate email registration with a 409 conflict response, and returns appropriate 401 Unauthorised responses, with the /auth/whoami endpoint verified to correctly distinguish authenticated and unauthenticated session states which as discussed in Section 5.2 underpins the MemberRoute protection mechanism. The notes tests confirmed full CRUD functionality and implicitly validated the AES-128 encryption cycle end-to-end, as a successfully decrypted GET response confirmed that no plaintext was persisting beyond the backend server memory. A particularly important boundary condition confirmed in the events tests was that an end time submitted before a start time correctly returns a 400 error rather than silently persisting malformed data. The GDPR account deletion tests verified that ON DELETE CASCADE correctly removed all adjacent user data across all dependent tables, confirming compliance with the right to erasure under Art. 17 GDPR – right to erasure (2016), ensuring no residual user data remained following account termination.

docs.title: 6.1 Evaluation Process
docs.text:
The evaluation of this project was conducted through systematic Postman-based API testing documented in Appendix 2, covering fifty-seven individual test cases across all core subsystems: authentication, notes, events, ICS import and export, account deletion, user settings, and university timetable synchronisation. This approach was selected because the most critical success criteria were the reliable and secure operation of the backend API endpoints, given that the entire Privacy-by-Design architecture depended on the correct behaviour of the AES-128 encryption cycle, the session management middleware, and the GDPR-compliant account deletion cascade. Testing directly against these endpoints provided the most direct and repeatable mechanism for verifying that the system met its defined requirements.

Each system was evaluated against the functional requirements labelled in Section 4.1. with each test case designed to both verify the expected success condition and the appropriate handling of invalid or boundary inputs. For example, the notes numerous tests successfully validated the decrypted GET response confirming that no plaintext persisted beyond the backend server memory. Similarly, the account deletion tests verified that ON DELETE CASCADE correctly propagated across all dependent tables, confirming compliance with the right of erasure under article 17 of GDPR. The timetable synchronisation tests confirmed core feasibility with integration by web scraping the presentation layer of the university’s legacy-like timetable system.

However, as discussed in Section 5.3, the pivot to sprint-based development meant that runtime debugging substituted for a formal automated testing framework such as Jest throughout the development lifecycle. This carries an inherent risk that edge-case behaviour within individual functions, particularly within the AES-128 encryption module and the TF-IDF algorithm, may have gone undetected, and represents a limitation of the current evaluation coverage that would need to be addressed in any future iteration of the project.

Nonetheless, the successful verification of all fifty-seven test cases across the core subsystems demonstrates that the system reliably automates the extraction and management of timetable and scheduling data, directly evidencing that the primary aim of reducing the manual data entry burden, and by extension the preventable academic stress identified in the literature, has been met.

docs.title: 6.2 Diversity, Equality & Inclusion
docs.text:
The project engaged with DEI considerations from its creation, driven by ethical obligations of the problem space itself. As identified in Section 2.1. students with specific learning needs such as dyslexia are disproportionately impacted by the cognitive demands of maintaining manual schedules, as established by Abbott-Jones (2021). This was a deliberate focus during project planning and design as to cater uniformly to students who both do and do not struggle with manual scheduling without it being burdensome.

In terms of accessibility, the post-MVP project utilises user settings, introduced to support themes being light, and dark mode, while also allowing for an auto mode dependent on the user's current browser theme. Font size and format preferences were similarly proposed through the user settings system, however, were unable to be added in time.

However, the timetable scraper is tightly coupled to the specific HTTP based authentication utilised and table formatting for UCLan’s TimeTable system, which limits institutional inclusivity of the applications. Students are other universities would be unable to benefit from the automatic timetable scraping. Supporting a broader range of timetable login systems for different institutions, or in the event of being unable to scrape, offering the manual ICS import as a fallback would significantly improve the inclusivity of the solution in future. Additionally, the React frontend has not been evaluated against the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (Kirkpatrick et al., 2018), which define the internationally recognised standard for web accessibility covering visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive disabilities, and ensuring conformance would be a necessary extension for any production deployment intended to serve students with disabilities.

docs.title: 6.3 Evaluation Discussion
docs.text:
The primary aim of this project was to develop a web-based adaptive student study planner that removes the need for manual data entry for timetables, thereby reducing the preventable academic stress caused by disorganisation.

Objectives 1 and 2 were largely achieved. The investigation confirmed that the university timetable system lacked any publicly accessible API endpoints, necessitating the wrapping strategy described by Bisbal et al. (1999), and the custom backend scraper successfully authenticated into the legacy system and parsed timetable events into the database, definitively proving the viability of the integration. The ICS import and export functionality further addressed Objective 1 by providing a universally compatible pathway for third-party calendar data. Objectives 3 and 4 were fully met; the AES-128 encryption-at-rest architecture, UUID-derived key derivation, bcrypt password hashing, and ON DELETE CASCADE account deletion together constitute a robust Privacy-by-Design implementation compliant with UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act (2018). Objective 5 was fully achieved and validated through twelve dedicated test cases. Objective 6 was partially met; synchronisation was implemented as a user-triggered request rather than the fully automated time-interval background service originally specified. Objective 7 was met through the React SPA dashboard, which aggregates recent notes, upcoming events, and a calendar view into a unified interface. Objective 8 was partially met; comprehensive Postman testing was conducted across all API subsystems, however the absence of a formal automated unit testing framework means coverage falls short of the comprehensive unit testing originally specified.

The one objective entirely descoped was the OCR feature planned under Objective 1. As discussed in Section 5.1, this decision was made deliberately to prioritise the reliable completion of the core backend features within the available timeframe, and the ICS import pathway provides an alternative mechanism for importing external schedule data.

The system demonstrably removes the need for manual timetable entry through automated synchronisation, provides a secure GDPR-compliant notes and events platform, and directly reduces the scheduling burden that Pascoe, Hetrick and Parker (2019) and Pérez-Jorge et al. (2025) identify as a significant contributor to academic stress and impaired executive functioning. To the question of whether the artefact solves the problem it set out to solve, the answer is substantially yes; the core problem of manual timetable data entry has been eliminated for the target demographic, and the unified dashboard addresses the disorganisation cycle described in the literature review.

In terms of commercial viability, the timetable scraper is tightly coupled to UCLan's authentication mechanism and HTML table structure, requiring rearchitecting for deployment at other institutions. A configurable integration layer abstracting the scraping logic behind an institution-agnostic interface would be necessary for any wider commercial deployment. The subscription-based freemium model outlined in the original proposal, centred on daily note limits, remains architecturally feasible given the existing server-side session and settings infrastructure.

docs.title: 6.4 Critical Reflection
docs.text:
The project’s methodology underwent significant changes from the originally proposed to final delivery. The initial waterfall approach outlined in section 3 proved appropriate for the requirements gathering, security-planning, and initial design phase, as these foundational stages were required in the sequential process before any meaningful implementation could proceed. However, the transition to frontend development revealed limitations of maintaining a strictly sequential methodology. As discussed in section 4.2, the decision to pivot from the Vanilla JavaScript to React introduced fundamental architectural changes that were not initially anticipated during planning phases due to inexperience with the React Framework, forcing an adaptive shift from Waterfall to a sprint-based development approach, with concurrent testing rather than deferred validation as originally planned.

In retrospect, this methodology change was essential to the project's success, though it came at a considerable cost. The React migration, while ultimately producing a significantly more maintainable and scalable frontend architecture, consumed development time that had been allocated to feature expansion. Due to React being a technology without prior experience, the time also had to account for the learning curve, which was initially underestimated when learning custom hooks, contexts, state management, and the component lifecycle. Consequently, the OCR functionality initially planned under Objective 1 was deliberately descoped to prioritise reliable completion of the core timetable integration, note-taking and calendar subsystems. This was the correct decision given the project's time constraints, as attempting to implement all originally envisioned features would have risked delivering a partially functional system rather than a robust final product for the show and tell. Supervisor feedback during the MVP demonstration validated this pragmatic approach, confirming that establishing solid foundational functionality was more valuable than pursuing feature completeness at the expense of system stability.

From a technical perspective, the project built upon foundational concepts from previous year's work in Flutter, particularly around state management. However, applying these concepts to a React and Node.js stack required significant adaptation. The practical challenges encountered, particularly implementing HTTP basic authentication for the timetable scraper, choosing a stable library for handling AES-128 cryptographic data flow for encryption-at-rest, and mastering React's hook-based state management, forced deeper engagement with these technologies than any academic coursework had previously demanded. The authentication flow implementation, detailed in Appendix 4, exemplifies this progression; designing the AuthProvider context pattern and the protected routing system required synthesising knowledge from disparate sources and online information to deduce a workable system. The TF-IDF algorithm was straightforward to implement; however, as discussed in Section 5.2, queries consisting primarily of stop words presented an edge case. Standard tokenization filters common terms during preprocessing, causing such queries to return zero results. The implementation addresses this through fallback tokenization that retains stop words when the filtered query produces no terms, alongside post-calculation bonuses for exact title matches, partial title matches, and content matches to ensure relevant notes surface regardless of stop word presence.

However, the project also exposed areas requiring further development. Time estimation for unfamiliar technologies proved consistently optimistic; the React migration alone took nearly double the allocated timeframe, a miscalculation that cascaded through subsequent sprint planning. Additionally, while the systematic Postman-based API testing documented in Appendix 2 provided comprehensive backend validation, the absence of automated frontend testing represents technical debt that would need addressing in any production deployment. The reliance on runtime debugging rather than a formal testing framework such as Jest, while pragmatic given the time constraints, meant that regression testing was manual and potentially incomplete. Edge-case behaviour within individual React components, particularly those handling asynchronous state updates in the calendar view, may have gone undetected without comprehensive unit test coverage.

docs.title: 6.5 Conclusions and Further Work
docs.text:
This project successfully achieved its primary aim of developing a web-based adaptive student study planner that eliminates manual timetable data entry through automated synchronisation. The delivered system demonstrably addresses the core problem identified in the literature review: the preventable academic stress and impaired executive functioning caused by the disorganisation cycle that Pascoe, Hetrick and Parker (2019) and Pérez-Jorge et al. (2025) establish as significant contributors to student wellbeing deterioration. Seven of the eight project objectives were substantially met, with the secure GDPR-compliant architecture, automated timetable scraping, comprehensive note management system, and unified dashboard all functioning reliably as verified through the fifty-seven test cases documented in Appendix 2.

The OCR functionality planned under Objective 1 remains the most significant piece of descoped work requiring future implementation. Integrating Tesseract.js or a comparable optical character recognition library would enable students to upload examination timetable images and automatically extract relevant dates, completing the originally envisioned feature set. However, as discussed in Section 5.1, the deliberate decision to prioritise core functionality over feature completeness ensured the delivery of a robust and reliable foundation upon which such enhancements can be built.

Further work beyond OCR would need to address the institutional portability limitations identified in Section 6.2. The current timetable scraper implementation is tightly coupled to UCLan's specific HTTP basic authentication mechanism and HTML table structure, requiring substantial rearchitecting for deployment at other institutions. Developing a configurable integration layer that abstracts the scraping logic behind an institution-agnostic interface would be essential for commercial viability, potentially using a plugin-based architecture where each institution-specific parser implements a common interface. Additionally, the client-side TF-IDF search algorithm, while preserving privacy by operating exclusively on decrypted in-memory notes, presents scalability limitations as note volume increases. Future iterations could explore server-side search implementations using homomorphic encryption or secure enclaves to maintain privacy guarantees while offloading computational burden from the browser.

The absence of automated frontend testing represents technical debt that would require addressing in any production deployment. Implementing a formal testing framework such as Jest with comprehensive component-level unit tests would ensure regression coverage currently missing from the manual runtime debugging approach. Similarly, the React frontend has not been evaluated against Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (Kirkpatrick et al., 2018), and ensuring WCAG conformance would be necessary for any deployment intended to serve students with disabilities. Production deployment would also require proper HTTPS configuration with valid SSL certificates to secure data transmission between client and server, as the current development environment operates over HTTP, except for HTTPS requests made by the timetable web scraper to the university system.

While the honours degree project may not lead to solving the big global societal problems such as but not limited to: - Climate Change (e.g. Energy Monitor App) - Crime (e.g. Security Notification System) - War (e.g. )
