NodeJS is needed to run JavaScript, the ExpressJS is used to simplify the creation of the server and the process of requests and return responses.

The only logic that needs to be written is the backend handling of the API's processing and data handling logic.

A database driver is also needed / SDK to enable the code to access the database and query it.

docs.title: Statelessness
docs.text:
In REST

The server does not store client state between requests. Each request must include all the information needed to process it, with any required long-term data stored separately (e.g. in a database).

docs.title: OpenAPI
docs.text:
API documentation is essential, or no one would know to use the API. The standard approach to documentation was defined by the OpenAPI Specification as a project of the Linux foundation.

This documentation approach was originally called Swagger until the specification was donated to OpenAPI initiative under the linux foundation, so OpenAPI maintain the current standard but some of their tools used in document creation are called Swagger.

Three common approaches to API documentation: - Design-First - API-First - Code-First

Each of these results in an OPenAPI Specification document (formerly Swagger).

docs.title: Design-First
docs.text: Design-First approach is used when the business works closely with engineers to create a design that satisfies the business requirements either before code is written or potentially to create coding stubs to get a feel for how instances could be used.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: • Common in large organisations that have many complex APIs.

docs.title: API-First
docs.text:
API-First approach is where the endpoints of the documentation/contract are formally defined using an API specification language. I.e. OpenAPI, formally swagger.

The OpenAPI documentation is written in YAML or JSON. Which can be written in either a general text editor, or the swagger web tool.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: • These specifications could be written by product owners or engineers or ideally both together before coding starts

docs.title: Code-First
docs.text:
The Code-First approach, comments need to be added to the openAPI (swagger) YAML style to enable document generation from code comments.

This keeps the documentation with the code and enables it to be manually served as a documentation API endpoint itself for easy access.

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text: • Could be argued that this approach makes the code file messy, although a counter argument is that the code and documentation are in one place.

docs.title: Top Level Elements of OpenAPI Spec
docs.text:
• info - used to inform users and make API discoverable
  • servers - list of servers running the API can run on
  • paths - a list of endpoints, methods, and parameters
  • components - data entities for reuse.
  • tags - used to group endpoints and other elements together. I.e. so they appear as a group in the final documentation i.e. separating payment and user endpoints into their own groups.
  • $ref - reference to reusable blocks (components).

docs.title: KONG API Gateway
docs.text:
The KONG API Gateway is a single point of entry for all applications, therefore removing the need for multiple public IP addresses, and ports. The gateway acts like a reverse proxy forwarding requests to applications, managing what is available to the public.

All interactions between the containers and gateway are private so they don't need encryption unless extra security is required.

flowchart TB
    %% Client
    User["💻 User Laptop"] -->|Public internet<br/>52.151.73.23:80/vm1/frontend.html| Internet((☁ Internet))

    %% Azure network
    subgraph Azure["Azure Private Network"]
        direction TB

        subgraph Public["Public Subnet"]
            Kong["Kong Gateway<br/>Public IP: 52.151.73.23<br/>Port: 80"]
        end

        subgraph Private["Private Subnet"]
            subgraph FrontendVM["Frontend Application VM<br/>Private IP: 10.0.0.9"]
                FrontendContainer["Frontend Docker Container<br/>Port: vm2:4000<br/>Serves frontend.html"]
                BackendContainer["Backend Docker Container<br/>Port: vm1:4001"]
            end
        end

        Kong -->|Internal Azure network<br/>http://10.0.0.9:4000| FrontendContainer
        FrontendContainer <-->|Internal container communication| BackendContainer
    end

    Internet --> Kong

The user connects to the kong's public ip address with the required path. I.e. 52.151.73.23:80/vm1/frontend.html. Kong will forward to the private ip of the vm1 e.g. internally http://10.0.0.9:4000 on the Azure private network to the VM's docker container.

The containers communicate between each other on a private docker network if on the same VM. E.g. Vm2 makes a request to Vm1 at its DNS name vm1:4001.

Important

The gateway and applications are independently scalable.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Avoid replicating functionality such as rate limiting and authentication as Kong plugins can handle these.
  • Single point of entry so HTTPs can be implemented once.
  • Aggregation of API calls E.g. one request to multiple API calls, to reduce bandwidth.
  • Acts as a reverse proxy to protect services from the internet. Users never see the endpoint IP.
  • Operates in two different modes: With Database & Database-Less Mode

docs.title: With Database
docs.text: Typically Postgres or Cassandra which centrally stores all configuration data.

docs.title: Database-Less
docs.text: In db-less config is stored on each node which is simpler for deployment as no database dependency is needed. - Uses declarative code, whereas db approach uses imperative due to API.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Request Routing: route client requests to the appropriate microservices based on the URL or request parameters
  • Load Balancing: load balancing evenly among multiple instances of the same microservice
  • Security: authentication, authorization, and security in one place
  • Rate Limiting: restricts the number of requests per min. Prevents abuse, protects backend resources
  • Throttling: sets rate of processed requests, often by slowing down responses (queue) to smooth traffic spikes
  • Caching: cache microservice responses. Reduce backend load and improve response times
  • Logging and Analytics: provide logging to analyse traffic patterns and API usage
  • Aggregation: aggregate multiple microservice responses into a single client response
  • reduces latency for client as they can make one rather than several individual calls

docs.title: Drawbacks
docs.text:
• Single point of failure. Must be designed to be resilient and scalable - multi-node with load balancer
  • Extra hop may introduce a bit of extra latency
  • Adds complexity to the architecture - needs configuring, monitoring and maintenance (e.g. patching)
  • Extra cost: cost to run and knowledgeable staff to understand the technology so adds to cost
  • Security, this is an advantage but, as all services are accessible from here, it increases the attack surface for hackers so security of the gateway must be carefully designed

docs.title: How To Use
docs.text:
The gateway is simple to use, as routes are defined in the kong.yaml and assocaiated with a forwarding address.

- name: vm1
  url: http://10.0.2.4:4000
  routes:
    - name: vm1
      paths:
        - /vm1
      strip_path: false
VM1 Route in Kong YAML

http:// 52.151.73.23/yin is matched on path then origin changed to http://10.0.2.4:4000/yin because strip_path is false.

- name: vm2
  url: http://10.0.2.4:4001
  routes:
    - name: vm2
      paths:
        - /vm2
      strip_path: true
VM2 Route in Kong YAML

http://52.151.73.23/yang/home is forwarded to http://10.0.2.4:4001/home because strip_path is true so yang is removed.

Important

strip_path is true by default and will remove from the source path, the path element specified in the path property

Example

Quote

  • Can be useful for example, for versioning: kongIP/api/v1-1-2/books/:media could be routed to 10.0.2.3/books/:media by specifying /api/v1-1-2 in the paths and strip_path: true

  • KongIP/api/v1-2-0/books/:media could be routed to 10.0.3.5/books/:media as kong will match the source path to the paths definition to find a match, then remove the source path and replace the IP address

For more complex path filtering, regex can be used

docs.title: Asynchronous VS Synchronous JavaScript
docs.text:
JavaScript is single-threaded, meaning it has one call stack and executes one task at a time.

The difference between synchronous and asynchronous code is that synchronous code blocks the execution of subsequent code until the current task finishes, whereas asynchronous code can start a task and continue executing other code without waiting for that task to complete.

Once the asynchronous task completes, its callback or Promise is handled when the call stack is empty.

docs.title: Asynchronous Messaging
docs.text:
Asynchronous Messaging involves microservices posting messages to a queue.

A producer sends a message to a message broker, which stores it in a queue. The producer does not wait for the consumer to process the message and can continue executing immediately.

docs.text:

  • Dynamic FIFO data structure.
  • M1 doesn't need to know if M2 can handle a large amount of messages at once.
  • M1 is unaffected if M2 does down.

docs.title: Basic Information
docs.text: RabbitMQ uses the AMQP (Advanced Message Queueing Protocol) standard which is a platform agnostic protocol to transfer information between applications. The source and destination are the Producer and Consumer.

docs.title: Connection
docs.text: This is a network connection between an app and the queue. Similar to a database connection

docs.title: Channel
docs.text:
Virtual connection inside a connection. Multiple channels can be created within a single connection, allowing for concurrent operations and communication between different parts of a client application

Example

May have one channel for produced messages and another for consuming messages within the same connection to RabbitMQ

docs.title: Queue
docs.text: A FIFO-based message storage and delivery component ▹ It holds messages sent by producers until they are consumed by consumers

docs.title: RabbitMQ Docker Container
docs.text:
It can implement queues and message routing through a message exchange component which can route messages to various queues based on a routing key.

It has a management interface to setup and monitor the queues

docs.title: Producer / Publisher
docs.text: An application that sends a message to the broker. The broker confirms the message is queued.

docs.title: Consumer / Subscriber
docs.text: Application that consumes the message. Consumer informs rabbitmq that it received the message (acknowledges it) so it can be removed from the queue.

docs.title: Exchange
docs.text: Receives messages from producers and routes them to the correct queue based on rules associated with a routing key.

docs.title: Routing Key
docs.text: This can be a word, series of words, wildcard. e.g. all messages that contain pr* as a post code are sent to a queue for consumers of Preston based messages e.g. for a survey.

docs.title: Virtual Host
docs.text: Segregates applications using the same rabbitmq instance. Think of it as separate broker instances each with different permissions and credentials but built into a single instance, e.g. a single container.

docs.title: Direct
docs.text: A producer and consumer are using one queue based on the binding key (we use this & default exchange).

docs.title: Topic
docs.text: A wildcard match between the routing key and the routing pattern determines the queue. Like the earlier example.

docs.title: Fanout
docs.text:
Routes a message to all the queues. E.g. message sent to multiple microservices - pub / sub pattern

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text: The purpose of this report is to present the formal specification and modelling of a real-time temperature regulation system designed for smart laboratory equipment. The system monitors multiple temperature sensors and controls heating and cooling components to maintain stable operating conditions.

docs.title: 2.1. Requirements Table
docs.text: Requirement Type Requirement Purpose Functional System must continuously read temperature values from multiple sensors. Ensure real-time data is maintained throughout the equipment. Functional System must compare each sensor reading to a configurable target temperature range. Determine whether current state deviates from acceptable operational limits. Functional System must activate cooling or heating components immediately when temperature deviates from set range. Restore environment to target state within acceptable timeframe. Functional System must log readings and monitor performance to identify potential faults, triggering alerts when thresholds are breached. Enable immediate safety interventions when system deviates from normal operation. Non-Functional System must ensure all temperature readings are accurate within ±0.1°C. Maintain integrity of sensitive laboratory equipment. Non-Functional System must respond to temperature changes within 1 second. Prevent breaching of temperature threshold. Non-Functional System must ensure consistent operation under varying conditions and be resilient against errors; heating elements default to OFF on failure. Prevent uncontrolled behaviour and ensure fail-safe reliability.

docs.title: 2.2. System Decomposition
docs.text:
The first module to decompose in the system is the SensorInput module, which acquires the temperature data from multiple sensors. The module detects and handles sensor failures or disconnections and communicates these events to the SystemMonitoring module.

The second module is the TemperatureController module, which compares sensor readings against the configurable target temperature range and determines the appropriate corrective action, whether heating, cooling, or in standby mode. The module implements control logic to maintain system stability and must operate within the 1-second real-time constraint to ensure temperature deviations are addressed promptly.

The third module is the ActuatorControl module, which translates control decisions from the TemperatureController into commands for heating and cooling components. It executes these commands and manages the fail-safe mechanism to ensure all heating elements default to OFF in the event of system failure.

The fourth module is the SystemMonitoring module, which logs all sensor readings and system events. The module monitors performance against defined thresholds and triggers alerts when temperature deviations exceed acceptable limits or sensor failures occur.

docs.title: 4.1. JML/OCL Specification
docs.text:
// SystemStatus.java
public enum SystemStatus {
    HEATING,
    COOLING,
    IDLE,
    ERROR
}

// TemperatureController.java
public class TemperatureController {
    private float currentTemp;
    private float targetTemp;
    private float tolerance;
    private SystemStatus status;
    private boolean isOn;

    // CLASS INVARIANT
    //@ invariant -50.0 <= currentTemp && currentTemp <= 150.0;
    /**
     * Sets the target temperature
     * @param t the new target temperature
     */
    //@ requires currentTemp < t;  // PRECONDITION
    //@ ensures isOn == true;      // POSTCONDITION
    //@ ensures targetTemp == t;   // POSTCONDITION
    public void setTarget(float t)
    {
        this.targetTemp = t;
        this.isOn = true;
    }

    /**
     * Updates the control loop
     */
    //@ requires isOn == true;
    //@ ensures status != null;
    public void updateLoop() 
    {
        // Check temperature and adjust
        if (currentTemp < targetTemp - tolerance) 
        {
            status = SystemStatus.HEATING;
        } 
        else if (currentTemp > targetTemp + tolerance) 
        {
            status = SystemStatus.COOLING;
        } 
        else 
        {
            status = SystemStatus.IDLE;
        }
    }

    /**
     * Monitors system safety
     */
    //@ requires -50.0 <= currentTemp && currentTemp <= 150.0;
    //@ ensures \result == true || status == SystemStatus.ERROR;
    public boolean monitorSafety() 
    {
        if (currentTemp < -50.0 || currentTemp > 150.0) 
        {
            status = SystemStatus.ERROR;
            return false;
        }
        return true;
    }

docs.title: 4.2. Design by Contract Principles
docs.text:
Design by Contract (DbC) is a software developmental approach which defines precise and mathematically verifiable specifications for software components. The DbC approach establishes contractual relationships between software modules through preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. The preconditions specify conditions that must be satisfied before method execution, while the postconditions define guarantees provided upon successful completion. The invariants establish properties that remain true throughout the object lifetime. This methodology ensures software components interact correctly and prevents invalid system states (Meyer, 1992).

The class invariant in the temperature regulation program represents the temperature bounds, which reflect the regulated temperature range acceptable for the physical hardware of the sensors. The TemperatureController class constrains the currentTemp attribute to remain within -50.0°C to 150.0°C. This invariant is specified in JML (Java Modelling Language) as: //@ invariant -50.0 <= currentTemp && currentTemp <= 150.0;. The invariant must hold true before and after every public method call (Leavens et al., 2006). This constraint prevents the system from operating if it falls outside of the temperature boundary limits, acting as a safety mechanism that protects hardware components from damage due to extreme temperature conditions.

The other formal language specification provided in the code is OCL (Object Constraint Language), which expresses constraints on object-oriented models that cannot be captured through visuals alone. OCL provides precise mathematical notation for defining invariants, preconditions, and postconditions on class operations, serving as the declarative language that complements UML structural diagrams (Object Management Group, 2014).

OCL is used in the temperature control system to formally specify constraints on the UML class diagram that define valid system states and operation behaviors. The class diagram implements an invariant constraint on the TemperatureController which ensures the currentTemp attribute remains within the safe operating range of -50.0°C to 150.0°C, acting as a boundary condition that must hold throughout all system operations. The precondition constraint on the setTarget() method specifies that currentTemp must be less than the target temperature before the method executes, providing a validation rule that prevents unnecessary heating activation when the system already meets or exceeds the desired temperature. The postcondition constraints guarantee that after setTarget() completes, the isOn attribute is set to true and the targetTemp stores the specified value, providing state guarantees that ensure correct system configuration. OCL constraints attached to the class diagram provide design-level specifications that guide implementation and serve as verification criteria during development, effectively creating formal documentation that bridges the gap between system requirements and executable code.

JML and OCL serve complementary roles in the formal specification process, operating as tools at different stages of the software development lifecycle. OCL operates at the design level by specifying constraints on UML models before implementation begins, capturing system requirements and design decisions (Object Management Group, 2014). JML operates at the implementation level by annotating Java source code with executable specifications that can be verified during compilation and runtime, translating design constraints into enforceable programming contracts (Leavens et al., 2006). The temperature control system uses OCL to specify constraints on the UML class diagram and JML to implement these same constraints in the Java code, utilizing a dual-specification approach that maintains consistency between design models and executable implementation. Both languages share similar syntax for expressing preconditions, postconditions, and invariants, providing a common foundation that enables seamless transition from design to code. The OCL constraint specifying the temperature invariant on the UML diagram corresponds directly to the JML invariant annotation in the TemperatureController class, ensuring design specifications are faithfully implemented in the final system.

Design by Contract principles prevent software faults through multiple defensive mechanisms that enforce correctness at method boundaries. The preconditions act as entry barriers which reject invalid method invocations before execution begins, serving as the first line of defense that prevents the system from processing incorrect inputs that could lead to undefined behavior (Meyer, 1992). For example, the setTarget() method precondition requires currentTemp < targetTemp, which prevents unnecessary system activation when the current temperature already meets or exceeds the desired value, providing validation that stops wasteful operations and potential state corruption. The postconditions provide verifiable guarantees about method behavior, ensuring operations complete correctly or fail explicitly rather than leaving the system in undefined states. The setTarget() postconditions guarantee that isOn becomes true and targetTemp stores the specified value, providing state guarantees that prevent scenarios where a target is configured but the system remains inactive. The class invariant establishes a continuous validation mechanism that must hold before and after every operation, providing the foundation that prevents the temperature control system from entering physically impossible or hardware-damaging states. When any contract is violated, the system immediately rejects the operation and provides diagnostic information rather than continuing execution with invalid data, utilizing a fail-fast approach that stops faults at their source before they can propagate through the system and cause cascading failures (Meyer, 1992).

The formal specifications enable comprehensive verification and testing approaches which significantly improve system reliability and correctness assurance. Static analysis tools examine the JML annotations and verify that method implementations satisfy their contracts without executing the code, providing a mathematical proof approach that can guarantee correctness for critical operations before deployment (Leavens et al., 2006). Runtime assertion checking validates that preconditions are satisfied before method execution and postconditions hold after completion, acting as a runtime defense mechanism that detects contract violations during development and testing phases. When contract violations occur during testing, the system provides immediate feedback identifying the specific condition that failed and the exact location of the violation, offering a diagnostic capability that accelerates debugging and fault localization by pinpointing errors at their source.

The formal contracts enable development of systematic test suites that validate precondition enforcement, confirm postcondition guarantees, and verify invariant preservation across sequences of operations. Test cases can verify that setTarget() correctly rejects calls when currentTemp >= targetTemp, confirming the precondition enforcement works as specified. The specifications provide objective criteria for measuring test adequacy and enable automated test generation tools to produce test inputs which exercise boundary conditions and edge cases, providing a comprehensive testing strategy that ensures the temperature control system handles all valid operational scenarios correctly while properly rejecting all invalid inputs that could compromise system integrity or hardware safety.

docs.title: 5. Concurrency & Real-Time Behaviour
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Main
    participant Scheduler as ScheduledExecutorService
    participant Controller as TemperatureController
    participant Actuators

    Note over Main: Initialize Hardware & Controller
    Main->>Controller: setTarget(22.0)

    Note over Main: Start Scheduler (2 threads)

    Main->>Scheduler: scheduleAtFixedRate(controlTask, 1s)
    Main->>Scheduler: scheduleAtFixedRate(tempChangeTask, 2s)

    loop Every 1 second
        Scheduler->>Controller: updateLoop()
        Controller->>Actuators: check sensors & toggle actuators
    end

    loop Every 2 seconds
        Scheduler->>Controller: setTarget(nextTemp)
    end

    Note over Main: After 20 seconds

    Main->>Scheduler: shutdown()
    Scheduler->>Controller: deactivate()
Sequence Diagram for scheduling execution of the temperature control system.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> IDLE

    IDLE --> HEATING : currentTemp < (target - tolerance)
    HEATING --> IDLE : currentTemp >= target

    IDLE --> COOLING : currentTemp > (target + tolerance)
    COOLING --> IDLE : currentTemp <= target

    IDLE --> ERROR : Temp < -50°C OR Temp > 150°C
    HEATING --> ERROR : Temp < -50°C OR Temp > 150°C
    COOLING --> ERROR : Temp < -50°C OR Temp > 150°C

    ERROR --> SafetyShutdown
    SafetyShutdown --> DeactivateActuators
    DeactivateActuators --> [*]
State Transition Diagram showing the temperature controller's operating modes and transitions between idle, heating, cooling, and error states.

The temperature regulation system is designed as a concurrent application to meet the strict real-time requirement of responding to environmental changes within one second. To achieve this, the implementation utilises a ScheduledExecutorService with a thread pool of size two, which ensures that the monitoring of sensors and the execution of control logic occur independently of administrative tasks like changing target parameters (Oracle, 2024a). The control task is scheduled at a fixed rate of 1 second, providing a deterministic execution window which prevents temperature drift and satisfies the performance constraints defined in the requirements.

// Main.java
// Monitors system safety
// requires -50.0 <= currentTemp && currentTemp <= 150.0;
//@ ensures \result == true || status == SystemStatus.ERROR;
public boolean monitorSafety()
{
   if (currentTemp < -50.0 || currentTemp > 150.0)
   {
       status = SystemStatus.ERROR;
       return false;
   }
   return true;
}

To manage communication and synchronisation between these concurrent tasks, the system employs thread-safe constructs which protect the integrity of the data. For instance, an AtomicInteger is used to track the index of target temperature changes, which prevents race conditions that could occur if multiple threads attempted to update the system's operational state simultaneously (Oracle, 2024b). This approach ensures that the TemperatureController always operates on consistent data when executing its updateLoop(), which maintains the integrity of the feedback loop between the TemperatureSensor and the Actuator classes.

Potential concurrency issues such as deadlocks or race conditions are mitigated by the system’s modular design which isolates critical tasks. By encapsulating the 'hardware' dependencies—the heater, cooler, and sensors—within the TemperatureController and using a single-threaded execution for the update cycle, the system effectively avoids resource contention. Furthermore, the fail-safe mechanism ensures that in the event of a system failure or scheduled shutdown, all actuators are explicitly deactivated which prevents uncontrolled heating or cooling and fulfils the non-functional requirement for resilient and safe operation.

docs.title: 6. Conclusion
docs.text: The development of the laboratory temperature regulation system demonstrates the effectiveness of integrating formal methods with real-time software engineering to ensure high-integrity operation. By applying Design by Contract principles, the system establishes a robust safety framework where JML and OCL constraints act as mathematical guarantees for software correctness. The implementation of the temperature safety invariant, which constrains the system to operate within the defined limits of -50oC and -150oC ensures that the 'hardware' components are protected from extreme conditions that could lead to physical damage. Furthermore, the modular decomposition of the system into distinct units for sensor input, control logic, and actuator management facilitates a maintainable architecture which supports complex concurrent behaviours. The use of real-time scheduling ensures that the system remains responsive to environmental fluctuations within the required one-second threshold, which maintains the stable conditions necessary for sensitive laboratory equipment. This transition from design-level OCL specifications to executable JML annotations provides a consistent verification path, which ultimately reduces the risk of runtime failures and enhances the overall reliability of the embedded control unit.

Choose one operation and formally express its precondition and postcondition to show how it affects system state.

docs.title: Part 4 - Implementing a Producer-Consumer in Java
docs.text:
Task 4.1 - Implement a Shared Buffer

Create a class Buffer with: - A fixed-size array (size = 5) - produce(item) method - consume() method

Use synchronized, wait(), notifyAll()

Task 4.2 - Implement Producer and Consumer Threads

Create the following: - Producer implements Runnable - Consumer implements Runnable - Producer - Generates 10 items - Consumer - Consumes 10 items

Start both threads from a main() method.

Code Example

public class ProducerAndConsumer
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        Buffer buffer = new Buffer();
        new Thread(new Producer(buffer)).start();
        new Thread(new Consumer(buffer)).start();
    }
}

class Buffer
{
    private String[] items = new String[5];
    private int count = 0;

    private sychronized void produce(String item)
    {
        while (count == items.length)
        {
            try
            { wait(); }
        }

        items[count++] = item;
        notifyAll();
    }

    public synchronized String consume()
    {
        while (count == 0)
        {
            try { wait(); }
        }
        String item = items[--count];
        notifyAll();
        return item;
    }
}

docs.title: Formality Benefits
docs.text:
• Precision
  • Clarity Specification
  • Forces greater thought
  • More chance that specification is correct
  • Identify inconsistencies in specification
  • Proof covers "all" possibilities
  • Tests only cover a sample of the possibilities
  • Potential for automated checking for
  • Specification Consistency
  • Proof

docs.title: Formality Problems
docs.text:
• Difficult to understand
  • Mathematical language
  • Difficult to write
  • Similar to programming
  • Errors still possibly
  • Complex
  • Especially if it covers all hardware details
  • Unable to express all requirements.

docs.title: What are Formal Methods
docs.text:
Formal methods use math to prove and verify that software works.

The reason formal methods are used to prove that a program works as intended.

docs.title: Formal Benefits
docs.text:
• find mistakes early
  • ensure reliable and safe systems
  • verify that software acts with intended behaviour.

docs.title: Application Examples
docs.text: Formal methods are utilised in numerous applications, some examples are as follows: - Safety-Critical Systems - Banking Software - Aerospace - Healthcare Systems

docs.title: Formal Methods Over-Time
docs.text:
Developed in the 1980s (Z & VDM (Vienna Development Method) popular) - These used abstract specifications (based on mathematical models) to specify how software should behave. - Developers would refine the abstract models and turn into code via series of refinement steps - Each refinement verified by formal reasoning to ensure no errors were introduced.

  • Much later systems like JML aim to make specification more "programmer friendly"
  • Over-Time researchers realised that traditional formal methods were too mathematical and difficult for the everyday programmer to use.

docs.title: Example Formal Method
docs.text:
double squareRoot(double val) // Signature
requires: val >= 0 // Pre-Condition
ensures: val == result * result // Post-Condition
SquareRoot Function Formal Method Example

docs.title: Example Explanation
docs.text:
Signature - Describes the function name, parameters, and return type. - The function squareRoot takes a double parameter for the variable val.

Pre-Condition: Defines what must be true for the function to run - val >= 0 - the input value must be greater than or equal to 0.

Post-Condition: Defines what must be true after the function finishes. - val == result * result - the returned value, when squared, must equal the original input. (Proving Correctness

docs.title: Applying Formal Methods
docs.text:
A systematic application of: - Mathematical notations - Mathematical reasoning (proofs)

The notations can be used for: - Functional requirements – defining what the system should do - Program design – outlining how the system will achieve it - Program proving – mathematically verifying that the design works correctly

The proofs can then be applied to: - Code development – ensuring the code correctly implements the design - Verification – confirming that the final code matches the specified behaviour

docs.title: Informal Specifications
docs.text:
Informal Specifications describe what a system or program should do without mathematics or formal logic.

Example

"When the user clicks a button I want them to see a message"

Describes what should happen, but is not specific or precise.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text:
There are issues that present themselves when working with informal specifications.

Some issues of informal specifications are as follows: - Ambiguity - Informal language can create different interpretations of the requirement. - Incompleteness - Often error error conditions - Inconsistency - Contradiction between two parts of the specifications - Lack of Expressive Power - Language cannot express intention - Somethings can be expressed through example

docs.title: Design By Contract
docs.text: Design by contract is a programming approach where the pre and post conditions define a contract between the method (which can also be referred to as the supplier) and the client (the code that calls it).

docs.title: The Contract Relationship
docs.text:
The Client must ensure the pre-condition is true before calling the method.

The Supplier can assume the pre-condition has been met, and must make the post-condition true before returning.

The Client after call can assume the post-condition is accurate and does not need to know how the solution was achieved.

docs.title: Contracts with JML
docs.text:
JML is a java-based language supporting the creation of "programmer friendly" specification and verification of methods and/or classes.

JML is supported in Visual Studio Code Extension

docs.title: Modelling System Behaviour
docs.text:
• Many systems can be described in terms of states and transitions.
  • A STD (State Transition Diagram) models how the system moves between states.
  • Arrows represent transitions; labels represent events or conditions that trigger them.
  • States are high-level abstractions, they describe what the system is doing and not how it has changed internally.

docs.title: Understanding System State
docs.text:
• A system's state is a snapshot of all its variable values at a specific time.
  • When an operation executes, it may modify variables causing a change in state.

Ordering Example

```mermaid stateDiagram-v2

direction LR [] → Created Created → Paid : Payment Received Created → Cancelled : Cancel Requested Paid → Shipped : Order Dispatched Paid → Cancelled : Cancel Requested Shipped → Delivered : Order Delivered Delivered → [] Cancelled → [*] ```

  • Variable Status in an order object:
  • Initial Status: Created
  • After Payment Status: Paid

  • After Delivery Status: Delivered

  • States: Created -> Paid -> Shipped -> Delivered -> Cancelled

  • Events: Payment Received -> Order Dispatched -> Cancel Requested

docs.title: State-Based Specification
docs.text:
• A state-based specification expresses the rules governing how state variables change.
  • Defined by a mathematical relationship between:
  • Variable values before an operation and

  • Variable values after an operation

  • These relationships are expressed as predicates which can be reasoned about logically.

  • This provides a precise description of system behaviour focusing on what must happen and not how it is implemented.

docs.title: State-Diagram Example
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> NEW 
    NEW --> RUNNABLE : start() 
    RUNNABLE --> RUNNING 
    RUNNING --> RUNNABLE : yield() 
    RUNNABLE --> BLOCKED : synchronized release 
    BLOCKED --> RUNNING : synchronized 
    RUNNING --> WAITING : wait() 
    WAITING --> RUNNABLE : notify(0) 
    RUNNABLE --> TIMED_WAITING : join(long) 
    RUNNING --> TIMED_WAITING : sleep(long) 
    TIMED_WAITING --> RUNNABLE : wait(long) 
    RUNNING --> DEAD : run end normal 
    RUNNING --> DEAD : abnormal end 
    DEAD --> [*]

docs.title: Predicates in Specifications
docs.text:
• A predicate is a logical statement that can either be true or false.
  • Used to express conditions, constraints or properties of system states.

docs.title: Where Predicates Used
docs.text:
• Pre-Conditions -> Must hold before execution
  • Post-Conditions -> Must hold after execution
  • Invariants -> Must hold always when the system is stable.
/*@
  @ requires x > 0; // Predicate: Pre-Condition
  @ ensures \result == x * x* // Predicate: Post-Condition
  @*/
public int square(int x)
{
    return x * x;
}

Here x > 0 and result == x * x are predicates defining logical truths about program states.

docs.title: Quantifiers
docs.text:
• Used to reason about collections or arrays.

  • Two key forms:

  • ForAll (∀) every element satisfies a condition. 
// ∀x: x > 0
List<Integer> nums = List.of(1,2,3,4);
boolean allPositive = nums.stream().allMatch(x -> x > 0);
  • Exists (∃) at least one element satisfies it.
List<Integer> nums = List.of(10,50,150,70);
boolean anyLarge = nums.stream().anyMatch(x -> x > 100);

docs.title: Design by Contract (DbC) Concept
docs.text:
• Builds on the principle of modularity and clear interfaces.
  • Traditionally an interface defines syntax (e.g. method signatures) but not behaviour.
  • DbC extends interfaces with behaviour specifications using contracts.

docs.title: Interfaces in Programming
docs.text:
• This defines what methods exist but not what they guarantee.
  • Design by Contract adds this missing behavioural dimension

Example

```java

// Interface defining the contract public interface Account {

void deposit(double amount); // Pre-condition: amount > 0

void withdraw(double amount) throws Exception; // Pre-condition: amount > 0 && amount <= balance

double getBalance(); // Post-condition: balance >= 0 }

// Class implementing the contract // Class invariant: balance >= 0 public class BankAccount implements Account {

private double balance = 0;

@Override public void deposit(double amount) { assert amount > 0 : "Precondition failed: amount must be positive";

 balance += amount;

 assert balance >= 0 : "Invariant violated: balance negative";

}

@Override public void withdraw(double amount) throws Exception { assert amount > 0 && amount <= balance : "Precondition failed: invalid withdrawal";

   balance -= amount;

   assert balance >= 0 : "Invariant violated: balance negative";

}

@Override public double getBalance() { return balance; } } ```

docs.title: Core Idea of DbC
docs.text:
• A contract defines obligations and guarantees between two parties:
  • Client (Caller): Must ensure the pre-condition holds before invoking the method.

  • Supplier (Callee): Guarantees the post-condition after execution.

  • The client doesn't need to know how the method works, only what it promises to deliver.

docs.title: Using Contracts To Specify Behaviour
docs.text:
• Precondition - What must be true before the method runs.
  • Postcondition - What must be true after the method runs.
  • Invariant - Must always hold for the object's valid state.

Contract by Behaviour Example

```java public class BankAccount {

private double balance; // Class Invariant: balance >= 0 public void deposit(double amount) { assert amount > 0 : "Precondition failed: amount must be positive"; double oldBalance = balance; balance += amount; assert balance == oldBalance + amount : "Postcondition failed: balance not updated correctly"; assert balance >= 0 : "Invariant violated: balance negative"; } public void withdraw(double amount) { assert amount > 0 && amount <= balance : "Precondition failed: invalid withdrawal"; double oldBalance = balance; balance -= amount; assert balance == oldBalance - amount : "Postcondition failed: balance not updated correctly"; assert balance >= 0 : "Invariant violated: balance negative"; } } ```

docs.title: Writing Post-Conditions
docs.text:
• Postconditions link the state before and after execution.
  • Postconditions must be pure, they cannot modify the program state.
public class BankAccount 
{

    private double balance;

    public void deposit(double amount) 
    {
        double oldBalance = balance;
        balance += amount;

        // Postcondition: balance must increase by the deposit amount
        assert balance == oldBalance + amount
            : "Postcondition failed: balance not updated correctly";
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount) 
    {
        double oldBalance = balance;
        balance -= amount;

        // Postcondition: balance must decrease by the withdrawal amount
        assert balance == oldBalance - amount
            : "Postcondition failed: balance not updated correctly";
    }
}

docs.title: Specifying Change & Stability
docs.text:
• When writing postconditions it's important to specify:
  • What changes the part of the state that should be modified

  • What stays the same, properties that must remain unchanged.

  • Omitting "what doesn't change" can lead to incomplete or ambiguous specifications.

docs.title: Handling Exceptional Behaviour
docs.text:
• Postconditions can also describe what happens when operations fail.
  • Different outcomes (normal or exceptional) can be expressed with implication (->) and logical AND (^).
  • For example, specifying postconditions for exceptions ensures consistent system state in the error cases.
public class BankAccount
{
    private double balance;

    public void withdraw(double amount) throws Exception
    {
        if (amount <= 0)
        {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Amount must be positive")
        }

        if (amount > balance)
        {
            throw new Exception("Insufficient Funds");
        }

        balance -= amount;
    }
}

docs.title: Class Invariants
docs.text:
• Class invariants are predicates that must always hold true for an object, except temporarily while a method is executing.

For Example

Invariant: balance > 0 must always hold. They define what it means for an object to be in a valid or consistent state. Class invariants are checked before and after every public method call.

JML invariants are written using the invariant clause within a class.

Example

public class BankAccount
{
    private double balance;

    public BankAccount(double initialDeposit)
    {
        this.balance = initialDeposit
        assert invariant();
    }

    public void despoit(double amount)
    {
        if (amount <= balance)
        {
            balance -= amount;
        }
        assert invariant();
    }

    public void withdraw(double amount)
    {
        if (amount <= balance)
        {
            balance -= amount;
        }

    assert invariant();
    }

    private boolean invariant()
    {
        // Class Invariant: balance should never be negative
        return balance >= 0;
    }
}

docs.title: Aims & Objectives
docs.text:
• To understand the role and importance of formal specification methods in software engineering.
  • To describe key techniques such as set notation, sequences, and recursion.
  • To understand how formal methods improve software reliability and safety.
  • To explore modern tools and real-world applications of formal methods in industry.

docs.title: Formal Specification Concepts
docs.text:
• Sets
  • Sequences
  • Recursion

docs.title: Sets
docs.text:
• A set is a collection of distinct elements

  • Used to describe system states, valid inputs, or relationships.

  • A collection of elements which:

  • Unordered

  • Contains no duplications

  • {6, ..., 9} represents a spread operator meaning {6, 7, 8, 9}

  • {} or Ø meaning empty set.

  • Other mathematical data types also exist, such as sequences, which do preserve order and may allow duplicates

docs.title: Set Operators
docs.text:
• ∈ means “is an element of”
  • Example: 2 ∈ {1, 2, 5}
  • ∉ means “is not an element of”
  • Example: 1 ∉ {2, 3, 5}
  • ⊆ means “is a subset of”
  • Example: {1, 2} ⊆ {1, 2, 3}
  • ⊂ means “is a proper subset of”
  • Example: {1, 2} ⊂ {1, 2, 3}
  • ∪ means union (elements in either set)
  • ∩ means intersection (elements common to both sets)

docs.title: Set Notation Example
docs.text:
A banking system: - {A1, A2, A3} representing all active customer Accounts. - another set, z = {A2}, might represent accounts with negative balance.

  • Overdrawn (⊆) Accounts This means:
  • Every element in Overdrawn is also an element of Accounts

  • A2 ∈ Overdrawn and A2 ∈ Accounts

  • We can verify the subset relationship:

  • ∀x (x ∈ Overdrawn ⇒ x ∈ Accounts)

  • This notation allows us to clearly describe system states and reason about conditions such as:

  • "All overdrawn accounts must be valid customer accounts”

docs.title: Sequence
docs.text:
• A sequence is an ordered collection.
  • Represents event histories, message queues, or ordered data.

docs.title: Sequence Notation
Recursion
docs.text:
• Recursion defines an operation in terms of itself.
  • Essential for reasoning about inductive definitions and loops.
public static int fac(int n) {
    return (n == 0) ? 1 : n * fac(n - 1);
}

docs.title: Why Use Formal Methods?
docs.text:
• Specify and prove system properties mathematically.
  • Detect inconsistencies early.
  • Improve reliability and safety.
  • Support certification for critical systems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Understand UML class and behavioural diagrams for system modelling
  • Learn how to apply OCL constraints: invariants, preconditions, and postconditions
  • Apply OCL to real-world examples (e.g. BankAccount)
  • Model system behaviour using sequence or activity diagrams

docs.title: UML Class Modelling
docs.text:
Purpose - Represent system structure: classes, attributes, operations and relationships

Key UML Elements: - Classes & Attributes - Associations, Multiplicities, Aggregations, & Compositions - Inheritance / Generalisation

BankAccount

Class: BankAccount Attributes: - balance: Real - accountNumber: String - Operations: - deposit(amount: Real) - withdraw(amount: Real) - Association: Customer -> BankAccount (1..*, 1..1)

docs.title: What is the Object Constraint Language (OCL)
docs.text:
• A declarative language used to describe rules about UML models.
  • Designed to be used alongside UML models
  • Based on set theory and first-order logic
  • Used for constraints (Invariants), behavioural specification (pre/post), derived values
  • Ensures model consistency and integrity:
  • No side effects
  • Purely evaluative (no data modifications)

docs.title: Why UML Alone Is Not Enough?
docs.text:
• Missing constraints
  • Ambiguity in natural language

docs.title: Object Constraint Language (OCL)
docs.text:
OCL is a formal declarative, side-effect language.

Purpose - Express constraints that cannot be captured in diagrams.

Types of OCL Expressions: - Invariants - must always hold - Preconditions - must be true before operation - Postconditions - must be true after operation

docs.title: Background OCL?
docs.text:
• OCL was created to make UML models more precise and verifiable by expressing constraints that diagrams alone couldn't show
  • It started as a part of the UML standardisation process in the mid-1990s

docs.title: Why OCL?
docs.text:
• UML alone is insufficient to specify detailed constraints
  • Examples: "No negative values", "deprived attribute formulas", "operation contracts"
  • Complements UML designs with precision
  • Formally specifies rules that cannot be shown visually
  • Improves consistency, traceability, and verifiability of models
  • OCL bridges the gap

docs.title: Core Principles of OCL
docs.text: Principle Meaning Formal Meaning Formal Syntax and semantics are mathematically defined — no ambiguity Side-effect Free OCL expressions only query the model — they never change system state Declarative States what must hold, not how to implement it Rooted in FOL & Set Theory Uses quantifiers (forAll, exists), logic (and, or, implies) and set operations Model-Level, not Code-Level Attached to UML artifacts (class, operation, association) rather than implementation

docs.title: OCL Syntax Basics
docs.text:
• Expressions begin with a UML context
  • Use self to refer to current object
  • Operations similar to programming languages
  • and, or, not, implies

  • =, <>, <, >

  • Collection operations: forAll, exists, size, select, collect

docs.title: Types of OCL Constraints
docs.text:
• Invariants - must always hold
  • Preconditions - must be true before operation
  • Postconditions - must be true after operation

docs.title: OCL & First-Order Logic
docs.text:
• OCL constraints are not invented in isolation, they are grounded in formal logic.
  • Formal link enables precision, tool support and verifiability.

docs.title: Key First-Order Logic (FOL) Concepts
docs.text:
FOL Concept Symbol OCL Equivalent / Usage Universal quantifier \(\forall\) forAll() over collections Existential quantifier \(\exists\) exists() over collections Logical AND \(\land\) and Logical OR \(\lor\) or Negation \(\neg\) not implication \(\rightarrow\) implies ## Overview on FOL First-Order Logic is a formal system used to describe objects, their properties and relationships.

Provides a precise, unambiguous way to specify conditions, constraints and rules.

Key Concepts: - Predicates: Properties or Relationships E.g. isCustomer© or owns(c, a) - c being the customer variable - a being the account variable.

\[\forall a \in \text{BankAccount}: \text{balance}(a) \ge 0\]

docs.title: OCL Preconditions Example
docs.text:
BankAccount(withdraw) - context BankAccount::withdraw(amount: Real) pre SufficientFunds: amount > 0 and amount <= self.balance - Withdrawals are only allowed if the account has enough funds.

OCL & FOL Withdraw Example

context bankAccount::withdraw(amount: Double) pre SufficientFunds: amount <= self.balance

∀a ∈ BankAccount: balance(a) ≥ 0

∀a ∈ BankAccount, ∀amt ∈ Double: deposit(a, amt) → balance(a)_after = balance(a)_before + amt

docs.title: OCL Postconditions Example
docs.text:
BankAccount(deposit) - context BankAccount::deposit(amount: Real) post BalanceIncreased: self.balance = self.balance@pre + amount - After deposit, the balance increases by the deposited amount.

OCL & FOL Deposit Example

```OCL

context BankAccount::deposit(amount: Double) post BalanceIncreased: self.balance = self.balance@pre + amount

```FOL
 ∀a ∈ BankAccount, ∀amt ∈ Double: deposit(a, amt) → balance(a)_after = balance(a)_before + amt

docs.title: OCL Invariants Example
docs.text: BankAccount(balance) - context BankAccount inv PositiveBalance >= 0 - The balance must never be negative.

docs.title: UML Behavioural Modelling
docs.text:
Purpose - Show dynamic behaviour of the system.

Diagram Types: - Sequence Diagram: Interactions between objectives over time - Activity Diagram: flow of operations or control

E.g. - BankAccount despoit sequence: - Customer calls deposit(amount) - BankAccount updates balance - Notify Customer

docs.title: Sequence Diagram Example
docs.text:
• Shows interactions between objects in time order
  • Focus on messages / calls across lifelines
  • Useful for scenario walkthroughs (e.g. use-case realisation)

docs.title: Combing UML & OCL
docs.text:
• UML Diagrams show structure and behaviour
  • OCL adds formal precision: invariants, preconditions, postconditions

Example mapping: - UML ElementOCL ConstraintBankAccount.balanceinv PositiveBalanceBankAccount.withdraw()pre SufficientFunds, post BalanceUpdatedFan.activate()

docs.title: Positive for...
docs.text:
• Improves model accuracy
  • Detects design errors early
  • Supports tool-based verification
  • Encourages disciplined thinking

docs.title: However...
docs.text:
• Can be complex for beginners
  • Doesn't specify system behaviour (not executable)
  • Requires modelling tool support

docs.title: Strengths
docs.text:
• Precise & unambiguous - removes informal interpretation
  • Declarative & side-effect free - safe for specification
  • Fits UML natively - Attaches to classes, operations, states
  • Rich Expressiveness - Supports FOL-style quantifiers & sets
  • Good for Contracts - Invariants, Pre/Post Conditions, & guards

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• No execution / behaviour - only constraints, does not simulate
  • Not Turing Complete - cannot express arbitrary algorithms
  • Learning Curve - Logic-based thinking can challenge modellers
  • Tooling Uneven - Supports varies by UML environment
  • Can be ignored - constraints not enforced unless tooling integrated.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• UML + OCL = Precise, Verifiable Models
  • OCL Types: invariants, preconditions, and postconditions
  • Behavioural Diagrams show object interactions / workflow
  • Applying examples (BankAccount, Temperature Control) demonstrates real-world usage.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Differentiate between structural and behavioural modelling
  • Model components, classes, and interactions using UML
  • Represent system behaviour using state machines

docs.title: Components Diagrams
docs.text:
Purpose - Show the high-level structure of a system. How components interact through interfaces.

Key Elements: - Component - Modular part of a system. (e.g. UserInterface, Controller, Database) - Interface - Defines provided/required operations. - Dependency - Shows how one component relies on another.

E.g. User Interface -> Controller -> Database Service

docs.title: UML Class Diagrams (Structural View)
docs.text:
• Class diagrams model:
  • Attributes
  • Operations
  • Associations
  • Generalisation / Inheritance
  • Relationships:
  • Association - "uses a" or "has a"
  • Aggregation - whole-part (weak)
  • Composition - whole-part (strong, lifecycle bound)
  • Inheritance - "is a" relationship

E.g. BankAccount -> SavingsAccount -> PremiumAccount

docs.title: Class Relationships
docs.text: Relationship Description Example Association "Uses" or "knows" another class Customer -> BankAccount Aggregation Whole-part (independent lifecycles) Department -> Employee Composition Whole-part (dependent lifecycles) Order -> OrderItem Inheritance Generalisation (is-a) SavingsAccount -> BankAccount

docs.title: Adding Precision with OCL
docs.text:
• OCL (Object Constraint Language) adds mathematical precision to UML:
  • Ensures model consistency, validity, and completeness
  • Prevents illegal states (e.g. negative balances, invalid references)
  • Supports tool-based verification and test generation

  • Independent of implementation - works at the model level

  • -> UML + OCL = precise, verifiable models before coding

docs.title: Behavioural Modelling in UML
docs.text:
• Behavioural diagrams capture how objects and components interact over time.

  • Types of behavioural diagrams:

  • Sequence Diagrams - Message interactions between objects
  • Activity Diagrams - Workflows and process logic

  • State Machine Diagrams - System states and transitions

  • These diagrams complement class and component diagrams by showing dynamic behaviour.

docs.title: UML Sequence Diagrams (Concept)
docs.text:
• Show how objects interact through message exchanges over time.
  • Illustrate communication between components
  • Emphasise lifelines, message activation bars, return messages.
  • Explain why sequence diagrams help visualise workflows and scenarios

docs.title: From Behaviour to State Modelling
docs.text:
• State:

  • Configuration of object attributes at a given time.

  • Event:

  • An occurrence that triggers a change of state.

  • Transition:

  • Movement from one state to another due to an event.

  • Example

  • withdraw(amount) (amount <= balance) / balance := balance - amount

docs.title: State Machine - Core Concepts
docs.text:
• A state machine (state transition system) consists of:
  • S - Set of States
  • Σ - Set of events or inputs
  • δ – Transition function

  • s₀ – Initial state

  • Formal Representation:

  • M = (S, Σ, δ, s₀)

docs.title: ATM System Example (Behavioural View)
docs.text:
• States:
  • Idle -> Card Inserted -> Pin Verified -> Transaction Selected -> Processing -> Card Ejected
  • Transitions:
  • insertCard()
  • verifyPIN()
  • selectTransaction()
  • completeTransaction()

  • ejectCard()

  • UML State Diagram:

  • Show transitions with event labels and guard conditions.

docs.title: Bank Account State Model
docs.text:
• States:
  • Active
  • Overdrawn
  • Closed
  • Transitions
  • deposit(amount)
  • withdraw(amount)
  • close()
  • Guards:
  • withdraw(amount) [balance >= amount] / balance := balance - amount
  • Each transition must preserve the invariant balance >= -limit.

docs.title: Part 3 - OCL in the Modelling Lifecycle
Where OCL Fits in the Lifecycle
docs.text:
• OCL is used after modelling and before implementation
  • UML gives structure & behaviour
  • OCL adds precision and rules not expressible in diagrams
  • Constraints checked before code exists -> cheaper fixes

Requirements -> UML Models -> OCL Constraints -> Code/Tests -> Deployment

docs.title: What Can Be Used in OCL
docs.text:
• OCL Supports:
  • Basic types: String, Boolean, Integer, Real
  • Classes & Attributes from UML models
  • Query operations: methods that do not alter state
  • Associations: navigate related objects

E.g. context Jar inv PositiveWeight: self.totalWeight() > 0

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• UML provides the visual structure and behaviour.

  • OCL provides formal rules for correctness. Together both provide precise verifiable models before code

  • Behavioural diagrams show object interactions and workflows

  • Structural models ensure clarity and maintainability
  • Applying both gives early defect detection and consistent design.

CO3408 Lecture 6 - Concurrency in Software Modelling

docs.title: CO3408 Lecture 6   Concurrency in Software Modelling
docs.text: CO3408 Advanced Software Modelling CO3408 Lecture 5 - From Structure to Behaviour with UML & OCL

docs.title: Lecture Documents
docs.text: CO3408 Lecture 6.pdf CO3408 L6 - Lab 6 - Concurrency.pdf

docs.title: Aims & Objectives
docs.text:
• What are the concepts of concurrency and why do they matter?
  • Show how concurrency can be represented and reasoned about in models
  • Provide concrete Java examples of concurrent programming

docs.title: What is Concurrency
docs.text:
• Concurrency is when multiple tasks appear to execute at the same time.
  • Making process independently and potentially overlapping in time.
  • It enables a system to:
  • Handle multiple events or requests simultaneously
  • Perform background work while staying responsive
  • Interleave tasks even on a single processor (via scheduling) Exploit multi-core hardware when available.

docs.title: Why Concurrency?
docs.text:
• Concurrency is needed because software must now:
  • Remain responsive under load.
  • Serve multiple actors at once.
  • Scale performance beyond a single CPU.
  • Exploit parallel hardware.

docs.title: Real-World Examples of Concurrency in Java
docs.text:
Scenario Concurrency Concept Example / API Web server handling many users Thread pool for parallel requests. ExecutorService Chat or messaging app Multi-threaded communication Runnable, Callable Banking transactions Synchronisation for shared data synchronized, ReentrantLock Download manager Parallel chunk processing CompletableFuture, ForkJoinPool GUI applications Background threads for responsiveness SwingWorker, Platform.runLater() Sensor/IoT data Producer-consumer coordination BlockingQueue Game engine Thread-safe resource sharing ConcurrentHashMap E-commerce checkout Consistent updates under load Thread-safe collections ## Handling Concurrency - Threads - Simultaneously executing components - Use one thread to manage an external actor
  • Event Handlers
  • Blocks of code triggered by an event
  • Event Queue - Handles events sequentially

docs.title: Concurrent Components
docs.text:
• Application
  • Complete program

  • OS may run several

  • Process

  • Code + Data + State of Execution
  • Heavyweight

  • Has own memory space

  • Thread

  • Code + Data + State of Execution
  • Lightweight
  • Shares memory space with other threads

docs.title: Does Parallel = Concurrency?
docs.text:
• Parallel Systems

  • Multiple processors working simultaneously

  • Concurrent Systems

  • Executing multiple programs at the same time

All programs should be treated as parallel regardless of if concurrency is involved.

docs.title: Java Concurrency
docs.text:
• Threads built into the language
  • Portability
  • Synchronisation primitives built in to objects
  • Each object has a “lock”
  • Well-behaved threads seize lock before manipulating the object
  • Ensures mutual exclusion
  • Low-level – can be misused
  • No protection against deadlock

docs.title: Basics of Java Concurrency Examples
docs.text:
class Task extends Thread
{
    private String name;

docs.title: Locks
docs.text:
• The first task to seize a lock can proceed.
  • Later tasks seeking the lock are suspended
  • Until the lock is released.

I have no interest in the mars pathfinding situation or issues that occurred with it therefore I have changed this to focus on the priority invasion idea.

docs.title: Core Idea
docs.text:
Priority inversion occurs when a high-priority thread is forced to wait because a low-priority thread holds a lock, and a medium-priority thread prevents the low-priority thread from running.

In effect the system behaves as if priorities are reversed.

The typical sequence is: - A low-priority thread acquires a lock. - A high-priority thread later attempts to acquire the same lock and becomes blocked. - A medium priority thread runs and pre-empts the low-priority thread. - The low-priority thread cannot run to release the lock - The high-priority thread remains blocked longer than expected.

This is dangerous in real-time and concurrent systems because high-priority tasks can miss deadlines even though the CPU is available.

Key idea: Locks can unintentionally distort scheduling unless priority inversion is explicitly handled.

docs.title: Aims & Objectives
docs.text: By the end of the lecture, should be able to: - Explain the concept of concurrency and why multi-threading is useful. - Describe the Java thread lifecycle and key thread states. - Use thread priorities and understand issues such as priority inversion. - Create aand start threads correctly and use join() for coordination - Identify race conditions and explain why operations like value = value + 1 are not atomic - Distinguish between: - Synchronization (mutual exclusion) - Coordination (condition-based waiting) - Explain why simple synchronization fails in producer - consumer problems - Use atomic variables (AtomicInteger, etc) as lock-free solution for thread-safe operations - Evaluate safe thread-stopping mechanisms (volatile, interrupt()), and recognise deprecated/unsafe methods.

docs.title: Thread Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Threads can be in states:
  • New -> Runnable -> Running -> Waiting -> Terminated
  • Created using new Thread()
  • Started with start()
  • Can be paused or terminated gracefully

docs.title: The Life of a Thread
docs.text:
• The scheduler gives the thread processor time:
  • the thread executes part of its run method.

docs.title: Thread States & Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> New

    New --> Ready : thread created - start()

    Ready --> Running : scheduler dispatches

    Running --> Ready : time slice expired / yield

    Running --> Blocked : waiting for I/O / lock / sleep
    Blocked --> Ready : event completed / notified

    Running --> Terminated : run() completes / uncaught exception

    Terminated --> [*]

docs.title: Summary of Different Thread States
docs.text: State Description Ready The thread is ready to run and waiting for the CPU. Running The thread is executing on the CPU. Waiting The thread is waiting for some event to happen. Sleeping The thread has been told to sleep for a time. Blocked The thread is waiting for I/O to finish.

docs.title: Thread Priorities
docs.text:
• Threads inherit the creator's priority
  • Priority constants: MIN_PRIORITY (1) -> MAX_PRIORITY (10)
  • Methods: getPriority(), setPriority()
  • Higher-priority threads are scheduled first but not guaranteed

docs.title: Priority Inversion Problem
docs.text:
• A low-priority thread holds a lock needed by a high-priority thread.
  • A medium-priority thread prevents the low-priority one from releasing the lock.
  • Result: high-priority thread is effectively blocked.

docs.title: Race Condition Demonstration
docs.text:
• A race condition occurs when:
  • Two or more threads across shared data
  • At least one thread writes to it

  • Access is not synchronized

  • Result: unexpected, inconsistent, or corrupted values.

  • The run() body: 

    public void run()
{
    int val;
    for (int i = 0; i < numInc; i++) // numInc = Number of Increments
    {
        val = value; // Read 
        val = val + 1; // Compute
        value = val; // Write
    }

    value = value - numInc;
}

docs.title: Why?
docs.text:
• Multiple threads reading and writing value cause inconsistent results.
  • "value = value + 1" is not atomic (multiple CPU instructions).

docs.title: Fixing Race Condition
docs.text:
Option 1 - Synchronized 

public synchronized void increment()
{
    value++;
}
Option 2 - AtomicInteger 
AtomicInteger value = new AtomicInteger(0);

docs.title: Atomic Variables in Multithreading
docs.text:
• Java provides atomic classes in javaa.util.concuurrent.atomic
  • AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean, AtomicReference<T>
  • What makes them atomic?
  • Operations like increment, get, and finally compare and set happen as one indivisble step
  • No other thread can observe aa half-updated value
  • Prevents race conditions without using synchronized
  • What use atomic variables?
  • Faster than sychronized for simple counters/flags
  • Lock-free, non-blocking operations
  • Useful for: 
    AtomicInteger count = new AtomicInteger(0);
count.incrementAndGet(); // atomic increment

docs.title: Atomic VS Non-Atomic Counter
docs.text: Atomic Counter (AtomicInteger) Non-Atomic Counter (int) Uses: atomicCount.incrementAndGet() Simple increment: count++ Thread-safe without sychronized Not thread-safe Operation is performed as one indivisible step Increment is not atomic (3 separate steps)- Read Value- Add 1- Write Value Back Uses low-level CPU primitives (CAS = Compare-And-Set) Multiple threads can interleave these steps -> race condition No race condition -> final result is correct Final result is often lower than expected

docs.title: Creating, Starting & Awaiting Thread Completion (Join)
docs.text:
• Creating threads using Runnable / extending Thread.
  • Starting a thread using .start()
  • Why .run() is not the same as .start()
  • Waiting for thread completion using .join()

Use case - Ensuring tasks finish before continuing, sequencing work.

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
public class JoinExample
{
    // A simple task for the thread to run
    static class Worker implements Runnable
    {
        private String name;
        Worker(String name)
        {
            this.name = name;
        }

        @Override
        public void run()
        {
            System.out.println(name + " starting work.");

            // Simulate some work
            try
            {
                Thread.sleep(500);
            } 
            catch(InterruptedException e)
            {
                System.out.println(name + " interrupted.");
            }
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        System.out.println("Main Thread Starting:");

        Thread t1 = new Thread(new Worker("Worker-1"));
        Thread t2 = new Thread(new Worker("Worker-2"));

        // Start Threads
        t1.start();
        t2.start();

        // Wait for both to finish
        try
        {
            t1.join(); // Main Thread waits for t1
            t2.join(); // Main Thread waits for t2
        }
        catch (InterruptedException e)
        {
            System.out.println("Main Thread interrupted while waiting.");
        }
        System.out.println("Both Workers Finished. Main Continues");
    }
}

docs.title: IncrementTest Example (Priorities + Join)
docs.text:
• Scenario: multiple threads incrementing a shared counter.
  • Focus on thread priorities as a scheduling hint.
  • Using .join() to ensure all worker threads finish before reading the final result.
  • Key message: priorities do not guarantee order or fairness.

docs.title: Code Example
docs.text:
public class IncrementTest implements Runnable
{
    static int numThreads = 5;
    static Thread[] threads;

    @Override
    public void run()
    {
        System.out.println(Thread.currentThread.getName()
            + "running with priority"
            + Thread.currentThread.getPriority());
    }

    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        threads = new Thread(numThreads);

        // Create & Start Threads with Random Priorities
        for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++)
        {
            threads[i] = new Thread(new IncrementalTest(), "Worker-"+i);

            int p = 1 + (int)(Math.random() * 5); // Priority 1 - 5
            threads[i].setPriority(p);
            threads[i].start();
        }

        // Wait for All Threads to Finish
        for (Thread t : threads)
        {
            try { t.join(); } catch (InterruptedException e) {}
        }

        System.out.println("All worker threads complete.");
    }
}

docs.title: Coordination VS Synchronization
docs.text: Synchronization - Ensures the correctness of shared data access. Coordination - Ensures threads wait for certain conditions before proceeding. Example - A thread must wait until data becomes available. Coordination - Requires explicit mechanisms (e.g. wait/notify)

docs.title: Producer-Consumer Problem
docs.text:
Producers - generate data items Consumers process them Needs Coordination access to a shared buffer.

Problems: - Producers may overfill the buffer. - Consumers may try to consume when empty.

docs.title: Why Synchronization Alone Fails
docs.text:
• Synchronized blocks ensure mutual exclusion But they do not provide a way for a thread to pause until a condition becomes true.

Example - Consumer enters synchronized block but buffer is empty -> no built-in waiting. Leads to inefficient busy-waiting loops. Solution use wait() / notify()

docs.title: wait(), notify(), notifyAll()
docs.text:
Due to synchronized not being sufficient alone due to a lack of coordination, despite providing mutual exclusion.

Some threads must wait for a condition to become true: - Buffer not empty - Buffer not full - Item available - Consumer ready

Only the following methods can be called inside a synchronized block/method and operate on the object's monitor lock: - wait() - notify() - notifyAll()

docs.title: Solution - Buffer Class
docs.text:
graph LR
    p1[Producer]
    p2[Producer]
    p3[Producer]

    b1[Buffer Zone]

    p1 --Inserts--> b1
    p2 --Inserts--> b1
    p3 --Inserts--> b1

    c1[Consumer]
    c2[Consumer]
    c3[Consumer]

    b1 --Extracts--> c1
    b1 --Extracts--> c2
    b1 --Extracts--> c3
- Synchronized Methods: insert(), extract() - Guarantees mutual exclusion But problems waiting for items / space: - Can't wait inside exclusion zone - No other thread can get in to add / remove items - Can't wait outside exclusion zone - Another thread might grab lock first.

docs.title: Other Thread Methods
docs.text:
sleep(long milliseconds) - Suspend the task for a fixed period - Unless interrupted - Keeps hold of the monitors

interrupt() - Interrupt the task - stops, wait, sleep

join() - Wait for the thread to finish

suspend() / stop() - Deprecated - may deadlock if thread holds a lock.

docs.title: Stopping a Task
docs.text:
volatile int finished;

setDone()
{
    finished = true;
    this.interrupt();
}

run()
{
    while (!finished)
    {
        // Do Things.
        try
        {
            sleep();
        }
        catch (InterruptedException e)
        {
            continue;
        }
    }
}
