docs.title: Introduction (10%)
docs.text: Facial emotion recognition is a significant area in the field of computer vision and artificial intelligence, focusing on identifying human emotional states from an individual’s facial expressions. Emotions such as sadness, anger, surprise, fear happiness, and neutral states are critical to recognising and understanding human communication, often conveying more than words alone and the ability to recognise these fundamental expressions is imperative in isolating the necessary features that assign a correct label. FER has many practical applications, from human-to-computer interaction, mental health monitoring, and customer service experiences.

docs.title: Literature Review (10%)
docs.text: FER (facial expression recognition) is fundamentally reliant on the psychological theory that expressions are universal regardless of culture. This theory was established by Ekman, P. and Friesen, W.V. (1971), who conducted pivotal research with a pre-literate culture, isolated from Western media. They demonstrated that subjects could accurately identify and replicate the same distinct expressions as understood in the Western world and provided further evidence which confirmed that six base human emotions existed being, happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust regardless of cultural exposure, which critically showed that expressions are a universe human trait. This universality is the crucial pre-requisite for computer vision, as it validates expression of emotions as, distinguishable categories that can be standardised into differing classes.

docs.title: 2.1. Face Detection
docs.text: Before facial features can be extracted for analysis the fact must be accurately located and isolated within the image frame. The industry standard for this task is the Haar Cascades (Viola and Jones, 2001), which utilises simple rectangular features to quickly detect the presence of a face in an image. This approach ensures that the feature extraction is performed on the relevant region of interest in the images.

docs.title: 2.1. Feature Extraction
docs.text:
To accurately classify these universal emotions without deep-learning a robust appearance-based feature extraction, was created to evolve from the simple geometric approach. Early approaches to feature extraction utilised geometric tracking, which calculated the spatial distances between facial key identifiers like the corners of the mouth, or eyes (Pantic, M. and Rothkrantz, L.J.M. (2000)). The problem with the early method was a reliance on conditions, if the subject’s head pose varied or lightning conditions changed then these methods proved fragile and inaccurate. To resolve this problem further research shifted from special measurements to appearance-based methods, which analysis the texture and pixel intensity of the face as a whole, Lyons et al. (1998) demonstrated these methods were superior in this approach through the JAFFE dataset using Gabor wavelets. These are linear filters, analyse content in an image effectively replicating how the human eye detects edges.

Within the research of appearance-based extraction one method emerged for non-deep learning applications being LBP (Local Binary Patterns), which were found to be particularly useful for analysing facial texture. Shan et al. (2009) conducted a study on low-resolution facial images, demonstrating that LBP features remain stable and robust even when face images are downsized to resolutions as low as 14x19 pixels. Their experiments established that LBP is highly effective at capturing micro-textures such as skin deformities and wrinkling, making it ideal in detecting the subtly changes in facial movements associated with emotional expression. This makes LBP particularly suitable for distinguishing emotions where the structural shape of the face changes minimally, but the surface texture shifts significantly.

In contrast to LBP, which utilises a texture approach, the HOG approach focuses on capturing the structural shape of the face. Originally established by Dalal and Triggs (2005) for human pedestrian detection, it works by calculating the direction and intensity of gradients, effectively presenting edges within an image. By compiling these into histograms, the algorithm creates a robust representation of facial geometry such as the structural curve of the jaw or the angle of the mouth that remains stable even when lighting conditions vary. While HOG is effective for shape detection, this report prioritises LBP for its ability to capture fine even micro skin texture details despite potential deformations critical for emotional recognition.

docs.title: 2.2. Classification
docs.text:
Once the facial features are extracted it is important to select an appropriate classifier, particularly for datasets with smaller sample sizes, like JAFFE. The classifier algorithmically assigns a discrete label representing a specific emotional state to the image based on the features that were extracted. The classifier must map the image’s feature data through methods such as LBP and label it under one of the six categories of universal emotion. This process is critical for datasets with limited sample sizes, such as JAFFE where the algorithm must generalise from a small number of consistent high-quality training examples.

For small, controlled datasets like JAFFE, one classifier stands out as an optimal choice, the SVM (Support Vector Machine). Defined by Cortes and Vapnik (1995) the algorithm operates by finding the hyperplane that maximises the margin between classes, this approach prevents the model from overfitting to noise. SVMs are inherently binary classifiers meaning that they are only able to distinguish between two classes at a time, therefore in distinguishing between multiple classes a different approach is required.

For more complex, and high-variability datasets like Cohn-Kanade (CK), the Decision Tree classifier is an alternative to SVM. Decision Tree’s established by Quinlan (1986) is an algorithm which operates by recursively separating the data based on the feature values extracted, effectively creating decision rules to classify images. This method was established as a technique for classifying rules for higher-dimensional feature sets therefore allowing these logical rules to decompose the complex task of identifying emotions into a sequence of decisions. This approach is particularly beneficial for processing the consistent feature patterns inherent in the CK dataset. However, in comparison to the robust hyperplanes generated by SVMs, single Decision Trees can be sensitive to small variations in data, which is critical for image-based emotion recognition.

docs.title: 3. Datasets (10%)
docs.text:
Two widely publicly available datasets that were selected are the JAFFE (Japanese Female Facial Expression) and MMI Facial Expression dataset.

The JAFFE dataset contains a cumulative total of 213 grayscale images of female Japanese students, each with a several contrasting facial expressions ranging from happiness, surprise, neutral to sadness, anger, fear, and disgust. The images which are consistent in resolution, contain appropriate file names that are clear and well labelled, for example “KL.NE2.156” which indicates the individual subject in the image KL, the expression maintained in the image NE neutral being the 2nd variation of the expression being demonstrated by the subject, the final number in the filename is 156 indicates the frame number the image was taken from. The structured naming system makes pre-processing tasks such as label extraction simple, and the uniform consistent lightning and facial positioning makes it particularly suitable for working with traditional supervised machine learning methods like SVM.

The Cohn-Kanade (CK+48 (Shawon, A. (2018))) dataset, this project utilises a total of 927 PNG images which are sized to 48 x 48 pixels and organised by emotional state in named folders. This pre-processed format provides a consistent, high-quality data for training, which eliminates the need for frame extraction from the original CK+ which serves as a set of video sequences. One problem with this dataset is that it does not have all seven emotional categories, therefore as a resolution, the neutral folder was extracted from a smaller sample of the CK dataset and placed inside of the CK+48.

docs.title: 4.1. Data Pre-Processing
docs.text: The datasets, stored in Google Drive, require minimal pre-processing to prepare the images for classification. The data is processed using Python in a Google Colab notebook, utilizing the OpenCV and OS libraries to handle image data directly from the mounted drive directory.

docs.title: 4.1.1. Image Standardisation & Face Detection
docs.text:
The first essential step in handling the images is to ensure they are consistent in lighting and isolating the regions of the face. All images are loaded from the datasets and converted into grayscale resolution; this is imperative for ensuring consistency but also to remove redundant colour information so that the LBP algorithm can prioritise based on luminance-based structure patterns, then the images are processed and resized to 48 x 48 pixels to ensure that the image data remains consistent while also retaining sufficient detail for feature extraction.

For face detection the industry standard, Haar Cascade classifier was utilised to accurately locate and isolate the face within the image frame, once detected the image was detected the image was cropped to focus exclusively on the face region of the image, this is done to remove any irrelevant background noise on top of the conversion to Gray scaling.

docs.title: 4.1.2. JAFFE Data Processing
docs.text: Since the JAFFE dataset consists of a single directory containing all of the images, custom file parsing was implemented to reiterate through the filenames such as KL.NE2.156.tiff to extract the emotion type, by splitting the filename to isolate the emotion type such as NE for neutral which is then mapped to its corresponding emotion label.

docs.title: 4.1.3. CK+48 Data Processing
docs.text: The CK+48 dataset, being pre-organized by emotional state in named folders, allowed for a simpler loading process where the folder name was directly assigned as the emotion label.

docs.title: 4.1.4. Data Splitting & Training
docs.text: To ensure both models are evaluated on completed unseen data and therefore provide a robust measure of general capability, both CK+48 and JAFFE datasets were segmented using the train_split_test function which reserves 80% of the data for training, and the remaining 20% of the data for testing, the stratify parameter was set to the target labels to ensure that training and testing maintain a proportional distribution of emotional classes from the original data, therefore preventing model biases toward majority classes.

docs.title: 4.2. Feature Extraction with LBP
docs.text: A robust appearance-based feature extraction method was required to extract the facial expression data, for classification. The LBP (Local Binary Pattern) technique was selected over gradient-based methods like HOG for its established effectiveness in capturing micro-texture details. LBP, in research was found to be particularly useful for analysing skin deformities and wrinkling, which makes it ideal for detecting facial expression movements associated with a specific emotion. For LBP ideal parameters were chosen, these being LBP_RADIUS = 1, which is the radius to focus on micro-textures. Another parameter LBP_N_POINTS = 8, defines the number of sampled points. The LBP method uniform was chosen as to optimise the feature extraction.

docs.title: 4.3. Decision Tree Classifier
docs.text: The decision tree is a classifier which operates by recursively separating data based on the feature values extracted effectively creating decision rules to classify images. The DecisionTreeClassifier was applied with a random_state of 42 required for reproducibility, which is essential for the consistent results required to evaluate the model.

docs.title: 5. Model Evaluation
docs.text: The model selected for this project was Local Binary Patterns for feature extraction with Decision Trees as the classifier for the several differing emotions being sadness, anger, surprise, fear, happiness, and neutrality. Evaluation metrics were generated demonstrating different categories in how the model acted being Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and the F-1 Score.

docs.title: 5.1. JAFFE Results
docs.text:
The results for the JAFFE dataset, using the Local Binary Patterns (LBP) feature extraction and Decision Tree classifier, show significant challenges in accurately classifying emotions.

As shown in the classification report, the model achieved an overall accuracy of 13.95%. This performance is notably low, barely exceeding random chance, being approximately 14%. The confusion matrix further highlights this difficulty, revealing a scattered distribution of predictions. The model struggled to distinguish between more nuanced emotions, for example sadness, was considerably misclassified as neutral or happy, whereas fear was often confused with sadness. This suggests that the LBP features extracted, while capturing texture, may not have been robust enough to differentiate the subtle facial shifts in the JAFFE dataset, or that the small sample size of 43 test images was insufficient for the Decision Tree to learn generalisable rules.

Specific emotions like happy achieved a slightly higher precision, likely due to distinct features such as the position of the jaw or the visibility of the teeth, but sadness and fear returned a precision of 0.00, indicating the model failed to correctly identify a single instance of these classes. This poor performance underscores the limitations of using a single Decision Tree on a small, high-dimensional dataset without more advanced pre-processing methods.

docs.title: 5.1.1. JAFFE Facial Predictions
docs.text:
JAFFE EXAMPLE PREDICTIONS As shown in the JAFFE examples above, the model successfully distinguished certain emotions but struggled significantly to identify emotions like fear. While it correctly identified mouth features in some contexts it failed to differentiate between fear and happiness, misinterpreting the widening of the mouth, as the curve of a smile, this along with the arched brows led to the model incorrectly classifying those features of fear with surprise. ## 5.2. CK+48 Dataset Results The CK+48 dataset, benefiting from the dataset’s larger sample size of 927 images, demonstrated an improved performance with an overall accuracy of 31.53%. While this significantly outperforms the JAFFE dataset results being 13.95%, highlighting the inherent difficulty of classifying facial expressions using simple appearance-based features like LBP with a basic Decision Tree classifier.

As illustrated in the confusion matrix, the model showed a much stronger ability to detect distinct, high-intensity emotions compared to the JAFFE model. The Neutral emotion achieved the highest precision of 0.58, indicating that the absence of strong facial muscle deformation provided a distinct and recognisable pattern for this model.

However, significant confusion remained among emotions that share similar facial details. Surprise was frequently misclassified as disgust by 10 instances. The Angry state suggesting the model struggled to differentiate between the open-mouth shapes of surprise and the jaw tension of anger. Happy, usually one of the easiest emotions to classify, performed poorly with a precision of just 0.18. This indicates that while the larger dataset allowed the Decision Tree to learn some general rules, the LBP features alone were insufficient to capture the subtle differences required to reliably separate complex emotions.

docs.title: 5.2.1. CK+48 Facial Predictions
docs.text:
CK+48 EXAMPLE PREDICTIONS As shown in the CK+48 predicted examples above the model successfully distinguished happiness and sadness by leveraging distinct mouth features specifically the curvature of the lips. However, it failed to differentiate between surprise and anger, this suggests the model overfit the arched brows and mouth tension of the angry expression with emotive features associated with surprise. # Conclusion This report explored the application of traditional machine learning techniques for Facial Emotion Recognition. The model consisting of Local Binary Patterns for feature extraction and a Decision Tree classifier. To investigate the model against two distinct datasets, JAFFE and CK+48 and evaluate the model’s performance and ability to generalise emotions across different datasets.

The results demonstrated significant challenges of using single Decision Trees for image classification due to the accuracy achieved being 31.53% on the larger CK+48 dataset but performed poorly on the smaller JAFFE dataset with only 13.95% accuracy. The analysis highlighted that while LBP is effective at capturing texture details like wrinkling it lacks the structural ability to distinguish between similar but differing expressions like fear and surprise, which share similar mouth and brow deformations. Furthermore the Decision Tree classifier proved highly sensitive to noise and prone to overfitting, therefore failing to generalise between emotional states.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Facial emotion recognition is a significant area in computer vision and artificial intelligence. It focuses on identifying six human emotions from facial expressions. Emotions being happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, and neutrality are critical in understanding how people communicate to each other. The ability to accurately recognise and isolate the distinct necessary features to deduce an appropriate emotional label to an image.

FER has many practical applications spanning human-computer interaction, mental health monitoring, driver fatigue detection, and customer service experiences. As artificial intelligence has continued to advance, automating this recognition process has become increasingly more viable and commercially significant across multiple business markets.

In the previous assignment this problem was solved using traditional features engineering methods and struggled for good performance and found some problems and challenges. Traditional machine learning approaches to FER, such as customised feature extraction methods and basic classifiers, have demonstrated considerable limitations in generalising across varied lighting conditions, differing facial orientations, and primary subject visibility. These methods have struggled to capture the proper structural depth required to truly distinguish between visually similar emotions, resulting in poor classification accuracy and limited robustness.

This project proposes the use of EfficientNet-B0, a deep convolutional neural network, to overcome these limitations by learning hierarchical facial features directly from raw image data without the dependency on manual feature engineering. The model is trained and evaluated across two datasets previously used in Assignment 1, CK+48 and JAFFE, enabling a direct performance comparison between the traditional LBP and Decision Tree approach and the proposed deep learning solution across the six fundamental facial emotions.

docs.title: Literature Review
docs.text:
The application of deep learning to facial emotion recognition has been extensively explored and significantly outperforms traditionally custom crafted approaches. Li and Deng (2020) conducted a comprehensive survey of deep learning methods applied to FER. The survey shows that convolutional neural networks consistently outperform traditional appearance-based methods by learning layered feature representation directly from the raw image data, removing the dependency on manual feature engineering entirely.

Khaireddin and Chen (2021) demonstrated that transfer learning applied to VGGNet achieved 73.28% accuracy on the FER-2013 dataset. This shows that pre-trained networks that are fine-tuned on emotion specific data significantly outperform models trained from scratch. This approach leverages generalised visual features learned from large-scale datasets such as ImageNet, which are then adapted to the specific task of emotion classification. However, VGG architectures are computationally expensive due to their considerable depth and parameter count, limiting their practicality in more resource constrained environments.

As a resolution to this limitation, Tan and Le (2019) proposed EfficientNet, which applies compound scaling across network width, depth, and image resolution simultaneously using a principled scaling coefficient. This approach achieves superior accuracy with substantially reduced computational cost compared to other models like VGG and ResNet. Subsequent research by Savchenko (2022) further confirmed that EfficientNet variants consistently achieve state of the art results on FER benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalisation across diverse datasets.

Another alternative is ResNet. He et al. (2016) introduced ResNet with residual connections that help train deeper networks without the degradation problem. ResNet models can achieve good performance on image classification tasks. However, like VGG, ResNet can still struggle with domain shift when applied to small, low-resolution grayscale datasets like JAFFE and CK+48.

This project utilises EfficientNet with transfer learning on the small CK+48 and JAFFE datasets. The approach is different from many previous methods because those methods often train the network from scratch on large datasets. Here transfer learning is used to adapt pre-trained ImageNet weights to the very small sample sizes and low resolution of the chosen datasets. This helps the model start with useful features instead of learning everything from the beginning with limited data.

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text:
The two datasets selected to train and evaluate the EfficientNet model are the CK+48 and the JAFFE dataset, both of which were utilised in Assignment 1, enabling a direct quantitative comparison between the traditional machine learning approach and the deep learning model proposed in this project.

The CK+48 dataset (Shawon, 2018) contains 927 PNG images standardised to 48×48 pixels, organised into labelled folders by emotional category. The dataset spans six emotion classes used in this project, being anger, fear, happiness, neutral, sadness, and surprise, with disgust excluded to maintain consistency with the JAFFE dataset. The pre-processed folder structure eliminates the need for frame extraction from the original CK video sequences, providing a clean and consistently formatted input for training. As identified in Assignment 1, the dataset presents challenges in distinguishing visually similar emotions such as surprise and anger due to shared facial muscle activations, which the traditional LBP and Decision Tree classifier struggled to resolve, achieving only 31.53% accuracy. Data augmentation techniques including random horizontal flipping, rotation, and zoom were applied during training to address class imbalance and improve the model’s ability to generalise across subtle inter-class variations.

The JAFFE dataset contains 213 grayscale images of ten female Japanese subjects, each demonstrating posed facial expressions across seven emotion categories, with disgust excluded to maintain label consistency with CK+48. The images are consistently lit and uniformly positioned, with structured filenames used to extract the corresponding emotion label during pre-processing, for example the filename convention “KL.NE2.156” encodes the subject identifier, the emotion code, and the frame number respectively, making automated label extraction straightforward. As demonstrated in Assignment 1, where the JAFFE model achieved only 13.95% accuracy using LBP and a Decision Tree, the dataset’s small sample size presents a considerable challenge for generalisation, making it a meaningful benchmark for evaluating the improvement offered by transfer learning.

docs.title: Model Development
docs.text:
Prior to classification, a preprocessing pipeline was applied to standardise all input images across both datasets. The industry standard Haar Cascade classifier (Viola and Jones, 2001) was employed for face detection, utilising a pre-trained frontal face detection model to accurately locate and isolate the facial region within each image. This approach applies a series of rectangular feature filters across the image at multiple scales, rejecting non-face regions rapidly through a cascade of increasingly complex classifiers. Although both CK+48 and JAFFE images are largely pre-cropped, applying Haar Cascade detection ensured consistent localisation of the facial region across all samples, removing irrelevant background content and aligning the region of interest before resizing. Detected face regions were subsequently resized to 224×224 pixels to meet EfficientNet’s input requirements, with pixel values normalised to the range [0, 1] to stabilise gradient updates during training.

EfficientNet-B0 was selected as the primary architecture for this project, leveraging transfer learning to adapt a model pre-trained on ImageNet, a large-scale dataset containing 1.4 million labelled images across 1,000 categories. Through this pre-training, EfficientNet develops a robust understanding of low-level visual features such as edges, textures, and shapes, which are directly transferable to the task of facial emotion recognition. Rather than initialising the model with random weights and training from scratch, transfer learning retains these pre-learned representations and replaces only the final classification layer with a new dense layer outputting six emotion categories. This approach significantly reduces the volume of labelled data required to achieve strong performance, which is particularly critical given the limited sample size of the JAFFE dataset. The pre-trained weights therefore provide a strong initialisation point, allowing the model to converge faster and generalise more effectively across both datasets than any traditional machine learning approach could achieve.

The model was trained using Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) as the optimiser, updating the model’s weights iteratively by computing the loss across small batches of training images. A learning rate of 0.001 was selected to control the magnitude of each weight update, sufficiently conservative to allow stable convergence without overshooting the optimal solution. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) was chosen as the optimiser instead of Adam. SGD was preferred because it tends to be more stable when working with small datasets like CK+48 and JAFFE. Adam can sometimes converge too quickly and overfit on limited data, while SGD with a small learning rate updates the weights more gradually and helps the model generalise better in this case. Categorical cross-entropy was used as the loss function, measuring the divergence between the predicted probability distribution across the six emotion classes and the true label, penalising confident incorrect predictions more heavily than uncertain ones. The model was trained for up to 30 epochs with a batch size of 32, meaning 32 images were processed per weight update, balancing training stability with computational efficiency. To reduce overfitting, dropout regularisation was applied prior to the final classification layer at a rate of 0.5, randomly deactivating half of the neurons during each training step to prevent the model from becoming overly dependent on any single feature pathway. An early stopping callback monitored validation loss throughout training and halted the process if no improvement was observed after five consecutive epochs, restoring the best performing weights automatically. A learning rate reduction callback was additionally applied, halving the learning rate after three epochs of stagnating validation loss to allow finer convergence near the optimal solution.

docs.title: Model Evaluation
docs.text:
The performance of the fine-tuned EfficientNet-B0 model was evaluated on the held-out test sets of the CK+48 and JAFFE datasets. The analysis of the training logs reveals significant challenges in convergence and generalisation for this specific application.

On the CK+48 dataset, the model achieved a final test accuracy of 24%. The classification report indicates a severe class imbalance in the model's predictive capability. Precision and recall scores for the classes "angry", "fear", "neutral", and "sad" were recorded at 0.00, meaning the model failed to correctly identify a single instance of these four emotional states. The model only produced non-zero predictions for the "happy" and "surprise" classes. While the recall for "happy" was 0.60, the corresponding precision was low at 0.22, indicating that a large number of non-happy images were incorrectly labelled as happy.

Figure 1 - CK+48 Training History

The sample predictions provided for CK+48 corroborate this analysis. The model frequently misclassified "angry" as "happy" and "fear" as "surprise". This confusion is likely attributable to the visual similarities in the mouth region at the low resolution of 48x48 pixels. The training history plots further illustrate the issue of underfitting. Both training and validation accuracy remained largely static across the epochs, fluctuating minimally around the 20% to 30% range without a clear upward trend. The validation loss plateaued at approximately 1.78 with negligible decay, suggesting that the model was unable to learn a robust internal representation of the features necessary to separate the six emotion classes. The application of the ReduceLROnPlateau callback was triggered twice, yet the reduction in learning rate did not result in improved validation metrics, confirming that the model had reached the limit of its generalisation capacity given the data constraints.

Figure 2 - CK+48 Confusion Matrix

The confusion matrix for CK+48 reveals a model that has collapsed into predicting only two of the six available classes: happy and surprise. Of the 27 angry images in the test set, 21 were misclassified as happy and 6 as surprise, yielding zero correct angry predictions. Similarly, all 16 neutral and 12 of 17 sad images were incorrectly labelled as happy, demonstrating that the model has failed to learn any discriminative boundary for these classes. The fear class performed only marginally better, with 7 predictions assigned to happy and 8 to surprise. The happy class itself achieved the strongest performance, with 25 correct predictions out of 42, though 17 were still misclassified as surprise. The surprise class shows a comparable pattern, with 16 of 50 images correctly identified while the remaining 34 were absorbed into the happy prediction. This binary collapse between happy and surprise is consistent with the relatively open-mouth appearance shared by both emotions at 48×48 pixel resolution, where subtle differences in eye aperture and brow position are lost due to insufficient spatial detail after upscaling to 224×224 pixels.

CK+48 Sample Predictions

The results for the JAFFE dataset show significant challenges in accurately classifying emotions.

As shown in the classification report, the model achieved a test accuracy of 20%. This performance is notably low. The confusion matrix further highlights this difficulty, revealing that the model classified every single test image as "sad", regardless of the true expression shown by the subject. This resulted in a recall of 0.00 for "angry", "fear", "happy", "neutral", and "surprise". The class weight adjustments were intended to mitigate the impact of the small sample size of 147 training images, but the model still defaulted to predicting only one class. This suggests that the transfer learning from ImageNet weights was not effective for this dataset. The difference between high-resolution natural images and the grayscale, posed expressions of the JAFFE dataset likely prevented the model from extracting useful features, resulting in no ability to distinguish between the emotion classes.

Figure 4 – JAFFE Training History

The training history plots for the JAFFE dataset show significant challenges in convergence and generalisation. Both training and validation accuracy remained largely static across the epochs, fluctuating minimally around the 0.17 to 0.22 range with no clear upward trend. The validation accuracy stayed almost completely flat at 0.20 for the entire training process. The validation loss also showed very little improvement and remained around 1.79 throughout, with only small fluctuations. This pattern indicates that the model was unable to learn useful features from the JAFFE images even with transfer learning from ImageNet weights.

Figure 5 - JAFFE Confusion Matrix

The confusion matrix for the JAFFE dataset illustrates a complete prediction collapse, representing a more severe failure than observed on CK+48. Every single test image across all six emotion classes was classified as sad, with no predictions assigned to any other label. Specifically, 6 angry, 7 fear, 6 happy, 6 neutral, 6 sad, and 6 surprise images were all labelled sad, resulting in a precision of zero for five of the six classes and a recall of zero for all classes except sad. The total test set of 37 images produced not a single correctly classified instance outside the sad category, meaning the model's reported 20% accuracy reflects purely the proportion of genuinely sad images in the test set rather than any learned discriminative capability. This outcome indicates that the model failed to learn meaningful decision boundaries on this small dataset.

Figure 6 - JAFFE Sample Predictions

As shown in the JAFFE sample predictions above, the model completely failed to distinguish between the different emotions. Every single test image was predicted as “sad” regardless of the true label. Neutral faces, angry faces, surprise faces, fear faces, and happy faces were all labelled as sad. This matches the confusion matrix results and shows the total prediction collapse on the JAFFE dataset. The model could not learn any meaningful differences between the six emotion classes due to the small number of training images.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
This project implemented a deep learning approach to facial emotion recognition using the EfficientNet-B0 architecture with transfer learning from ImageNet weights. The model was trained and evaluated on two publicly available datasets, CK+48 and JAFFE, with the objective of classifying six fundamental emotions: anger, fear, happiness, neutral, sadness, and surprise. A preprocessing pipeline incorporating Haar Cascade face detection, image resizing to 224×224 pixels, and pixel normalisation was employed to standardise input data. Training utilised Stochastic Gradient Descent with a learning rate of 0.001, categorical cross-entropy loss, and regularisation techniques including dropout at a rate of 0.5, early stopping, and learning rate reduction on plateau.

The results obtained from model evaluation highlight significant limitations in applying a large pre-trained architecture to low-resolution facial expression data. On the CK+48 dataset, the model achieved a test accuracy of 24%, with zero predictive capability for the anger, fear, neutral, and sadness classes. The model predominantly predicted the happy and surprise categories, demonstrating a tendency to collapse predictions into a narrow subset of available labels. Analysis of the training curves indicated that both training and validation loss plateaued early in the training process, with minimal improvement observed despite reductions in learning rate. This underfitting suggests that the model was unable to extract sufficiently discriminative features from the 48×48 pixel inputs after upscaling, and that the transfer learning benefit was diminished by the resolution gap between ImageNet and the target datasets.

Performance on the JAFFE dataset was even more problematic. Although the test accuracy was recorded at 20%, inspection of the confusion matrix and sample predictions revealed a complete failure of the classification mechanism. The model assigned the label sad to every single test image, regardless of the true expression. This behaviour indicates that the model converged to a degenerate solution where the final dense layer weights were biased entirely toward a single output class. Given the extremely limited training set of 147 images, the model lacked sufficient exposure to diverse facial configurations to learn meaningful decision boundaries, and the class weighting applied during training was insufficient to counteract this collapse.

Several future directions could be pursued to address the shortcomings identified in this work. First, a custom convolutional neural network designed specifically for low-resolution inputs of 48×48 pixels would likely preserve critical texture information that is lost during upscaling to 224×224 pixels. Second, more aggressive data augmentation strategies such as random erasing or CutMix could artificially expand the effective size of the CK+48 dataset and improve generalisation. Third, for the JAFFE dataset, few-shot learning techniques would be more appropriate than standard transfer learning, as they are explicitly designed to operate with very limited labelled examples. Fourth, employing a larger and more diverse emotion dataset such as FER2013 or AffectNet would provide a stronger foundation for fine-tuning a model of EfficientNet's capacity.

Through the completion of this project, the selection of a deep learning architecture must be carefully matched to the characteristics of the available data. While EfficientNet is a state-of-the-art model for large-scale image classification, its application to small, low-resolution facial expression datasets proved ineffective in this instance. The experience underscored the importance of critically evaluating training dynamics, such as loss curves and confusion matrices, rather than relying solely on aggregate accuracy metrics. Furthermore, the project reinforced the understanding that transfer learning is not a universal solution and that domain-specific adaptations are essential for achieving robust performance in specialised computer vision tasks.

docs.title: Arrays
docs.text:
A NumPy array is basically a table (or grid) of numbers that are all the same data type (for example, all integers or all floats).

  • Each value in the array can be located using indexes — numbers that tell you where the value is along each axis (like row and column numbers in a spreadsheet).
  • The number of axes an array has (for example, 1D, 2D, 3D, etc.) is called its rank or number of dimensions.
  • The shape of the array is a tuple (a list of numbers in parentheses) that tells you how big the array is in each dimension. 
    a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
    One Dimensional NumPy Array 
    b = np.array([[1,2,3],[1,2,3]])
    Two Dimensional NumPy Array

docs.title: Additional Research
docs.text:
Perceptron The perceptron is a simple building block for neural networks that classify patterns that are linearly separable.

The data can be divided into two distinct classes separated by a 'hyperplane' in higher dimensions, which act as a decision boundary.

However, if the classes become too close or overlay they become non-linearly separable, therefore rendering the perceptron inefficient for this activity.

Perceptron consists of a single neuron with adjustable synaptic weights and bias.

The perception algorithm first introduced by Frank Rosenblatt in 1958, adjusts the parameters during training.

Rosenblatt proved that if patterns used to train the perceptron are from two linearly separable classes then the perceptron algorithm will successfully converge and position the hyperplane accurately between the two classes.

docs.title: Lab Work
docs.text:
![[Pasted image 20260119140145.png]] A perceptron is a type of artificial neuron used in machine learning, it simulates the way a single biological neuron processes inputs and produces an output.

The perceptron is the simplest form of a neural network.

docs.title: Key Components
docs.text:
• Inputs (Features) - The data which is fed into the model. E.g. Hours Studied and Hours Slept
  • Weights - The important assigned to each input
  • Bias - Adjusts the output to make better predictions
  • Output - The perceptron's prediction E.g. Pass or Fail

docs.title: Perceptron
docs.text:
# Perceptron Function
def perceptron(inputs, weights, bias):
    weighted_sum = sum(x * w for x, w in zip(inputs, weights)) + bias
    return 1 if weighted_sum >= 0 else 0

# Inputs and Parameters
inputs = [4, 3] # Hours studied and slept
weights = [0.6, 0.4]
bias = -0.5

# Prediction
output = perceptron(inputs, weights, bias)
print("Predicted (Pass = 1, Fail = 0): ", output)
The weights determine the slope of the line whereas the bias determines where the line sits on the x-axis shifted from the centre. - Without biases the decision line is placed at 0,0 origin point but it is unable to adjust. - With bias the line can be unpinned and shifted to best fit.

docs.title: Visualizing the Decision Boundary
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Paraneters
weights = np.array([0.6, 0.4])
bias = -0.5

# Decision Boundary
# w1*x1+w2*x2+b=0
x1 = np.linspace(0,10,100)
x2 = -(weights[0] * x1 + bias) / weights[1] # Solve for x2

# Plot Data Points
plt.plot(x1, x2, label="Decision Boundary")
plt.fill_between(x1, x2, 10, color="lightblue", alpha=0.5, label="Pass Region")
plt.fill_between(x1, x2, 0, color="lightcoral", alpha=0.5, label="Fail Region")
plt.scatter(4, 3, color="green", label="Student (4 hrs study, 3 hrs sleep)")
plt.xlabel("Hours Studied")
plt.ylabel("Hours Slept")
plt.title("Perceptron Decision Boundary")
plt.legend()
plt.show()
Decision Boundary - The line where the perceptron switches its decision between pass and fail. Blue Region - Represents where students pass. Red Region - Represents where students fail. Green Dot - Represents the specific student (4 hours studied, 3 hours slept) that was predicted.

def train_perceptron(X, y, learning_rate=0.01, epochs=20):
    # Initialize weights and bias
    weights = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    bias = 0

    # Loop through the dataset multiple times
    for _ in range(epochs):
        for i in range(len(X)):
            linear_output = np.dot(X[i], weights) + bias
            y_pred = activation(linear_output)

            # Calculate error
            error = y[i] - y_pred

            # Update weights and bias
            weights = weights + learning_rate * error * X[i]
            bias = bias + learning_rate * error

    return weights, bias

docs.title: House Price Prediction
docs.text:
Quote

As solved in the lecture, LR provides a simple yet effective baseline model for house price prediction. Model performance is evaluated using metrics like MSE and RMSE, complemented by visualizations to analyze the fit. Though straightforward, the model's effectiveness depends on the feature set and data quality.

Before running into the code. The California Housing dataset is loaded and converted into a Pandas DataFrame for manipulation.

Features (independent variables) include housing characteristics like average income, housing age, and more. The target variable (dependent variable) is PRICE, representing median house prices.

The dataset is divided into training (80%) and testing (20%) sets using train_test_split, ensuring a balanced evaluation.

A Linear Regression model is initialized and trained on the training data (X_train and y_train).

The model calculates coefficients for each feature, indicating their influence on house prices, and an intercept value for the baseline prediction.

The trained model predicts house prices for the test dataset (X_test), generating y_pred. Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) are used to assess model perfor- mance.

Lower values indicate better accuracy. Scatter Plots: Show the relationship between actual (y_test) and predicted (y_pred) prices.

Line Plots: Highlight trends in actual and predicted prices across sorted indices. Result Analysis: A summary DataFrame compares actual and predicted prices for deeper insights. Sorting and plotting help identify patterns and discrepancies.

Please run the following code for house price prediction: - First, import necessary libraries where numpy for numerical operations. pandas for data manipulation and analysis. - train_test_split to split data into training and testing sets. - LinearRegression for creating and training a linear regression model. - mean_squared_error for model evaluation. ~ - matplotlib.pyplot for data visualization. - fetch_california_housing to load a sample dataset of California housing prices.

Python work same as lab work.

docs.title: Biological Inspiration
docs.text:
• Neurons: Inspired by biological neurons in the brain.
  • Synapses: The "Weights" (\(w\)) mimic the synaptic strength between neurons. A higher weight means a stronger connection.

  • All-or-None Law: Just like a biological neuron either fires an action potential or doesn't, the Perceptron uses an activation function to output a crisp 1 (Fire) or 0 (Don't Fire) based on whether the signal crosses a threshold.

  • These neurons receive signals from other neurons

  • Depending on the strength, the neuron can either active or off/stay.

docs.title: A Perceptron Example

docs.title: Abstract Neuron Model
docs.text:
Neuron in a model processes the information by taking inputs and applying weights to them, adding a bias then finding whether it should activate based on the result.

$\(y=\theta^Tx\)$ x is the vector of inputs to the neuron theta is the vector of weights (also called a pattern or filter) theta^T*x is the dot product between the weights and inputs.

Neuron Model Diagram

Bias is added to the weighted sum which helps the neuron adjust its threshold for activation.

docs.title: Problems with a Single Perceptron
docs.text:
Single-layer perceptron's can only solve linearly separable problems (Step Function, Linear Function).

An MLP can be defined as a combination of many neurons.

Multi-layer Perceptrons (MLPs) with hidden layers can approximate complex functions using non-linear activation functions.

docs.title: Feedforward Propagation
docs.text:
Data flows in one direction, from the input layer through one or more hidden layers to the output layer.

Feedforward Diagram with h^n layers

docs.title: Feedforward Deep Network Components
docs.text: Feedforward Propagation Components

docs.title: Input Layer
docs.text: The model receives raw features from the image, which is represented as a vector.

docs.title: Hidden Layer
docs.text:
Early hidden layers might detect low-level features i.e. edges, textures or gradients and are represented as a vector.

Hidden Layer Process

Hierarchy if representations with increasing level of abstraction each stage is a kind of trainable nonlinear feature transform.

Image Recogniton
pixel -> edge -> texton -> motif -> part -> object

Text
Character -> word -> word group -> clause -> sentence -> story

docs.title: Output Layer
docs.text:
The output layer produces the final prediction.

The number of neuron depends on the task.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
Regression - 1 neuron with linear activation function.

$$ y = w^th +b$$ Linear units - no nonlinearity.

Regression Output Layer

docs.title: Multi-Layer Regression
docs.text: n neuron with a linear activation function. $$ y = w^Th+b $$ Linear units - no nonlinearity.

docs.title: Binary Classification
docs.text: 1 neuron with a sigmoid activation function $$ y = sigma(w^Th+b) $$ Linear units - no nonlinearity.

docs.title: Multi-Class Classification
docs.text:
n neurons (one per class) with a softmax activation function.

y = softmax(z) where z = $$ z = W^Th+b $$ Example: Classify handwritten digits.

docs.title: Activation Functions
docs.text:
Considering a neuron.

\[ Y = \sum(weight * input) + bias \]

The value y can be anything ranging from -inf to +inf. The neuron doesn't really know the bounds of the value. How to know whether the neuron should fire or not?

docs.title: Linear Function
docs.text: A straight line function where activation is proportional to input: $$ f(x) = cx $$ Not appropriate for modelling complex nonlinear functions.

docs.title: Sigmoid Function
docs.text:
If the value of Y is above a certain value declare it activated.

\[ f(x) = 1 \div 1 + e^{-x} \]

if sigmoid (x) >= 0.5 predict class 1. if sigmoid (x) < 0.5 predict class 0.

Often used in binary classification tasks where a threshold of 0.5 is used to make decisions.

docs.title: ReLu (Rectified Linear Unit) Function
docs.text:
It is a non-linear function and is capable of modelling complex functions.

$$ f(x) = max(0,x) $$ For any input x > 0 the output is x (no change). For any input x <= 0 the output is 0 (the neuron is 'turned off').

The range of ReLu is [0, inf]. It ensures sparsity of activations.

docs.title: Softmax Function
docs.text:
In softmax the output is a vector of probabilities and there isn't a single threshold used in the same way as sigmoid.

Thresholding can be applied during classification: $$ mathrm{softmax}(x_i) = frac{e{x_i}}{sum_{j=1} $$} e^{x_j}

For multi-class classification after applying softmax typically the class with the highest probability is selected as prediction.

docs.title: Problem with Forward Propagation
docs.text:
MLPs have many weights and biases so how can they be updated to reduce error?

Forward Propagation Problem

docs.title: Backpropagation
docs.text:
Solution - Backpropagation calculates the gradients of the loss with respect to each weight and bias.

Backpropagation is a common method for training a neural network.

By optimising weights so that the neural network can learn how to correctly map arbitrary inputs to outputs.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: 1) Do forwards propagation 2) Compute the Loss/Error (for instance, MSE) 3) Backward Pass - Use the chain rule to compute gradients - Adjust weights and biases 4) Repeat forward and backward passes to reduce the loss over time.

docs.title: What is the problem with Deep ANN (Deep Artificial Neural Network)
docs.text:
• Consider an image classification problem of an indoor/outdoor scene)
  • Image size is 64 x 64 x 3 = 12288 (input layer)
  • Two hidden layers h1 = 1000 neurons, h2 = 500 neurons
  • Outputs = 2 neurons (one for each class)

How many parameters would need to be trained? input layer -> h1 -> h2 -> output layer -> 12288 x (1000) + (1000 x 500) + (500 x 2) = 12789000 (12.7 million) very small image and very small network.

Task

What if the image size is 256 x 256 x 3 and network has 4 layers with 1000 neurons and 1000 outputs?

256 x 256 x 3 = 196608 (input layer) 4 layers 1000 neurons each 1000 outputs

parameters = (neurons_prev × neurons_next) + neurons_next

196608 × 1000 ← input → L1

+1000 × 1000 ← L1 → L2 +1000 × 1000 ← L2 → L3 +1000 × 1000 ← L3 → L4 +1000 × 1000 ← L4 → output = 200,608,000

docs.text:
• Convolutional neural networks are a special kind of multi-layer neural network.
  • CNN is a feed-forward network that an extract the topological properties from an image.
  • Like almost every other neural network, they are trained with a version of back-propagation algorithm.
  • Convolutional neural networks are designed to recognise visual patterns directly from pixel images with minimal pre-processing.
  • Can recognise patterns with extreme variability i.e. handwritten characters

docs.title: Pooling Layer
docs.text:
A subsampling layer commonly referred to as the pooling layer which reduces the spatial size of feature maps helping achieve translation invariance and reduces computational complexity.

Ensures that the same result will be obtained even when the image features have small translations.

Important

Important operation for object classification and detection.

docs.title: Types of Pooling
docs.text: Max Pooling - Takes the maximum value from a given window. Helps preserve the most important features. Average Pooling - Computes the average value in the window, resulting in a smoother representation. Global Pooling - Reduces an entire feature map to a single value, often used before fully connected layers.

docs.text:
• Construct a CNN by placing a number of convolution and pooling layers in cascade:
  • Specify input size.
  • Specify filter size at each layer, etc.
  • Add a number of fully connected layers after convolution and pooling layers
  • Add a classifier at the end of the network.

docs.title: Deep Learning Frameworks
docs.text:
Deep learning frameworks are essential tools that simplify the process of designing, training, and deploying neural networks. Instead of implementing complex mathematical operations from scratch these frameworks provide pre-built functions optimised computation and GPU acceleration to speed up development.

  1. TensorFlow - A highly scalable framework from Google.
  2. Keras - A user-friendly API for deep learning
  3. PyTorch - A flexible and research-oriented framework from Facebook
  4. Caffe - A lightweight, fast framework for image processing.

Other frameworks (MXNet, Theano, CNTK) - Specialised frameowkrs with unique advantages

docs.title: TensorFlow
docs.text: TensorFlow is an open-source deep learning framework developed by Google Brain. It is widely used for: - Image and speech recognition - Natural Language Processing - Reinforcement Learning

docs.title: Keras
docs.text: Keras is a high-level deep learning API that runs on top of TensorFlow making it easier to build and train deep learning models. It is widely used for: - Rapid prototyping - Building neural networks - Accessing built-in pre-trained models.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Simple, intuitive synrax for building neural networks.
  • Support for multiple backends like TensorFlow, Theano, and CNTK.
  • Built-in pre-trained models like ResNet, VGG, and Inception.
  • Rapid prototyping for beginners and professionals alike.

docs.title: Weak AI
docs.text:
• Trained and designed for a specific task or a narrow range of tasks
  • Can't perform beyond its defined tasks

Example

Voice Assistants (Siri, Alexa, Google) Recommendation Systems (Netflix, YouTube, Spotify)

docs.title: Strong AI
docs.text:
• Can perform any intellectual task that a human can.
  • Ability to learn, reason, and understand across various domains.
  • Not restricted to any specific task.

Imagine

Imagine an AI system that can not only assist with voice commands like Siri but: - write essays - solve complex math equations - understand human emotions - drive a car - create art

Example

This would be an AI that could perform any task you ask of it, similar to a human with broad knowledge and abilities.

docs.title: Super AI
docs.text:
• Far exceeds human intelligence in all respects.
  • AI could learn, adapt and evolve much faster than humans.
  • Solving problem in innovative ways

Example

The Matrix or Ex Machina - AI Depictions not only outperform human intelligence but also gain consciousness and potentially control the human environment. - A Super AI might for example cure all diseases or design technologies far beyond current human capacities but it might also pose ethical risks if it behaves unpredictability. - AI can categorise into several types based: - Functionality - Capacity - Real-World Applications - Other Technologies.

docs.title: Reactive Machines
docs.text:
• Simplest AI that perform specific tasks by reacting to current conditions without storing any past experiences.
  • Cannot 'learn' from the previous actions or improve their performance based on experience.

docs.title: IBM's Deep Blue (Chess-Playing AI)
docs.text:
• Famously beat the chess champion Garry Kasparov is a reactive AI.
  • It analysed the chessboard's current state, evaluated possible moves, and chose the best one based on programmed algorithms.

The Problem?

It couldn't learn or adapt between games and was purely reactive to the current game's conditions.

docs.title: Limited Memory AI
docs.text:
• Can learn from historical data to make decisions.
  • Can store past experiences or data for a short time and use it to improve their predictions or performance.

Example

Self-Driving Cars (e.g. Tesla or Waymo) - Use limited memory AI - Analyse real-time data from sensors, cameras, and radar (like road conditions, traffic, and other vehicles' behaviour) to make decisions. - Use previous experiences (like patterns of traffic flow) to navigate better in future.

docs.title: Theory of Mind AI
docs.text:
• Designed to understand emotions, intentions and social situations.
  • To interpret human needs and respond accordingly.
  • To predict how humans will behave in certain situations and adjust its behaviour accordingly.

Currently Theoretical

  • In development however remains theoretical for now.
  • Research into emotional AI is underway.
  • No current AI system fully understands human emotions.

If Developed

  • Will be able to detect sad, or stressed based on facial expressions, voice tone, or physiological data.
  • Responds accordingly offering calm music if stressed or providing motivational content if down.

docs.title: Self-Aware AI
docs.text:
• Exists only in theory
  • Own consciousness and self-awareness
  • Understand its own state of existence
  • Recognise it's own identity
  • Have independent desires or motivations

Example

  • In films like Ex Machina AI systems become self-aware developing independent thoughts, emotions and even desires.
  • Systems start to question their purpose and existence. (Much like humans)

docs.title: Supervised Learning
docs.text: Supervised learning the training of a ML model on labelled datasets where both input data and the correct output (label) are known.

docs.title: Key Details
docs.text: The algorithm learns by mapping inputs to their corresponding outputs. - The algorithm learns by mapping inputs to their corresponding outputs. - Goal is to predict labels for new unseen data. - Performance is measured using the metrics: - Accuracy - Precision - Recall - F1-Score

docs.title: Common Algorithms
docs.text:
• Linear Regression - Predicts continuous values.
  • Logistic Regression - Used for binary classification.
  • Support Vector Machines (SVM) - Finds the optimal separating hyperplane.
  • Decision Trees - Tree-like models for classification or regression.

Example Applications

  • Image Classification (e.g. cat vs dog, mouse vs rat)
  • Spam Email Detection
  • Sentiment Analysis
  • Disease Diagnosis

docs.title: Lecture Example
docs.text: A database containing both cat and dog images are separated and labelled before being processed into a trained model which identify which are cat or dog by their assigned label.

docs.title: Unsupervised Learning
docs.text: Unsupervised learning trains a model on unlabelled data, meaning the correct outputs are unknown.

docs.title: Key Details
docs.text:
• The algorithm discovers hidden patterns or structures in data.
  • Goal is to group or reduce data dimensions without prior labels.
  • Performance is often evaluated using internal metrics (e.g. Silhouette Score, Davies–Bouldin Index).

docs.title: Common Algorithms
docs.text:
• K-Means Clustering – Groups data into k clusters based on similarity.
  • Hierarchical Clustering – Builds a tree of clusters.
  • Principal Component Analysis (PCA) – Reduces dimensionality while preserving variance.
  • Association Rule Learning (Apriori) – Finds relationships between variables in large datasets.

Example Applications

  • Customer Segmentation
  • Market Basket Analysis
  • Anomaly Detection
  • Topic Modeling

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning
docs.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent to make successive decisions by interacting with an environment to maximise rewards and minimise punishment.

docs.title: Key Details
docs.text:
• No labelled data — learning via trial and error.
  • The agent observes a state, performs an action, and receives a reward.
  • Goal is to learn a policy that maximizes total reward over time.
  • Evaluated by convergence speed and long-term reward.

docs.title: Common Algorithms
docs.text:
• Q-Learning – Learns value of actions using Q-values.
  • Deep Q-Network (DQN) – Combines Q-learning with neural networks.
  • Policy Gradient Methods – Directly optimize the policy function.
  • SARSA – On-policy version of Q-learning.

Example Applications

  • Game AI (e.g. AlphaGo, Chess, Dota 2 bots)

  • Autonomous Driving

  • Robotics Control

  • Dynamic Pricing

docs.title: Overfitting
docs.text:
• The model performs well on the training data but fails to generalise new data.
  • Usually occurs when the model learns noise or irrelevant details.

docs.title: For Model Training
docs.text:
• Model is too complex (i.e. Massive number of layers or DT with too many trees.)
  • Perfectly fit, capturing even the smallest variations/noise but fails to generalise (memorises instead of learning)
  • Training Accuracy is very high but the Test Accuracy is much lower.
  • A decision tree that splits the data repeatedly until each leaf node has only one data point.

docs.title: Underfitting
docs.text:
• The model is too simple and fails to capture the patterns in the data leads to poor performance even on the training data.
  • Model is too simple (Very few layers, or DT with few trees)
  • Happen if using a linear model for a dataset that has non-linear patterns.
  • Training Accuracy and Testing Accuracy are low because the model fails to learn the relationships between the features and the target.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text: Different algorithms are suited for types of problems.

docs.title: K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN)
docs.text:
• Supervised learning algorithm used for both regression and classification.
  • Based on the majority class of its nearest 'k' neighbours.

Example Applications: Simple classification, pattern recognition, recommendation system, etc.

  • KNN tries to predict the correct class for the test data by calculating the distance between the test data and all the training points.
  • Select the K number of points which is closest to the test data.

docs.title: KNN Steps
docs.text: 1) Select the number K of the neighbours 2) Calculate the Euclidean distance of K number of neighbours 3) Take the K nearest neighbours as per the calculated Euclidean distance. 4) Among these k neighbours count the number of data points in each category 5) Assign the new data points to that category for which the number of neighbour is maximum.

docs.title: KNN Example - Shop Example
docs.text:
Imagine owning a shop with two types of customers: those who buy Yellow t-shirts and those who buy Green t-shirts. The Red data point represents a new customer. By looking at which group of existing customers is standing closest to the Red point, the algorithm predicts which shirt the new customer is most likely to purchase.

In the following example K the amount of neighbours will be 4.

The Euclidian distance is calculated between the Red data point and the closest existing customers. Once the distances are calculated, the values are ranked in descending order. The votes are counted based on the class majority of K neighbour's distances with the closest majority class distance to the red data point, therefore the red data point (the new customer) will purchase the Orange t-shirt.

docs.title: Supervised Learning - Regression - Continuous Outputs
docs.text: Linear Regression is a statistical method used to model the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables.

docs.title: The Goal
docs.text:
Find the best-fitting line (or hyperplane in higher dimensions) which predicts the dependent variable based on the existing independent variable(s). Dependent Target - Outcome that is wanted to be predicted. (e.g. A house price) Independent Predicator - Variable used to make predictions. (e.g. Square Foot, Number of Bedrooms, etc)

Equation of a line: y = mx + b y - dependent variable m - slope of the line (change in y for a unit change in x) x - independent variable b - y-intercept (value of y when x = 0)

docs.title: What are SVMs
docs.text:
• Developed in the 1990s by [Vladmir N. Vapnik & Colleagues]
  • Powerful machine learning algorithm widely used for both linear & non-linear classification, as well as regression and outlier detection tasks.
  • SVMs are highly adaptable, making them suitable for various applications such as:
  • Text classification
  • Image classification
  • Spam detection
  • Handwriting detection
  • Gene expression analysis
  • Face detection
  • Anomaly detection

The idea behind SVM is to find a boundary (or decision boundary) that best separates data points of one class from data points of another class.

docs.title: Example Scenario - Email Spam Detection
docs.text:
• Imagine building a system to classify (spam & not spam)
  • Algorithms to classify incoming emails as either spam or not spam.

Emails incoming spam and not spam contents are the data points.

Goal - Model can learn to distinguish between these two classes using patterns in past emails.

Here are some features for each email that may be suspicious: - X1 - Frequency of the word free. - X2 - Frequency of the word urgent.

SVM selects the line (hyperplane) that maximises the margin between two classes (spam and not spam). This maximises the confidence in the classification.

docs.title: Why Maximise the Margin
docs.text:
• A wider margin reduces the risk of misclassifying emails
  • Helps to better generalise new emails.

docs.title: Equation of Hyperplane
docs.text: $$ mathbf{w} cdot mathbf{x} + b = 0 $$ where \(\mathbf{w}\) is the weight vector and \(b\) is the bias.

docs.title: Non-Linearly Separable
docs.text:
Problem with Linear Boundaries: - FER (Facial Expression Recognition) - i.e. Imagine building a model to classify facial expressions into six categories. (Angry, Happy, Sad, Neutral, Fear, and Surprise) - Each face image can be represented by features such as: - Edge Patterns - Texture - Texture Brightness - Key Points on Face (e.g. Position of eyebrows, mouth, etc)

Challenge with FER

These six expressions may not be linearly separable due to overlapping or similar features.

docs.title: Solution with Kernels
docs.text: SVM can use a kernel function to map the data into a higher-dimensional space wwhere it becomes easier to separate.

docs.title: Radial Basis Function (RBF) Kernel
docs.text: • Useful for non-linear data - helps separate classes by creating a more flexible decision boundary.

docs.title: One-Vs-One Strategy
docs.text: • SVM can classify pairs of expressions at a time. (e.g. one SVM model might classify "happy" vs "sad", another "angry" vs "neutral", etc for all combinations of emotions)

docs.title: One-Vs-All Strategy
docs.text:
• Score for each class is computed based on the output of the respective binary classifier that was trained to distinguish that class from all others.

CO3722 Assignment Brief, p.3

Introduction Businesses and organisations need to continually develop their systems and technologies in order to be able to meet the challenges of the modern globalised world. Their challenge, however, is to be able to make rational decisions about which technologies they should incorporate in their businesses.

Academia and other places of research continually invest in emerging technologies, including data science and analytics. However, do we understand their challenge and capability and thus, their design to provide impact.

What are the consequences and what steps do we need to carefully consider before applying machine decision-making models within our business domain.

CO3722 Assignment Brief, p.3

Consider example business/domain cases and user groups, such as: - Financial sectors and the considerations that need to be made on their customers regarding loan and banking decisions; - Medical informatics and the classification or predictions on medical ailments; - Crime prevention/prediction; - Shopping malls/stores and customer spending behaviours.

CO3722 Assignment Brief, p.3

Detailed Assignment Brief - You will choose an area of business or a specific user group in which data science is explored (or has the potential) to bring competitive advantage. You will critically discuss the use of data science, including:

  • the approach to data collection;
  • feature selection and justifications of choices;
  • strategies for data cleaning;
  • statistical analysis of early findings,
  • options for modelling and choices of algorithm.

Critically evaluate the case for or against adoption of data science for your chosen business or specific user group.

This preliminary activity of research and design will better prepare you for assignment 2 in which you will have the background and design knowledge to carry out your own investigations and data science project
