``` Research and question design:

You have demonstrated deep domain knowledge with a critical evaluation of dataset features. 

While you described the distributions visually, you did not calculate key statistical measures (mean, standard deviation) in the text to quantify this spread.

Research questions have been formulated well.

Good choice of algorithms. But the discussion is very brief and lacks critical contrast between the algorithms. 

Ethical analysis: Good identification of specific risks. This can be expanded with the inclusion of algorithmic and AI-related risk, along with proper references.

Introduction and recommendation: Strong business context, but the introduction lacks references to support your initial claims about the industry. The conclusion is very brief. You needed to propose specific next steps for questioning the data ```

The Research Report assignment will be in 4 sections:

docs.title: 1. Introduction (~10%)
docs.text:
Data-driven decision-making  has become a fundamental component within many modern business operations enabling organisations to extract insights from the quantitative data collected to identify patterns, predict outcomes and inform strategy decisions against competitors. Analytics has become imperative as a competitive advantage across almost every industry sector, from customer behaviour such as buying habits, to customer demand forecasting to predict and project potential risky business choices, while maintaining optimisation and efficiency through the business practices.

The entertainment and streaming industry represent a particularly fascinating domain for data science, where platforms such as Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Disney+ utilise it to potentially forecast statistics such as subscriber retention. In highly competitive environments, like streaming services, data-driven practices have developed from general business insights into a core strategy for business survival. This report focuses on a publicly available Kaggle dataset (Bansal, S. (2021)) focusing on the Netflix containing a cumulative total of 8,807 movies and tv show titles, the data is spread across these titles described by twelve attributes being: content type, director, country, release year, rating, duration, movie genre, and description.

docs.title: 2. Critical Discussion of the Proposed Dataset & Question Development (~40%)
2.1. Data Collection & Feature Selection
docs.text:
The chosen Netflix dataset represents a static and simple curation of a sample of the total catalogue’s metadata, as of mid-2021. For a streaming service this data is typically sourced from internal management systems, which aggregate information from customer behaviour, trending analytics and categorised popularity by geographic location such as with their current country’s top trending recommendation system. The value of this dataset is for a competitive advantage insight, allowing not just individuals to assess the Netflix dataset but other companies who may find their historical data relevant for business or delayed content release strategies.

The twelve attributes provide the information required to critically evaluate the dataset’s utility for data science. The show type attribute being either movie or tv show is fundamental for analysing past consumer content trends if mixed with an additional dataset providing user-engagement or review data for the same or similar catalogue sample. Time features like the release year and date added allow for analysis of the catalogue growth over time, which can indicate trends or business growth strategies such as the exponential increase in content for Netflix from 2016 onwards, as detailed in an article by Moses, 2024 which states that Netflix wrote the playbook for streaming and entertainment services. Attributes like the country, rating and genre are essential for understanding geographically trending movies or shows, or the audience segmentation between regional content. However, features like the director and cast provide challenges due to 30% of the directors and 9% of the cast being missing values.

docs.title: 2.2. Data Cleaning Strategy
docs.text:
The analysis scope for this project focuses on high-level data like trends, genre distribution, and geographical content. The director and cast attributes are not essential for the evaluation which is centred on the other remaining ten attributes which provide direct and clear insights. Therefore, to acknowledge the presence of the missing data in these categories, the decision was made to remove these two attributes from the overall analysis. Removing this data simplifies the cleaning process required and aligns the dataset more tightly with the purpose of the research.

The analysis scope for this project focuses on high-level data like trends, genre distribution, and geographical content. The director and cast attributes are not essential for the evaluation which is centred on the other remaining ten attributes which provide direct and clear insights. Therefore to acknowledge the presence of the missing data in these categories, the decision was made to remove these two attributes from the overall analysis. Removing this data simplifies the cleaning process required and aligns the dataset more tightly with the purpose of the research.

For the retained features, a targeted cleaning strategy is required. The country attribute, often containing multiple listed countries for a single title, presents a standardisation challenge. To resolve this for the purposes of analysing the content and geographical regional trends based on primary production country. This transforms the data from a complex multi-entry field into a clear single categorical feature suitable for analysis and visualisation for comparison of content from across multiple regions. While this approach does not capture a title’s full international distribution it successfully creates a clean dataset for analysing the core geographic origins of content within the catalogue.

The duration attribute presents a unique data cleaning challenge as its format entirely depends on the field’s content, as it stores the movies runtime, and the number of seasons for a tv show. To make this analytically useful, this single column will be separated into two distinct features being movie duration minutes, and tv show seasons. This separation allows for a proper statistical analysis of each content’s format length.

Furthermore, to address the absence of an explicit identifier for distinguishing original from licensed content. By comparing the release_year to the year extracted from date_added, it is possible to infer that the content’s acquisition to Netflix’s platform can be correlated with the specific title’s release year. It can be classified as an Original or First-Run under the assumption that Netflix releases its own productions immediately. Conversely a delineation between these dates can suggest a Licensed title reflecting the typical delay caused by Cinema-wide releases or prior broadcasting rights held by other networks.

Finally, the date added attribute must be converted into a standard date and time format to ensure consistent analyse of catalogue growth. These steps collectively format the data into a consistent clean dataset ready for analysis.

docs.title: 2.3.1. How has Netflix’s volume of content (as assumed by the dataset) increased from 2008 to 2021?
docs.text: This graph illustrates content graph from 2008 to 2021 the temporal shift in the growth of the Netflix catalogue, providing a clear visualisation for Netflix’s over thirteen-year expansion. The data demonstrates content additions during the years of 2008 and 2015 were minimal with fewer than 50 titles being added annually during this period. However, from 2016 onwards the graph demonstrates the dramatic acceleration peaking to around 2000 titles added in 2019. This shift reflects Netflix’s evolving business strategy transiting from a heavy reliance on third-party licensing toward large-scale investment in exclusive original content Lobato, R. (2019). The reason for this change could be due to the rise of competitive streaming platforms such as Amazon Prime, therefore making the original content the key differentiator between the platforms.

docs.title: 2.3.2. What are the dominant genres within the dataset and how is this correlated to the number of titles available?
docs.text:
The bar chart graph above shows the top 10 dominant genres in the Netflix dataset, which highlights a large disparity in content genres. International Movies represent a clear outlier peaking around 2,750 titles, followed by Dramas at around 2,400 titles, while Comedies trail behind significantly with roughly 1,600 titles.

This data demonstrates that the platform prioritises global content over local content, this trend correlates with Netflix’s “localised content strategy” as noted by Patov (2024), that Netflix’s heavily invests in regional productions such as Money Heist in Spain to drive subscriber growth in more diverse international markets. Furthermore, the separation of genres as seen in the group particularly the disparity between Dramas and TV Dramas reflects the usage of varied content formats to inform recommendation algorithms responsible for 80% of content discovery.

docs.title: 2.3.4. What is the frequency distribution of content duration for Movies compared to TV Shows?
docs.text:
The histograms above illustrate the distribution of duration for Movies and TV shows revealing distinct structural patterns in the platform’s catalogue as provided by the dataset. The data for movies approximates a normal distribution peaking significantly around 90-to-100-minute mark. This aligns with traditional industry standards for feature-length movies, historically leaning towards optimisation for Cinemas to produce high turnover and audience retention.

In contrast, the distribution for TV shows reflects a strong right-skewed pattern rather than a regular bell curve. The data indicates that most series—approximately 67% of the category—consist of only one season, whereas second seasons account for just 17% of TV shows (or 5% of the complete dataset). This right-skewed structure suggests that the Netflix catalogue is heavily weighted towards limited series or shows that were cancelled, with multi-season content being a comparative rarity.

docs.title: 2.3.4. How does the distribution of season counts reflect Netflix’s strategic shift towards binge-consumption?
docs.text:
The line graph above visualises the annual release for TV shows segmented by content type, which reveals distinct differences between Netflix’s internal production strategy and its acquisition of licensing agreements. The data for the originals approximates a solid growth curve rising sharply from 2015, reflecting a drive to produce more exclusive content to stimulate subscriber growth. This trajectory aligns with Netflix’s strategic shift from third-party licensing to new and original content that does not rely on third-party studios.

In contrast, the licensing line of the graph approximates a linear trend which remained steadily rising until 2016 before experiencing a distinct downturn in 2018. This inflection point reflects the industry-wide “repatriation” of content, where studios such as Disney and Fox began withdrawing their intellectual property to launch competing services, as described by Munson (2018). Consequently, the continued descent observed post-2018 indicates that Netflix’s reliance on licensed material has diminished, with the platform increasingly focusing on original content to offset the gap left by the withdrawn titles.

docs.title: 3. Critical Evaluation of Data Modelling including its Ethical Considerations
docs.text:
Based on the exploratory analysis in the 2.3.4. section which identified a high rate for single season shows. A predictive model could be deployed to optimise production investment, the primary purpose of which is to identify whether a new original series will secure a renewal for a second season or be cancelled. To address this, a binary classification model is proposed to estimate the probability of a new series securing a renewal. The target variable for this model would be defined based on the duration value where a value of 1 season is classified as 0 which indicates Risk or Cancelled and 2+ Seasons which is classified as renewed and successful.

To implement this, two algorithms that would work best for evaluation. Logistic Regression is a strong candidate for its interpretability, allowing acquisition managers to quantity exactly how specific features such as Genre or Country increase or decrease the odds of renewal. However, given the complexity of the dataset a Random Forest Classifier is the better choice as this method is superior for handling the dataset’s categorical variables without extensive pre-processing (Breiman, 2001) and provides ranking for features of the dataset allowing for easy evaluation of which of the important features directly impact the state of the current competitive streaming environment.

Critically the adoption of this model raises significant ethical concerns regarding the automation of creative media decision making. While analyse of the dataset revealed that international movies are the largest genre, this broad categorisation presents the risk of oversimplification. By categorising cultural movies into one single international genre, a predictive model may fail to distinguish between specific regional markets. Consequently, this could lead to a scenario where the algorithm favours content based on the historical patterns for specific international regions, therefore, the model must be deployed strictly as a decision-support tool and not as an autonomous decision-maker.

docs.title: 4. Conclusions & Recommendations
docs.text: This report has critically evaluated the Netflix dataset to determine its utility for driving business insight. The findings demonstrate that while the dataset provides strong signs regarding catalogue growth and the dominance of international genres, it requires careful feature engineering to address significant class imbalances, particularly the prevalence of single season shows. This imbalance is not merely due to statistics but reflects a documented business strategy as discussed by Lederer (2024), Netflix frequently cancels series that fail to meet a 50% completion rate threshold within their first four weeks, resulting in many unfinished narratives.

Task 1 - Computation Literature Examination

Driving around London City Centre

A paper (Hawke et al. 2021) questions whether all the fundamental problems of autonomous vehicles have been solved, acknowledging that at present during their research, 4 years ago in 2021, deemed the problem not feasible due to an a few prime factors as directly quoted:

Quote

1) technical scalability 2) safety-critical engineering effort 3) unit economics (profitability of an AV based on utilisation and costs) 4) Regulation

"technical scalability" is defined in the paper as:

Quote

the ability of the decision-making software systems to [generalise] to new situations quickly with sufficient performance for deployment."

This means that the software on-board autonomous vehicle needs to have critical-level decision-making abilities. For instance, avoiding or understanding how to properly cause the most none or the most minimal harm during a trolley problem like situation in unseen environments (i.e. London), and prevent accident or harm to the driver or passenger(s) while maintaining its ability and speed to recognise these situations is adequately quick enough that it is suitable for mainstream mass deployment to the public, and properly alert the user when it is unable to, so they can take control.

Translating Spoken English

This task is solved, as written in a paper from Seamless Communication (2023), which writes about the existing solution for

Quote

"X2T Into-Text Translation [&] Transcription" demonstrating how machine learning models with "trained on X-eng directions".

  • X2T = X-To-Text (X can either be Text or Speech)
  • X-Eng = X-To-English (X is any source of language)

The idea demonstrating how pre-trained models when used with the SeamlessM4T model can translate audio from speech-to-text which utilise

Quote

"[A] conformer-based encoder for speech input" and a Transformer-based Encoder (NIPS-2017-attention-is-all-you-need-Paper.pdf) for text input"

Writing an Intentionally Funny Story

This task continues to pose many challenges to humanity, the creation of humorous content as demonstrated in a paper by (Loakman et al. 2025) details the challenges and existing ways that have been attempted to create humour or at least the perception of it, through natural language processing.

The paper claims that the generation of humour computationally is highly "context-dependent" and requires an "extensive [level of] reasoning" to understand and create.

Task 1 - Task Name Here

In this activity, you are supposed to use the regression implementations from the sklearn package to fit regression models to a given dataset. The dataset is included in today’s resources, however there is no requirement to upload. Sklearn provide a small number of sample datasets that are already prepared and processed for modelling. Refer to link below for details on the datasets available.

Reference: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/datasets/toy_dataset.html Have a quick explore over the data – dataset provided in the practical resources folder on Blackboard. Explore sklearn further using: scikit-learn: machine learning in Python — scikit-learn 1.8.0 documentation

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from sklearn import datasets, linear_model
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error, r2_score

# Load Dataset
diabetes = datasets.load_diabetes()

diabetes_X = diabetes.data[:, np.newaxis, 2]

# Examine one feature, that being, the second index element (third) column:
# 80 : 20 for training/testing - Split the data into training and testing
diabetes_X_train = diabetes_X[:-20] # All but last 20
diabetes_X_test = diabetes_X[-20:] # Last 20

# Split the targets into training and testing sets
diabetes_y_train = diabetes.target[:-20] # All but last 20
diabetes_y_test = diabetes.target[-20:]   # Last 20

# Linear Regression Module using Training Data
regr = linear_model.LinearRegression()

# Train the model using the training sets
regr.fit(diabetes_X_train, diabetes_y_train)

# Make predictions using the unseen testing set
diabetes_y_pred = regr.predict(diabetes_X_test)

# Statistics and Plot Outputs
print('Co-Efficients: ', regr_coef_)
print('Mean Square Error: %.2f' % mean_squared_error(diabetes_y_test, diabetes_y_pred))
print('Varience Score: %.2f' % r2_score(diabetes_y_test, diabetes_y_pred))

# Plot Outputs
plt.scatter(diabetes_X_test, diabetes_y_test, color="black")
plt.plot(diabetes_X_test, diabetes_y_pred, color="blue", linewidth=3)
plt.xticks(())
plt.yticks(())
plt.show()

docs.title: What is Data Cleaning
docs.text:
Data cleaning is performed due to the basis that data analysis is only as good as the data used and therefore it is important to consider what is 'garbage' (duplicate, or missing data fields) and processing that 'garbage' into a usable quality dataset to support decision making. The following are problems that can exist in datasets that haven't been cleaned: - Incorrect Data - Corrupted Data - Incorrectly Formatted Data - Duplicate Data - Incomplete data within Dataset itself

Note

There is no absolute way to prescribe the exact steps in the data cleaning process, however establishing a method is good practice.

docs.title: Remove Unwanted/Duplicate Values
docs.text:
• Remove unwanted observations from the dataset including duplicate or irrelevant ones.
  • Duplication observations will happen most often during data collection.
  • May occur when you combine datasets from multiple places, scrape data, or receive data from clients or multiple departments.
  • Irrelevant observations are when you notice observations that do not fit into the specific problem that is attempted to be analysed
  • For example if data regarding millennial customers is wanting to be analysed but the chosen dataset includes different generations then it is important to filter for the irrelevant obervations; data outside of the millennial generation.

docs.title: Fix Structural Errors
docs.text: Structural errors are when measured or transferred data has strange naming conventions, typos, or incorrect capitalisation which can lead to inconsistencies in mislabelled categories or classses. - For example for you may find "N/A" and "Not Applicable" both appear but should be the analysed as the same category despite the difference.

docs.title: Filter Unwanted Outliers
docs.text:
Often there may be one-off anomalies in the data, where at a glance they do not fit the data that is being analysed and in this case where a legitmate reason can be provided then an outlier (improper data entry) can be removed helping to improve the performance of the data that is being worked with.

Sometimes the appearance of an outlier proves that a theory being worked on is valid, just because an outlier exists doesn't mean it is incorrect. Wherre an outlier proves irrelevant for analysis or a mistake then it is reasonable to consider it for removal.

docs.title: Handling Missing Data
docs.text: Missing data cannot be ignored because numerous algorithms do not accept missing values, at a glance there are three options that can be taken to resolve this issue: - First Option) Drop observations that have missing values however, this will result in the loss of information so it is important to be mindful of what information is being removed, why it is being removed, and how that is justified. - Second Option) Input missing values based on other observations, this option also results in the potential to lose data integrity. - Third Option) Might alter the way the data is used to effectively navigate null values.

docs.title: Quality Control
docs.text: For quality control it is important to validate the data to ensure it maintains integrity, consistency, and performance.

docs.title: Validating Data
docs.text:
• Does the data make sense?
  • Does the data follow the appropriate rules for its field?
  • Does it prove or disprove the working theory or bring any new insights?
  • Can trends be found in the data to help form the next working theory from the data?
  • If a next theory cannot be found, is it due to a quality control issue.

docs.title: Components of Quality Data
docs.text: Validity - The degree to which the data conforms to defined business rules or constraints. Accuracy - Ensure the data is close to the true values. Completeness - The degree to which all required data is known. Consistency - Ensure the data is consistent within the same dataset and/or across multiple datasets. Uniformity - The degree to which the data is specified using the same unit of measure.

docs.text: If a data distribution is approximately normal then: - 68% of the data values lie within one standard deviation - 95% are within two standard deviations. - 99.7% lie within three standard deviations.

docs.title: Standard Deviation - Z-Score (Variance)
docs.text:
The Z-Score simply means how many standard deviations a given value is away from the distribution mean.

Z-Score can either be a positive or negative value.

SM = Score Mean.

\[ (SM) \div SD \]

docs.title: Data Normalisation
docs.text:
Normalisation refers to the re-scaling numeric data from its real-value into a 0 to 1 range.

This form of normalisation is used in machine learning and data analytics make model training less sensitive to the scale of features, which allows the model to converge to better weights and overall leads to a more accurate model.

Normalization is useful when different attributes are measured on different scales. Without it, attributes with larger numerical ranges can overwhelm those with smaller ranges, even when both are equally important.

docs.title: Normalisation VS Standardisation
docs.text:
Normalisation is good to use when the distribution of data does not follow a Normal Distribution. This is useful in algorithms which do not assume any distribution of data.

Standardisation, can be helpful in cases where data follows Normal Distribution, unlike normalisation, standardisation does not have a bounding range so even if outliers are present in the data it will not be affected by standardisation.

The choice of using normalisation or standardisation depends on the problem, and the machine learning algorithm being utilised. Therefore, there is no hard-fast rule of when to normalise or standardise data.

One potential method is by fitting the model to raw normalised and standardised data and comparing the performance for the best results.

docs.title: Summarising, Aggregating and Grouping Data
docs.text:
The pandas library makes the calculation of different statistics very simple by including pre-built functions of mean, max, min, and standard deviation (std).

import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 12, 15, 20])
std_value = s.std()
print(std_value)

docs.title: GroupBy
docs.text:
Many cases require query-based summarisation. E.g. What's the total call duration in January for a call centre dataset.

To group these categories together the groupby() pandas function can be utilised. Essentially splitting data into differing groups depending on the variable of choice. E.g. the expression data.groupby('month') will split the current DataFrame by month.

The groupby() function returns a groupBy object but essentially descirbes how the rows of the original dataset has been split.

Note

Functions like max(), min(), mean(), first(), last(), etc can be applied to the GroupBy object to obtain summary statistics for each group.

Groups can also be applied to more than one available to allow for more complex queries.

Aggregating Statistics

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
• Evaluate basic statistics for data analysis
  • Examine descriptive and probability (inferential) statistics

docs.title: Types of Statistics
docs.text:
Descriptive Statistics is a method used to describe and understand the features of a specific dataset by giving short summaries about the sample and measures of the data. Mainly focused on the main characteristics of the data, it provides a summary of the data.

Inferential Statistics make inferences and predictions about a population based on a sample of data taken from the population in question. Generalising a large dataset and applies probability to draw a conclusion. It allows to infer data parameters based on a statistical model using sample data.

docs.title: Descriptive Statistics
docs.text: With descriptive statistics, it simply describes what is or what the data shows and are used to present quantitative descriptions in a manageable form.

docs.title: Inferential Statistics (Probability)
docs.text:
Probability is the measure of how likely an event is to occur. To be more precise probability is the ratio of the desired outcomes to total outcomes: - (desired outcomes) / (total outcomes). - The probabilities of all outcomes always sums up to 1.

Consider the famous rolling dice example: - On a rolling dice there are six possible outcomes. - Each probability only has one outcome so each has a probability of ⅙. - For example, the probability of getting a number '2' on the dice is ⅙.

docs.title: Measures of Centre
docs.text: There are three main measures of centre: Mean - Measure of the average of all values in the sample. Median - Measure of the central value of the sample. Mode - Most reoccurring value in the sample.

docs.title: Measures of Spread
docs.text: Range – How spread apart the values in a data set are (difference between the maximum and minimum values). Quartile – Describes the spread of a data set by dividing it into four equal parts, similar to how the median divides the data in half. Variance – Measures how much values differ from the expected (mean) value by averaging the squared deviations. Standard Deviation – Indicates how dispersed the data values are from the mean, expressed in the same units as the data.

docs.title: Standard Deviation - Z-Score (Variance)
docs.text:
By definition the z-score simply means how many standard deviations a given value is away from the distribution mean. A z-score can be positive or negative.

Calculate the score as (X-Mean) / SD

docs.title: Cumulative Distribution
docs.text: The cumulative distribution function (CDF) provides a visualisation of the probability distribution. As its name suggests it is simply the probability that a variable will take a value less than or equal to a particular value.

docs.title: Uniform Distribution
docs.text:
A uniform distribution is a type of distribution of probabilities where all outcomes are equally likely; each variable has the same probability that it will be the outcome.

  • A deck of cards has a uniform distribution because the probability that a heart, club, diamond or spade is pulled is the same.
  • A coin also has a uniform distribution because the probability of the head or tail in a coin toss is the same.
  • The dice tossing has a uniform distribution too, because each side of a dice has the same probability to be drawn.

docs.title: Binomial Distribution
docs.text:
If the probability for multiple trials is wanted to be known for example: - given 10 flips of a fair coin, what is the probability of getting 6 heads?

The answer to this question is to use Binominal Distribution, which is the probability distribution of a sequence of experiments where: - Each experiment produces a binary outcome - Each of the outcomes is independent of all the others

docs.title: Coin Toss Example
docs.text:
Quote

Experiment: 3 Heads, 2 Heads, 1 head, None • P(Three Heads) = P(HHH) = ⅛ • P(Two Heads) = P(HHT) + P(HTH) + P(THH) = ⅛ + ⅛ + ⅛ = ⅜ • P(One Head) = P(HTT) + P(THT) + P(TTH) = ⅛ + ⅛ + ⅛ = ⅜ • P(Zero Heads) = P(TTT) = ⅛

Distribution: Symmetric or skewed

docs.title: Normal (Gaussian) Distribution
docs.text:
Normal also known as Gaussian Distribution is a continuous probability distribution that is symmetric about mean, showing that data near the mean are more frequent inn occurrence than data far from the mean.

In graph form normal distribution appears as a bell curve.

One of the main reasons for the popularity of the Normal Distribution is that it occurs very commonly in most of the things we see in nature around us. For example: - Finance i.e. the salary distribution in an office. - Healthcare - Height/Weight Distributions - Grading Distributions

docs.title: Reflection on Different Distributions
docs.text:
The common distributions are common because they occur again and again in different and sometimes unexpected domains.

These distributions occur so often in many applications in life. Consider them as 3rd party libarires that have bee verified and tested so they can be directly used in problems.

It is useful to know, the probability density function for a sample of data, in order to know whether a given observation is unlikely an outlier or an anomaly and whether it should be removed.

Get familiar with common probability distributions as it will help to identify a given distribution from a histogram.

docs.title: Hypothesis
docs.text:
A statement or claim!

Examples of hypotheses': - All customers aged over 50 will be accepted for a loan - Loan acceptance requires higher levels of incomes - Previous history - Loan amount

docs.title: Feature Selection
docs.text:
• Data Overload - which columns are likely to contribute to results?
  • Is some data irrelevant? GIGO
  • What is relevant? (This is where feature selection is most beneficial)

How to know what is important? - Domain knowledge, expertise, experience

Examples: Retail data - focus perhaps on features that influence purchases a customer makes. Wine quality - Chemical constituents and how they affect preferences - Changing constituents could affect the levels of other substances.

Large datasets have many features. Data scientists may look to try different combinations to see what provides the best results.

docs.title: In Short...
docs.text:
• Domain knowledge is just as important than data analysis skills
  • Asking the right questions is more important than elaborate algorithms
  • It's about the 'right' data.

#include "CValueAssignment.h"
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

CValueAssignment::CValueAssignment()
{
    cout << "CValueAssignment constructor called" << endl;
    mpData = new int(0);
}
//copy constructor
CValueAssignment::CValueAssignment(const CValueAssignment& theOriginal)
{
    cout << "CValueAssignment copy constructor called" << endl;
    mpData = new int;
    *mpData = *theOriginal.mpData;
}

// Copy Assignment Operator: Handle deep copy and self-assignment
CValueAssignment& CValueAssignment::operator=(const CValueAssignment& other) {
    cout << "CValueAssignment copy assignment operator called" << endl;

    // Check for self-assignment
    if (this != &other) {
        delete mpData;          // Free existing memory     (why do this? - good practice for some data types)
        mpData = new int;       // Allocate new memory      (if size of object changes we need to reallocate e.g. when managing Arrays)
        *mpData = *other.mpData; // Copy the value (can just use this in this case and avoid freeing and allocating memory)
    }

    return *this; // Return reference to the current object
}

void CValueAssignment::Set(int data)
{
    *mpData = data;
}

void CValueAssignment::Display()
{
    cout << *mpData << endl;
}

//destructor
CValueAssignment::~CValueAssignment()
{
    cout << "CValueAssignment destructor called" << endl;
    delete mpData;
}
